SUL-ARCHITECTURE/Ch. 02 — Auth and Vault.md

1\. Purpose

The vault protects user data at rest via XChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD with TPM + DPAPI + password + biometric wrapping; the app-level auth layer gates launch before the WebView exists. Together they are the security baseline for the application. The vault is a storage subsystem that runs as a dedicated thread inside sul.exe; its threat model is about the encrypted file at rest, not about the runtime process.

2\. Architecture

2.1 App-level authentication

The vault has layered auth (\[vault], §2.5). The app does not. The entire app launch requires authentication, reusing the same auth primitives (sul-face-auth, sul-voice-auth, Windows Hello, passcode) that already exist for the vault. AND-logic, not OR. Every enabled factor must pass simultaneously. Disabling any factor is a Tier 1 event.

The auth prompt is a native Win32 modal rendered before the WebView loads — a compromised WebView cannot bypass auth by any XSS→RCE path because the WebView does not exist until auth succeeds. No recovery for the app-level auth layer; the only recovery is the user's credentials. Debug bypass (--dev-auth-bypass) is gated behind \[dev] dev\_auth\_bypass = true and refused in release builds (AST guard). Session token held in secure\_memory (DPAPI-protected, never written to disk), destroyed on app close or reauth expiry.

Config:

toml

\[auth]

enabled = true

require\_password = true

require\_windows\_hello = false

require\_face = false

require\_voice = false

reauth\_interval\_min = 120

reauth\_on\_idle\_min = 15

reauth\_for\_high\_risk = true

reauth\_for\_vault = false

anti\_debug = true

process\_hardening = true

memory\_lock = true

face\_match\_threshold = 0.65

voice\_far\_target = 0.005

voice\_challenge\_phrase = "auto"

Behaviour:

\[auth] enabled = true → launch prompts auth modal.

Fail or timeout (30s) → sul.exe exits without loading UI.

\[auth] enabled = false → Tier 1 event, persistent warning chip in overlay corner.

\[vault] enabled + \[auth] enabled + reauth\_for\_vault = false → app session covers vault unlock.

\[vault] enabled + \[auth] enabled + reauth\_for\_vault = true → separate vault prompt.

\[vault] enabled + \[auth] enabled = false → vault's own auth only, app not gated.

Enrollment: Settings → Security → Authentication. Set passcode (12+ chars, zxcvbn "strong"), optional Windows Hello, optional face (3-shot, ambient-light check), optional voice (3-shot challenge phrase). Confirmation: "If you forget your passcode and lose access to your enrolled biometric factors, you cannot recover SUL. Continue?" — must type I understand.

Auth store at %APPDATA%\\SUL\\auth\\ (Ed25519-signed, DPAPI-wrapped), separate from the vault.

Validator rules (auth-specific; cross-cutting rules in Ch. 1 §4.2):

AUTH-1: \[auth] enabled = true requires at least one auth factor (password, Windows Hello, face, or voice) to be enabled (E\_CFG otherwise — no way to authenticate).

AUTH-2: \[auth] face\_match\_threshold must be ≥ 0.65 (E\_CFG otherwise — too permissive).

AUTH-3: \[auth] voice\_far\_target must be ≤ 0.005 (E\_CFG otherwise — too permissive).

Failure modes: no fallback. Fail-to-unlock → app exits. Anti-debug / process-hardening / memory-lock are enforced at process level (Ch. 14 §14.11's Mode F harness and vtcode-process-hardening). The session token's destruction is verified by a Zeroize + Drop test.

AST guards (Ch. 1 §9 and Ch. 16 §16.15):

sul-auth-app must not expose a bypass path in release builds.

\[auth] enabled = false must be a Tier 1 event.

\[auth] require\_password = false with no other factor enabled must be rejected (E\_CFG).

Tier 1 events (R0, Tier 1-core per Ch. 1 §2.4): auth:disable, auth:disable\_factor, auth:change\_reauth\_for\_vault, auth:disable\_anti\_debug, auth:disable\_process\_hardening, auth:disable\_memory\_lock.

What app auth does not do: it does not encrypt anything. It gates launch. If app auth is bypassed, the vault still needs its own auth (§2.5). If the vault is disabled, app auth is the only gate. Both are needed for the full posture.

Local multi-user profiles (`[auth.profiles]`, R1, gated A.191): for shared machines, optional local profile isolation gives each OS/local profile its own vault key and `game_metadata` (zero cloud sync). WebAuthn/passkey UX patterns (inspired by openGym) map directly to Windows Hello + existing AND-logic biometrics.

Cross-references: vault layered auth (§2.5), startup Step 4.14 (§2.9), threat model (§2.17), AST guards (§2.18), A.114 (Appendix gates).

#### UX reference: Vaultwarden

Vaultwarden (https://github.com/dani-garcia/vaultwarden) is a lightweight Bitwarden-compatible password manager. It provides UX reference for unlock flows, session management, auto-lock behavior, and reauth intervals. SUL does not integrate Vaultwarden; the *patterns* are borrowed.

2.2 Vault overview and config

The vault is a storage subsystem that encrypts user data at rest. It is not an inference subsystem. It runs as a dedicated thread inside sul.exe, not a separate process (Ch. 1 §2.6). Its threat model is about the encrypted file at rest, not about the runtime process.

Purpose: XChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD, 4 KiB-aligned header, chunk-indexed XOR nonces (TLS 1.3 style), header-authenticated AAD, STREAM final-chunk flag, self-describing KDF parameters, fresh 16-byte salt + 12-byte base nonce per file, password zeroization. I/O pipeline over IOCP (triple-buffered) — the ground-up piece vs concryptor's Linux-only io\_uring implementation. Seek-aware reader decrypts only needed chunks. Key hierarchy: master key → HKDF-SHA256(vault\_uuid) → per-vault KEK → AES-256-GCM key-wrap of DEK → per-chunk AEAD keys. Rotating password re-wraps DEK under new KEK — no bulk re-encryption. DPAPI (user-scope) via windows-dpapi wraps KEK; TPM 2.0 sealing via hardwareseal (chosen over locket\_tpm for smaller API surface) wraps KEK.

What this gives you: the vault file is useless on another machine. A stolen laptop's disk image is useless. Two independent hardware roots; both must be defeated.

Config:

toml

\[vault]

enabled = false

path = "%APPDATA%/SUL/vault/"

key\_source = "windows\_hello" | "passphrase"

searchable\_index = false   # no plaintext index by default

strip\_metadata = false     # preserve EXIF/IPTC/XMP verbatim inside vault

extra\_paths = \[]           # extended via OS file picker only, never config edit

Validator rules (vault-specific; cross-cutting rules in Ch. 1 §4.2):

V-1: \[vault] extra\_paths cannot be extended via config edit — only via OS file picker.

V-2: \[vault] key\_source must be "windows\_hello" or "passphrase" (E\_CFG otherwise).

V-3: \[vault] enabled = true requires vault file exists at \[vault] path with valid header signature (else E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED at startup).

Tier 1 events (R0, Tier 1-core per Ch. 1 §2.4): vault:disable\_auth\_factor, vault:disable\_anti\_debug, vault:disable\_decoy, vault:change\_kdf\_profile, vault:change\_aead\_cipher, vault:enable\_searchable\_index, vault:add\_extra\_path\_via\_config.

AST guards (Ch. 16 §16.15):

sul-vault-core must not import HTTP client.

sul-vault-core must not expose the DEK outside the vault thread.

sul-vault-core must not write plaintext to disk at any point (fuzz test at every write boundary).

sul-face-auth and sul-voice-auth must not store plaintext embeddings.

\[vault] extra\_paths must only be extended via OS file picker (AST check against config edit path).

2.3 Vault AEAD construction

Portable construction: XChaCha20-Poly1305, 4 KiB-aligned header, chunk-indexed XOR nonces (TLS 1.3 style), header-authenticated AAD, STREAM final-chunk flag, self-describing KDF parameters, fresh 16-byte salt + 12-byte base nonce per file, password zeroization. The AEAD construction is portable — the reference implementation is concryptor's io\_uring-based Linux-only pipeline. SUL implements the same construction over IOCP.

Chunk layout:

Field	Size	Notes

Header	4 KiB	4 KiB-aligned; contains KDF parameters, cipher ID, wrapped DEK, base nonce, salt. Header-authenticated as AAD.

Chunk N	variable	AES-GCM / XChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypted with chunk-indexed XOR nonce.

STREAM final chunk	varies	Final-chunk flag distinguishes final chunk from non-final; prevents truncation attacks.

Nonce derivation: chunk\_nonce = base\_nonce XOR chunk\_index. Base nonce is per-file (12 bytes); chunk index is 8 bytes, zero-padded to 12. XOR-based nonce derivation ensures unique nonces per chunk without counter tracking (TLS 1.3 style). A fresh 16-byte salt + 12-byte base nonce is generated per file.

KDF parameters: self-describing (stored in the header). Current default is Argon2id with parameters chosen at vault creation. Changing the KDF profile is a Tier 1 event (vault:change\_kdf\_profile); rotating KDF parameters re-wraps the DEK under a new KEK without re-encrypting the vault contents.

Password zeroization: the user's password is held in secrecy/redoubt (encrypted-at-rest-in-memory) and zeroized on drop. The passphrase is never written to disk, never logged, never included in diagnostic bundles.

AEAD adversarial cases (fuzz-tested):

Truncation (final chunk removed → STREAM final-chunk flag catches).

Chunk reorder (chunk N swapped with chunk N+M → chunk-index nonce catches).

Chunk substitution (chunk from another file → header AAD + base-nonce mismatch catches).

Header tamper (KDF params, cipher ID, wrapped DEK, base nonce, salt modified → header AAD catches).

Zero-length file (valid).

Single-chunk file (valid).

Non-final chunk flagged as final (STREAM flag catches).

Final chunk flagged as non-final (STREAM flag catches).

Salt reused across files (only possible by attacker copying header; the wrapped DEK won't unwrap).

Base nonce reused (only possible by attacker copying header; same as above).

Same chunk index in two files (chunk nonces are per-file; no cross-file attack).

Empty plaintext chunk (valid; AAD still authenticates chunk metadata).

Non-contiguous chunk read (seek-aware reader handles).

Partial chunk read (seek-aware reader handles).

Header-only file (no chunks; valid empty vault).

Concurrent write mid-chunk (fuzz at every write boundary — see §2.8).

Concurrent read mid-chunk (fuzz at every read boundary).

Concurrent write + read (IOCP pipeline isolation).

Key rotation mid-write (blocked by vault lock).

Truncated header (rejected by header signature check).

Success criterion: all 20+ cases must be rejected or handled correctly before A.92 passes (§2.12). Any case that decrypts tampered data is a hard fail.

2.4 Vault key hierarchy

text

Master key (KDF-derived from user password + salt)

&#x20;   ↓ HKDF-SHA256(vault\_uuid)

Per-vault KEK

&#x20;   ↓ AES-256-GCM key-wrap (wrapped by DPAPI + TPM)

DEK (Data Encryption Key)

&#x20;   ↓ per-chunk AEAD key derivation

Per-chunk AEAD keys

Key wrapping: the KEK is wrapped by two independent hardware-rooted keys:

DPAPI (user-scope) via windows-dpapi — bound to the Windows user account. A disk image restored to a different user account cannot unwrap.

TPM 2.0 sealing via hardwareseal — bound to the specific machine. A disk image moved to another machine cannot unwrap.

Both must be defeated simultaneously to unlock. If either is unavailable (e.g., TPM cleared, DPAPI profile corrupted), E\_VAULT\_HARDWARE\_ROOT\_UNAVAILABLE fires and the user is offered passphrase-only mode as a Tier 1 event (§2.9).

Password rotation: changing the password re-derives the KEK from the new password + new salt, and re-wraps the DEK under the new KEK. No bulk re-encryption — the vault contents remain encrypted under the same DEK. Password rotation is O(1) in vault size. This is the design property that makes password rotation practical for large vaults.

KDF profile rotation: changing KDF parameters (Argon2id memory/time/parallelism) similarly re-derives the KEK and re-wraps the DEK. Tier 1 event.

DEK never leaves the vault thread. The DEK is held in secrecy/redoubt (encrypted-at-rest-in-memory) inside the vault thread. There is no API to extract the DEK. The AST guard verifies this (§2.18).

Memory protection while unlocked: mlock/VirtualLock on key material (so the OS does not page it to disk). secrecy/redoubt for encrypted-at-rest-in-memory secrets. secmem-alloc for guard pages around the key material. These are the runtime defenses; they are not a substitute for process isolation (there is none — the vault runs in the same process as sul.exe), but they raise the bar for a memory-scraping attacker.

2.5 Vault layered auth

All configured factors must pass (AND-logic, not OR):

Factor	Required?	What it proves	Hardware-rooted

Password	Always	Knowledge of passphrase	No

Windows Hello	Recommended default	Presence at machine	Yes (OS-backed)

Face (RetinaFace/ArcFace)	Optional	Presence of user's face	No

Voice (sherpa-onnx speaker verification)	Optional	Presence of user's voice	No

AND-logic, not OR-logic. Disabling any factor is a Tier 1 event (vault:disable\_auth\_factor). The vault does not unlock unless every enabled factor passes.

Face auth (sul-face-auth, §2.15): RetinaFace detection + ArcFace embedding + cosine matching (threshold ≥0.65) + anti-spoof heuristics. Face embeddings stored in the vault header (encrypted). Enrollment is 3-shot with ambient-light check.

Voice auth (sul-voice-auth, §2.16): Challenge-phrase generation (regenerated every unlock, so replays are useless), sherpa-onnx speaker embedding, cosine matching (≤0.5% FAR target), replay-attack detection (chroma-based liveness). Enrollment is 3-shot.

No password recovery. The only recovery path is the user's credentials. Vault creation flow forces explicit acknowledgment (same as app auth, §2.1).

Reauth: \[auth] reauth\_for\_vault = false means the app session covers vault unlock (default). reauth\_for\_vault = true means a separate vault prompt — the user must re-authenticate to unlock the vault even if the app session is active. Tier 1 event to change.

2.6 Vault file integrity

Ed25519 signatures on every vault artifact:

Header (KDF params, cipher, wrapped DEK) — Ed25519-signed.

Manifest (encrypted index of files inside) — Ed25519-signed.

User-marked files — Ed25519-signed.

SHA-256/BLAKE3 file hashes recorded in the signed manifest.

Tampering behavior:

Tampered file (hash mismatch) → sul-quarantine (copy → verify → record → verify → remove into encrypted quarantine), manifest entry marked integrity\_failed, original not deleted. The user can inspect the quarantined file.

Tampered vault header (signature mismatch) → vault refuses to open entirely; whole vault to quarantine.

Tampered manifest (signature mismatch) → same as header — vault treated as untrusted.

Unknown file (in vault but not in signed manifest) → treated as potentially injected, quarantined, surfaced to user.

Hive-mind signed revocation lists: Hive-mind backend publishes signed manifests and signed revocation lists. Client verifies against maintainer key, applies to local trust store. Backend never sees user files — it publishes policy only. Revoked file → quarantined immediately on next access.

Signing keys: the user's Ed25519 key is stored at %APPDATA%\\SUL\\trust\\ with the same protections as the vault KEK (DPAPI + TPM wrapping). An attacker who steals the key can sign anything, but stealing the key requires defeating the same hardware roots as the vault itself.

2.7 Vault active defense

Decoy vaults: same format, different DEK, plausible-looking fake files. Any access triggers VaultDecoyAccessed telemetry + hive threat log + user notification + optional cooldown on the real vault. The decoy is a tripwire — an attacker who tries the wrong passphrase gets a plausible-looking vault that logs the attempt. Disabling the decoy is Tier 1-core (vault:disable\_decoy).

Rate limiting:

5 failed unlock attempts → 5 min lock.

20 failed attempts → 24 h lock and require TPM PIN to reset.

Rate limiting state is stored in the vault header (signed); tampering with the rate-limit counter invalidates the header signature and triggers VaultTamperDetected.

Anti-debug:

cynapse — in-memory tampering detection.

astraguard — anti-debug + anti-VM primitives.

anti-dbg proc-macro on the vault unlock path.

Detection triggers VaultTamperDetected and immediate lock. Disabling anti-debug is Tier 1-core (vault:disable\_anti\_debug).

Process hardening:

win\_mitigations (CFG, ACG, CIG, blocking child-process creation from vault process).

vtcode-process-hardening pre-main (disables core dumps and debugger attach).

Memory protection while unlocked:

mlock/VirtualLock on key material (so the OS does not page it to disk).

secrecy/redoubt for encrypted-at-rest-in-memory secrets.

secmem-alloc for guard pages.

Anti-tampering layers (decoy vaults + rate limiting + anti-debug + process hardening + memory protection) are the vault's anti-tampering layers. There is no separate §11.22 — the content is here.

2.8 Vault I/O pipeline

IOCP triple-buffered pipeline (via tokio-rs/mio, already a workspace dep) — roughly 3–4 weeks of work. Three buffers: read buffer (filled by IOCP completion), decrypt buffer (holds decrypted chunk), write buffer (holds new plaintext pending re-encryption). This is the ground-up piece vs concryptor's io\_uring-based Linux pipeline.

Seek-aware reader: decrypts only the chunks needed for a seek target plus the containing chunk. A 20 GB file with a 4 KiB chunk size has \~5M chunks; a seek to offset N only decrypts the chunk containing N plus the STREAM metadata. Random-access reads are O(1) in vault size.

Zero plaintext leak on crash mid-write: fuzz at every write boundary (before read completes, after read completes, before decrypt, after decrypt, before encrypt, after encrypt, before write, after write, before fsync, after fsync). If the process crashes at any point, the vault file must be recoverable to a consistent state and no plaintext may be left on disk.

Throughput targets: ≥500 MB/s read, ≥500 MB/s write (median); p99 800 MB/s. 20 GB file streams with peak RSS <100 MB (the vault never holds the whole file in memory — streaming chunk-by-chunk).

Encryption overhead: XChaCha20-Poly1305 is \~1–3 GB/s on AVX2 CPUs; the bottleneck is disk I/O, not AEAD. The IOCP pipeline overlaps encryption with disk I/O, so the throughput is disk-bound.

2.9 Startup: vault check (Step 4.14)

If \[vault] enabled = true, verify:

Vault file exists at \[vault] path.

Header signature valid (E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED if not — whole vault to quarantine).

TPM/DPAPI wrapping available.

Auth factors configured.

Failure modes:

Condition	Error	Behavior

Vault file corrupt	E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED	Whole vault to quarantine; session continues without vault access; user notified; hive threat log.

Auth factors missing	E\_VAULT\_MISCONFIGURED	Vault remains locked.

TPM unavailable, DPAPI available	E\_VAULT\_HARDWARE\_ROOT\_UNAVAILABLE (partial)	Allow user to proceed with DPAPI + passphrase (Tier 1 event) or abort unlock.

TPM and DPAPI unavailable	E\_VAULT\_HARDWARE\_ROOT\_UNAVAILABLE	Allow user to proceed with passphrase-only (Tier 1 event) or abort unlock.

Rate-limited	E\_VAULT\_RATE\_LIMITED	Vault remains locked; 5 min or 24 h lock per §2.7.

Auth factors fail	E\_VAULT\_UNLOCK\_FAILED	Vault remains locked; rate-limit counter increments.

The vault check runs at startup, but the actual unlock is user-initiated (unless \[auth] reauth\_for\_vault = false and \[auth] enabled = true, in which case app auth covers vault unlock — §2.1).

Deferred vault sync (`[vault.sync]`, research-only, D-136): `enabled = false`. Cloud library sync is out of scope; if ever unlocked, it will follow Ente's client-side encryption + presigned S3 ciphertext upload pattern so master keys never leave the device.

VaultStatusIndicator UI: shows vault locked/unlocked state, active auth factors, decoy-vault warning state. Shown only when \[vault] enabled = true. Not opt-in — always visible when vault is active. Subscribes to VaultUnlocked / VaultLocked / VaultDecoyAccessed / VaultTamperDetected.

2.10 Vault anti-tampering layers (during operation)

The vault check at startup (§2.9) is the one-time check. During operation, sul-watchdog verifies:

The vault file's SHA-256 has not changed since last session (a modified vault file is rejected — E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED on next access).

The auth models (RetinaFace/ArcFace/sherpa-onnx) are SHA-256 verified on every session start.

The vault config section is signed as part of config.toml; a tampered config triggers a signature mismatch.

The vault's own Ed25519-signed header and manifest are verified on every open.

The decoy vault's DEK is different from the real vault's DEK (this is a build-time invariant, not a runtime check).

Mode D quarantine lifecycle: E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED / E\_VAULT\_DECOY\_ACCESSED → vault refuses to open; whole vault to quarantine; session continues without vault access; user notified; hive threat log. Mode E (persistent) per Ch. 14 §14.11.

VaultDecoyAccessed / VaultTamperDetected also append to the hive-mind threat log (Ch. 14 §14.13).

Auto-updater does not touch vault files (Ch. 14 §14.5). The vault file format is versioned and the AEAD construction version is immutable — once a file is encrypted with format v1, it stays v1 until the user explicitly runs a re-encryption migration (Tier 1 event, requires A.92 re-review). Updates to the runtime do not change the format; the runtime always supports the current format version plus one previous version for migration.

Auth model updates (RetinaFace/ArcFace/sherpa-onnx) follow the standard model-file signing chain. Changes to KDF parameters trigger a background re-KEK without re-encrypting the whole vault — Tier 1 event.

Baselines (baselines.md vault section; status per Ch. 1 §8):

\[vault] read\_mb\_s = { median = 500, p99 = 800, higher\_is\_better = true, status = target }

\[vault] write\_mb\_s = { median = 500, p99 = 800, higher\_is\_better = true, status = target }

\[vault] unlock\_ms = { median = 1500, p99 = 3000, higher\_is\_better = false, status = target }

Benchmarks (xtask vault-bench):

vault-bench.py::throughput — measures vault read/write throughput. Produces \[vault] read\_mb\_s, write\_mb\_s.

vault-bench.py::unlock — measures vault unlock latency. Produces \[vault] unlock\_ms.

vault-bench.py::rss\_20gb — 20 GB stream peak RSS. Produces \[vault] peak\_rss\_at\_20gb\_mb.

vault-bench.py::adversarial — runs the 20+ AEAD adversarial cases from §2.3. Any case that decrypts tampered data is a hard fail.

vault-bench.py::fuzz\_crash — fuzz at every write boundary; asserts zero plaintext leak.

vault-bench.py::key\_rotation — asserts key rotation works without bulk re-encryption (measured by comparing vault file size before and after — should be identical).

History file (vault\_history.json in the diagnostics bundle, Ch. 1 §3.6): per-session vault state. Records VaultUnlocked, VaultLocked, VaultDecoyAccessed, VaultTamperDetected events. Never contains filenames, file content, key material, or plaintext. Only event type, factor set that succeeded, timing, and reason codes.

bash

vt-2 — tamper detected; asserts whole vault to quarantine.

vt-4 — decoy accessed; asserts telemetry + hive threat log.

2.12 Deferred: A.92 vault encrypted storage

A.92 is the gate for shipping the vault (in SUL-LEDGER/gates.md). Full text:

XChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD + IOCP pipeline + DPAPI + TPM wrapping + Ed25519 signatures + decoy vaults + rate limiting + anti-debug + memory protection. Ships when: (a) zero plaintext leak on crash mid-write (fuzz at every write boundary), (b) AEAD construction resists truncation/chunk-reorder/chunk-substitution/header-tamper (20+ adversarial cases), (c) key rotation works without re-encrypting the whole vault, (d) throughput ≥500 MB/s read and write, (e) 20 GB file streams with peak RSS <100 MB, (f) one external crypto review of the AEAD construction and nonce derivation before release. This is a hard release gate; the vault cannot ship without (a), (b), and (f) at minimum.

2.13 Vault failure codes

Full vault failure taxonomy (VT-1 through VT-5):

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery

VT-1	Vault unlock fail	Auth factors fail or TPM unavailable	Vault remains locked; E\_VAULT\_UNLOCK\_FAILED.

VT-2	Vault tamper detected	Header/manifest signature mismatch	Vault refuses to open entirely; whole vault to quarantine; E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED.

VT-3	Vault hardware root unavailable	TPM + DPAPI both unavailable	Allow passphrase-only mode with Tier 1 confirmation; or refuse; E\_VAULT\_HARDWARE\_ROOT\_UNAVAILABLE.

VT-4	Vault decoy accessed	Decoy vault opened	VaultDecoyAccessed telemetry; hive threat log; user notification; optional cooldown on real vault.

VT-5	Vault rate limited	Too many failed unlock attempts	5 min lock (5 failures); 24 h lock + TPM PIN reset (20 failures).

Mode F classification:

E\_VAULT\_UNLOCK\_FAILED — informational (no mode transition; vault remains locked, session continues without vault access).

E\_VAULT\_RATE\_LIMITED — informational (same).

E\_VAULT\_HARDWARE\_ROOT\_UNAVAILABLE — informational (same; the user's choice to proceed with passphrase-only is Tier 1).

E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED — Mode E (persistent; vault refuses to open; session continues without vault access; user notified; hive threat log).

E\_VAULT\_DECOY\_ACCESSED — Mode E (same).

Error class additions:

rust

// sul-vault-core

E\_VAULT\_UNLOCK\_FAILED, E\_VAULT\_TAMPER\_DETECTED, E\_VAULT\_HARDWARE\_ROOT\_UNAVAILABLE,

E\_VAULT\_DECOY\_ACCESSED, E\_VAULT\_RATE\_LIMITED,

2.14 sul-vault-core crate contract

Purpose: Encrypted vault storage with XChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD over IOCP, DPAPI + TPM wrapping, Ed25519 signatures, decoy vaults, rate limiting, anti-debug, memory protection.

Architecture:

text

crates/sul-vault-core/

├── Cargo.toml

├── src/

│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API

│   ├── aead.rs                         # XChaCha20-Poly1305 construction

│   ├── stream.rs                       # STREAM final-chunk flag

│   ├── nonce.rs                        # chunk-indexed XOR nonces (TLS 1.3 style)

│   ├── header.rs                       # 4 KiB-aligned header + AAD

│   ├── key\_hierarchy.rs                # master key → HKDF → KEK → DEK → per-chunk

│   ├── key\_wrap.rs                     # DPAPI + TPM wrapping

│   ├── iocp\_pipeline.rs                # triple-buffered IOCP reader/writer

│   ├── seek\_reader.rs                  # seek-aware reader (decrypt only needed chunks)

│   ├── manifest.rs                     # Ed25519-signed manifest of files

│   ├── integrity.rs                    # SHA-256/BLAKE3 file hashes + signature verification

│   ├── decoy.rs                        # decoy vault (same format, different DEK)

│   ├── rate\_limit.rs                   # 5-fail/20-fail rate limiting

│   ├── anti\_debug.rs                   # cynapse + astraguard + anti-dbg

│   └── ipc\_bridge.rs                   # VaultUnlocked/VaultLocked/VaultDecoyAccessed/VaultTamperDetected

└── tests/

&#x20;   └── ...

Dependencies: ring (AEAD primitives), chacha20poly1305 (fallback path), blake3 (fast hashing for manifest), windows-dpapi (DPAPI wrapping), hardwareseal (TPM 2.0 sealing), secrecy/redoubt (encrypted-at-rest-in-memory secrets), secmem-alloc (guard pages), mlock/VirtualLock (via windows crate), tokio-rs/mio (already a workspace dep, used for IOCP).

Compatibility: AEAD construction is portable; the reference is concryptor's io\_uring-based pipeline. SUL implements the same construction over IOCP. The vault file format is versioned; runtime supports current format + one previous version for migration.

Failure taxonomy: VT-1 through VT-5 (§2.13).

Fallback chain: TPM + DPAPI + password + (Hello/face/voice) → password + (Hello/face/voice) → password only (Tier 1) → refuse.

Performance contract: ≥500 MB/s read, ≥500 MB/s write (median); p99 800 MB/s. 20 GB file streams with peak RSS <100 MB. Unlock latency median 1500 ms, p99 3000 ms.

Test requirements: Miri clean on AEAD construction and IOCP pipeline. Zero plaintext leak on crash mid-write (fuzz). AEAD construction resists truncation/chunk-reorder/chunk-substitution/header-tamper (20+ adversarial cases). Key rotation works without re-encrypting the whole vault. Throughput ≥500 MB/s read and write. 20 GB file streams with peak RSS <100 MB. Fail-injection: VT-1 through VT-5 each tested. Tampered file quarantined; tampered header/manifest → vault refuses to open. Decoy vault access triggers telemetry without touching real vault. Rate limit: 5 fails → 5 min lock; 20 fails → 24 h lock.

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=vt-1 through vt-5.

Release: shipping (A.92).

2.15 sul-face-auth crate contract

Purpose: Face authentication — RetinaFace detection, ArcFace embedding, cosine matching, anti-spoof heuristics.

Architecture:

text

crates/sul-face-auth/

├── Cargo.toml

├── src/

│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API

│   ├── enroll.rs                       # multi-shot enrollment

│   ├── detect.rs                       # RetinaFace detection

│   ├── embed.rs                        # ArcFace embedding

│   ├── match.rs                        # cosine similarity + threshold

│   └── anti\_spoof.rs                   # anti-spoof heuristics

└── models/

&#x20;   ├── retinaface.onnx                 # detection

Test requirements: enrollment works with ≥3 shots; matching threshold ≥0.65; anti-spoof rejects printed photos on scripted test set; embeddings stored in vault header (encrypted); no plaintext embeddings on disk.

2.17 Vault and auth threat model

The vault protects data at rest via XChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD with TPM + DPAPI + password wrapping. It does not protect against a fully compromised host process that reads the DEK while the vault is unlocked. It does not protect against a malicious OS that fakes TPM sealing (though DPAPI's user-account binding is orthogonal and would still need to be defeated). It does not protect against an attacker who has the user's password, Windows Hello credentials, and physical access to the machine. The threat model is "an attacker with the vault file cannot read it without defeating TPM + DPAPI + password + any configured biometric factors simultaneously." This is a computational infeasibility claim, not a mathematical impossibility claim.

§2.17.1 Vault file theft. Threat: attacker steals the vault file (via a stolen laptop, a disk image, a backup, malware on the machine, etc.). Defense: The vault is XChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypted. The DEK is wrapped by a TPM-sealed key AND a DPAPI-protected key AND the user's password (via HKDF-derived KEK). All three must be defeated simultaneously to unlock. TPM 2.0 sealing ties the vault to the specific machine; a disk image moved to another machine cannot unlock. DPAPI ties the vault to the specific Windows user account; a disk image restored to a different user account cannot unlock. The password is the user's knowledge factor. The layered auth (password + Windows Hello + optional face/voice) is AND-logic — all configured factors must pass. No password recovery exists; the only recovery path is the user's credentials. Decoy vaults provide an early-warning signal if an attacker tries the wrong passphrase. Rate limiting (5 fails → 5 min lock; 20 fails → 24 h lock + TPM PIN reset) makes brute-force attack computationally infeasible. Anti-debug (cynapse + astraguard + anti-dbg) detects in-memory tampering and debugger attach; detection triggers VaultTamperDetected and quarantine.

§2.17.2 Vault file tampering. Threat: attacker modifies the vault file (to inject a malicious file, to modify an existing file, to corrupt the header, to replace the manifest). Defense: Ed25519 signatures on the header (KDF params, cipher, wrapped DEK), the manifest (encrypted index of files), and every user-marked file. SHA-256/BLAKE3 file hashes recorded in the signed manifest. A tampered file (hash mismatch) → quarantine, manifest entry marked integrity\_failed, original not deleted. A tampered header (signature mismatch) → vault refuses to open entirely; whole vault to quarantine. A tampered manifest → same as header — vault treated as untrusted. An unknown file (in vault but not in signed manifest) → treated as potentially injected, quarantined, surfaced to user. Hive-mind signed revocation lists allow the maintainer to revoke a compromised file's signature; the client verifies against the maintainer key and applies to the local trust store.

§2.17.3 Vault runtime compromise (memory). Threat: attacker compromises the running sul.exe process to read the DEK from memory while the vault is unlocked. Defense (layered): memory protection while unlocked — mlock/VirtualLock on key material so the OS does not page it to disk. secrecy/redoubt for encrypted-at-rest-in-memory secrets (zeroization on drop). secmem-alloc for guard pages around the key material. Anti-debug — cynapse (in-memory tampering detection), astraguard (anti-debug + anti-VM primitives), anti-dbg proc-macro on the vault unlock path. Detection triggers immediate lock + VaultTamperDetected. Process hardening — win\_mitigations (CFG, ACG, CIG, blocking child-process creation from the vault process). De-elevated sul.exe — the WebView host is not the vault host; a WebView compromise cannot read vault memory (the vault runs in a separate thread in the same process, but the WebView2 renderer process is a child process with its own memory space; the vault thread is in the main process). Honest claim: "A compromised SUL process can read the DEK while the vault is unlocked. The defenses make this compromise harder (anti-debug, process hardening, de-elevation) but do not eliminate it. The vault is designed to protect the vault file at rest, not to protect the DEK against a fully compromised host process. This is a fundamental limitation of user-space encryption."

§2.17.4 App-level auth bypass. Threat: attacker attempts to bypass the app-level auth modal (e.g., via XSS→RCE against the WebView, via a debug bypass, via a config edit disabling auth). Defense: The auth modal is a native Win32 window rendered before the WebView loads — a compromised WebView cannot bypass auth by any XSS→RCE path because the WebView does not exist until auth succeeds. The --dev-auth-bypass flag is gated behind \[dev] dev\_auth\_bypass = true and refused in release builds (AST guard). \[auth] enabled = false is a Tier 1 event with a persistent warning chip. No recovery path exists; an admin reset would open a bypass vector and is not implemented. The session token is held in secure\_memory (DPAPI-protected, never written to disk) and destroyed on app close or reauth expiry. reauth\_interval\_min and reauth\_on\_idle\_min force re-authentication after active use or idle time. reauth\_for\_high\_risk forces re-auth before Tier 1 config changes, vault unlock (if \[vault] unified = false), disabling safety invariant, and \[auth] changes. AND-logic across all configured factors means an attacker must defeat every factor simultaneously.

2.18 Vault and auth AST guards

Enforced by cargo xtask ac-regression on every PR:

sul-vault-core must not import HTTP client.

sul-vault-core must not expose the DEK outside the vault thread.

sul-vault-core must not write plaintext to disk at any point (fuzz test at every write boundary).

sul-face-auth and sul-voice-auth must not store plaintext embeddings.

\[vault] extra\_paths must only be extended via OS file picker (AST check against config edit path).

sul-auth-app must not expose a bypass path in release builds.

\[auth] enabled = false must be a Tier 1 event.

\[auth] require\_password = false with no other factor enabled must be rejected (E\_CFG).

SUL-ARCHITECTURE/Ch. 03 — Game Library, Virtualization Core, and Mod Toolchain.md
1. Purpose
The game library, emulation surface, mod toolchain, VFS, and Steam integration. Wraps external emulators, ships one from-scratch core (sul-gb), ships one from-scratch savestate ring (sul-savestate), ships the libretro frontend (sul-emu-libretro), integrates the frame-generation layer, and provides the mod manager + virtual filesystem + sandbox. Every subsystem here interacts with the anti-cheat posture defined in Ch. 16.

2. Architecture
2.1 Game library
Centralized hub for local game libraries (Steam titles: Elite Dangerous, Helldivers 2). Steam library parsing via WilliamVenner/steamlocate (libraryfolders.vdf), ShadowDara/vdfparser, CosmicHorrorDev/vdf-rs, Tormak9970/Steam-Art-Manager. Manifest codes via SteamDB. Unified launcher references: JosefNemec/Playnite, Heroic-Games-Launcher/HeroicGamesLauncher, hydralauncher/hydra.

Tauri bridge and Steam IPC: see §3.14.

Per-game registry: game_registry.json (§3.24) carries launch profiles for both titles plus any user-added game. It declares per-game: executable name, storage root, log filename pattern, telemetry parsing mode, save version, overlay monitor, VFS enable, optimizer enable, flip-model override, run_ahead_frames, combat block, vision block, frame_gen block, audio block, and anti_cheat block. The anti-cheat block is hash-verified against an Ed25519-signed baseline in sul-trust at every launch (§3.14.3 / §3.24); a mismatch triggers a hardcoded safe-default.

2.2 Emulation settings
Per-title executable paths, parameters, optimization flags. run_ahead_frames (0 = off, 1–2 = 1–2 frames). Run-Ahead is a per-game toggle; see §3.5.2 (sul-emu run-ahead module) and gate A.44.

2.3 Emulation integration core (crates/sul-emu)
Wraps external emulator executables with per-title launch profiles, host-side Vulkan/DX12 config, CPU-affinity pinning per hardware profile (cores 4–5). Three phases:

Phase 1 — libretro. One integration covers NES, SNES, Genesis, GB/GBC/GBA, N64, PSX, Saturn, Dreamcast, MAME, FBNeo, Atari 2600/5200/7800/8-bit. Primary ref: lifning/ferretro. Preferred: purpose-built sul-emu-libretro (§3.7) — direct symbol resolution via libloading, fixed-size env vtable dispatch, persistent-mapped texture upload via glMapBufferRange, fence-based frame sync via glFenceSync. Saves 1–2 frames input latency and 15–25% CPU vs generic frontends. ferretro is fallback. Libretro API documentation in R.6.

The performance wins in sul-emu-libretro are structural, and each is worth specifying because they are the reason the frontend exists rather than just using RetroArch:

Direct symbol resolution via libloading instead of dlopen+dlsym per call. Cached once per core load; the dispatch cost of a core function call drops from ~30 ns (dlsym lookup) to ~3 ns (cached function pointer).

Fixed-size vtable env dispatch ([Option<unsafe extern "C" fn(...)>; 64]) instead of a match on env command. Each env query drops from ~30 ns (branchy match) to ~3 ns (array index).

Cache env queries across frames: the frontend caches RETRO_ENVIRONMENT_GET_CAN_DUPE, RETRO_ENVIRONMENT_GET_SYSTEM_DIRECTORY, RETRO_ENVIRONMENT_GET_SAVE_DIRECTORY, and pixel-format queries on first call, so per-frame env traffic drops to nearly zero.

Persistent-mapped texture upload via glMapBufferRange with GL_MAP_PERSISTENT_BIT | GL_MAP_COHERENT_BIT. Zero-copy — the core writes directly into GPU-mapped memory, no CPU→GPU round trip per frame.

Fence-based frame-ready detection via glFenceSync + glClientWaitSync: the frontend renders the next core frame while the current one is still in flight on the GPU. ~2 ms/frame saved vs blocking on glFinish.

Frame-skip in the frontend, not the core: the frontend drops frames on the presentation path instead of asking the core to skip, which preserves audio-timing and input-lag integrity. ~3–5% CPU saved.

Frame pool allocator: zero heap allocation per frame in the hot loop. Pre-allocated texture slots, audio buffers, and video frame descriptors.

The measured aggregate is 1–2 frames of input latency reduction and 15–25% CPU savings vs. a generic frontend on the same core. Both numbers are reproduced on the reference rig in §3.16's emu_bench.py::libretro_boundary.

Phase 2 — Native (priority order fixed):

PCSX2 (PS2)

Dolphin (GC/Wii)

Ryujinx forks (Switch)

DuckStation (PSX)

melonDS (DS)

RPCS3 (PS3)

Cemu (Wii U)

Per-emulator adapter: config-file reader, CLI-flag launcher, save-directory detection, shader-cache layout. 20–40 h each; full set 3–6 months.

Phase 3 — CLI fallback: generic wrapper for any emulator executable with CLI flags.

Core discovery: scan %APPDATA%\\SUL\cores\*.dll at launch, call retro_get_system_info on each, cache (path, name, extensions), present discovered list.

2.4 Full emulator reference list
Preserved from R.6: libretro/RetroArch, lifning/ferretro, RetroPie/EmulationStation, es-de/emulationstation-de, JoeOsborn/retro-rs, danielwolbach/rust-libretro-frontend, mprobinson/rust-libretro, Tinic/libretro-runtime, koute/pinky, stenzek/duckstation, grumpycoders/pcsx-redux, PCSX2/pcsx2, RPCS3/rpcs3, Inori/GPCS4, AlexAltea/orbital, hrydgard/ppsspp, Vita3K/Vita3K, SourMesen/Mesen2, snes9xgit/snes9x, project64/project64, mupen64plus/mupen64plus-core, dolphin-emu/dolphin, melonDS-emu/melonDS, PSI-Rockin/Corgi3DS, Ryujinx forks, ekeeke/Genesis-Plus-GX, FCare/Kronos, flyinghead/flycast, xenia-project/xenia, Cxbx-Reloaded/Cxbx-Reloaded, xqemu/xqemu, mamedev/mame, finalburnneo/FBNeo, stella-emu/stella, atari800/atari800.

2.5 Why integrate rather than rebuild
The performance wins in the emulator layer are in the boundary, not the cores. sul-emu-libretro's direct-symbol resolution, fixed-size vtable dispatch, persistent-mapped texture upload, and fence-based sync deliver 1–2 frames input-latency and 15–25% CPU savings regardless of which core is loaded. sul-fg's Vulkan implicit layer delivers frame generation without touching the core. sul-savestate delivers run-ahead at ~137 µs of snapshot/restore per frame, without the libretro C-ABI UB risks. Rebuilding PCSX2, DuckStation, Dolphin, or RPCS3 from scratch would trade a decade of accuracy work and a moving upstream for a slightly cleaner call boundary — and the resulting core would be worse than the one upstream ships. All mature cores integrate; none are rebuilt.

Four from-scratch builds. Every other emulator system integrates, but four subsystems are built from scratch because the performance win is structural, not incidental:

sul-gb — Game Boy / Game Boy Color core (new). The strongest from-scratch case in the entire emulator surface. Mizu, boytacean, and gb-emulator demonstrate that the hardware is simple enough for a mature Rust implementation, the accuracy is testable against Blargg cpu_instrs (11/11) and dmg-acid2/cgb-acid2, and the save-state ring can be built in pure Rust without the libretro C-ABI boundary. sul-gb ships as an alternative to the libretro Gambatte core, not a replacement — the user picks per-game, with Gambatte as the fallback for any title where sul-gb fails the accuracy gate. The Game Boy core is the only emulator in SUL built from scratch. Everything else is integration. Contract in §3.5.1; gate A.90.

sul-emu-libretro — libretro frontend. Not "an emulator" — the boundary that loads emulators. Direct symbol resolution via libloading, fixed-size vtable dispatch, persistent-mapped texture upload, fence-based sync. The 1–2 frame input-latency and 15–25% CPU wins come from this crate, not from any core. Contract in §3.7.

sul-savestate — Rust-native save-state ring and run-ahead subsystem (new). The libretro C-ABI boundary has documented UB risks — repeated retro_init() panics, data races from unsynchronized worker-thread queries, aliasing-invariant violations in retro_unserialize, NUL-termination hazards in disk-control callbacks (the audit is referenced in R.6). A Rust-native ring that owns its own buffers avoids all of them. It provides the ring, the compression, and the async savestate worker; sul-gb implements the SavestateSource trait natively (~32 KB state), and sul-emu-libretro implements the same trait by wrapping retro_serialize/retro_unserialize in a Box<[u8]> that the ring owns. One ring, one save/restore API, one run-ahead subsystem for both native and libretro cores. Contract in §3.6; gate A.91.

sul-fg — Vulkan implicit layer for frame generation. Same logic — the performance win is in the layer, not the core. Contract in Ch. 9 §9.1.

The four crates are the entire performance-critical emulator stack. Everything else is integration via the frontend adapters (PCSX2, Dolphin, RPCS3, DuckStation, melonDS, Cemu, Ryujinx forks, RetroArch, and the libretro cores). The Rust-native experimental cores — Trapezoid (PSX), RustyNES (NES), AccuNES (NES), x-nes (NES) — are reference implementations for specific subsystems, not shipping dependencies.

2.5.1 sul-gb — Game Boy / GBC core
Purpose: Cycle-accurate GB / GBC emulator in Rust, purpose-built as the from-scratch alternative to the libretro Gambatte core. Ships when the accuracy gate (A.90) passes; Gambatte remains the fallback for any title where sul-gb fails.

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-gb/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API + SavestateSource impl
│   ├── cpu.rs                          # LR35902 (GB CPU) — cycle-accurate
│   ├── ppu.rs                          # scanline-accurate PPU with mode timing
│   ├── apu.rs                          # 4-channel APU at 48 kHz, sample-accurate mixing
│   ├── mmu.rs                          # memory bus, MBC1/2/3/5
│   ├── rtc.rs                          # MBC3 real-time clock
│   ├── cart.rs                         # cartridge header parsing, ROM loading
│   ├── timer.rs                        # DIV/TIMA/TMA/TAC
│   ├── interrupt.rs                    # IE/IF/IME
│   ├── link.rs                         # serial port (stub for single-player)
│   ├── savestate.rs                    # SavestateSource impl
│   └── frame_pool.rs                   # pre-allocated framebuffer ring
└── tests/
    ├── blargg.rs                       # cpu_instrs (11/11), instr_timing, mem_timing
    ├── acid2.rs                        # dmg-acid2, cgb-acid2
    ├── mbc.rs                          # MBC1/2/3/5
    └── perf.rs                         # per-frame time budget
Performance contract:

Metric	Target	Test
CPU step	cycle-accurate	Blargg instr_timing (all tests)
PPU mode timing	scanline-accurate	dmg-acid2, cgb-acid2
APU mixing	sample-accurate at 48 kHz	spectrum match vs gambatte reference ±1 dB, 20 Hz – 20 kHz
Frame time (median)	< 2 ms on reference rig at 60 fps	perf test, 60 s median
Frame time (p99)	< 2.5 ms	perf test, 60 s p99
Allocations per frame	0 (hot loop)	custom global allocator panic test
Savestate size	~32 KB	info output
Savestate snapshot cost	< 20 µs	SavestateSource test
Savestate restore cost	< 20 µs	SavestateSource test
Memory footprint at load	< 5 MB (with 8 MB max ROM)	measured
Accuracy gate (A.90): Blargg cpu_instrs: 11/11 pass. Blargg instr_timing: all pass. Blargg mem_timing: all pass. dmg-acid2: pixel-exact match. cgb-acid2: pixel-exact match. MBC1/2/3/5: all supported; MBC3 RTC accuracy within 1 s over 24 h. APU: spectrum within ±1 dB of gambatte reference on a scripted ROM set across 20 Hz – 20 kHz. Top 50 GB/GBC title compatibility list: all run without graphical or audio glitches on a curated list (per-system).

Integration: SavestateSource impl: snapshot(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> Result&lt;usize&gt; writes the full state to buf; restore(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> Result<()> restores. The buffer is owned by sul-savestate and preallocated. Zero allocation in the hot path. The frame pool is a pre-allocated [u32; 160*144] ring of 3 framebuffers; the frontend reads from one while the core writes the next.

Out of scope: MBC5 rumble, HuC1, and MBC6 are out of scope for the shipping release — they are rare and add cartridge-specific complexity. The core reports E_GB_MAPPER_UNSUPPORTED if it encounters one and refuses to load; Gambatte is the fallback for those titles. Link cable is a stub for single-player; two-instance link is out of scope for A.90.

Dependencies: #[deny(unsafe_code)] except for the AVX2 audio mixing path. No external deps beyond the workspace.

Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_GB_MAPPER_UNSUPPORTED	GB mapper unsupported	MBC5 rumble / HuC1 / MBC6 cartridge	Refuse to load; Gambatte fallback offered (Mode B)
E_GB_ACCURACY_GATE_FAILED	Accuracy gate fail	A.90 gate fails on current hardware	Forced to libretro_gambatte for the session (Mode B)
E_GB_ROM_CORRUPT	ROM corrupt	Cartridge header parse or ROM-size consistency mismatch	Quarantine lifecycle (Mode D)
Test requirements: Miri clean on all unsafe blocks (there are very few — the core is #[deny(unsafe_code)] except for the AVX2 audio mixing path). All Blargg and ACID2 tests pass in CI. Per-frame allocation count = 0. Frame time median < 2 ms, p99 < 2.5 ms on reference rig. Savestate round-trip is byte-identical after 100 iterations on each test ROM. Deterministic: same inputs produce identical framebuffer output across runs.

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=gb-1 (mapper unsupported).

Release: gated shipping component (A.90). R1 per releases.md.

2.5.2 Run-ahead
Frontend exposes run_ahead_frames and the save-state ring; implementation is in the emulator core (ares, RetroArch, GroovyMAME, Azahar 2127.0). The frontend does not reimplement Run-Ahead — it configures the core. Gate in A.44.

The libretro run-ahead API is documented in R.6: "Run-ahead relies on save states; higher frame counts demand more CPU. Single-instance mode disables audio and video, saves state, runs extra frames, re-enables, loads state. Two-instance mode uses a primary core for audio only and a secondary core for video." SUL implements single-instance run-ahead (retro_run N+1 times per displayed frame, snapshot once, restore once). Two-instance run-ahead (secondary core for audio only) is A.92 research — the added complexity is not justified for the shipping release.

Cost budget: Run-ahead at run_ahead = 2 costs ~6.2 ms per displayed frame, of which snapshot + restore is ~137 µs — 2.2% of the cost. The rest is the actual emulation of the extra frames. Run-ahead at run_ahead = 1 is comfortably within budget on the reference rig; run_ahead = 2 is marginal and should be measured per-emulator before defaulting.

Mutual exclusion with Frame Generation (A.44 / A.74): Run-Ahead and Frame Generation are mutually exclusive per emulator instance by default. Enabling FG on an instance with Run-Ahead active: the governor surfaces a two-line confirmation, then disables Run-Ahead and enables FG. Enabling Run-Ahead on an instance with FG active: same confirmation, inverse outcome. Override flag: [frame_gen] allow_with_run_ahead = false (default). If true, both are enabled, and the governor logs a FrameGenRunAheadConflict warning; this is a Tier 1 event. The FG side of this exclusion is in Ch. 9 §9.8.

Why the save-state ring is Rust-native, not libretro-bound: The libretro C-ABI boundary has documented UB risks (aliasing violations in retro_unserialize, data races from unsynchronized worker-thread queries, NUL-termination hazards in disk-control callbacks, repeated-retro_init() panics). The Rust-native ring avoids all of them. The ring owns its own buffers, compresses with zstd, and uses a single savestate worker thread with a FIFO job queue — the emu thread keeps only the snapshot and the apply; compression and file I/O are on the worker. This is the PPSSPP async-savestate pattern applied to the emulator-agnostic ring (R.6). Measured: a full PSP save state is ~35–70 MB uncompressed; zstd at default level compresses the changed blocks ~3×, so the ring takes about a third of the memory. SUL's ring targets the same shape: the ring is sized to the emulator's snapshot size, not to a fixed slot count.

2.6 sul-savestate — Rust-native save-state ring and run-ahead subsystem
Purpose: A save-state ring that owns its own buffers, avoids the libretro C-ABI UB risks, and drives run-ahead for both native cores (sul-gb) and libretro cores (sul-emu-libretro). Single worker thread, zstd-compressed changed blocks, pre-allocated slots.

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-savestate/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API + SavestateSource trait
│   ├── ring.rs                         # pre-allocated ring of slots
│   ├── worker.rs                       # single savestate worker thread
│   ├── compress.rs                     # zstd-compressed changed blocks
│   ├── run_ahead.rs                    # run-ahead orchestration
│   └── shim_libretro.rs                # SavestateSource impl for libretro cores
└── tests/
    ├── round_trip.rs                   # byte-identical serialize/deserialize
    ├── perf.rs                         # snapshot/restore cost budgets
    └── async.rs                        # worker + emu thread interaction
Public API:

rust
pub trait SavestateSource {
    fn snapshot(&mut self, buf: &mut [u8]) -> Result<usize, SavestateError>;
    fn restore(&mut self, buf: &[u8]) -> Result<(), SavestateError>;
    fn state_size(&self) -> usize;
}

pub struct SavestateRing {
    slots: Box<[Slot]>,
    worker: SavestateWorker,
    // ...
}

impl SavestateRing {
    pub fn new(source: Box&lt;dyn SavestateSource&gt;, capacity: usize) -> Result<Self, SavestateError>;
    pub fn snapshot(&mut self) -> Result<SlotHandle, SavestateError>;
    pub fn restore(&mut self, handle: SlotHandle) -> Result<(), SavestateError>;
    pub fn set_run_ahead(&mut self, frames: u8);
    pub fn stats(&self) -> RingStats;
}
Performance contract:

Metric	Target	Test
Snapshot (GB, ~32 KB)	< 20 µs	round_trip test
Restore (GB, ~32 KB)	< 20 µs	round_trip test
Snapshot (PS2, ~35 MB)	< 500 µs	round_trip test
Restore (PS2, ~35 MB)	< 500 µs	round_trip test
Run-ahead snapshot+restore at run_ahead = 2	< 200 µs p99	run-ahead budget test
Allocations in hot path	0	custom global allocator panic test
Ring capacity	≥ 3 slots for run_ahead = 2	default
Worker thread	1 (single savestate worker)	info output
Compression	zstd level 1 on changed blocks only	measured
Design rationale: The ring owns the buffers, not the emulator. The libretro C-ABI documents UB risks in retro_unserialize (aliasing), unsynchronized worker-thread queries (data races), NUL-termination in disk-control callbacks, and repeated-retro_init() panics. A ring that owns its own Box<[u8]> buffers and calls retro_serialize/retro_unserialize with those buffers avoids the aliasing and NUL-termination risks entirely. The C-ABI itself is still called — it has to be — but the buffer it operates on is Rust-owned.

The worker pattern matches PPSSPP's async savestates (R.6): the emu thread does the snapshot and the apply, the worker does the compression and the file I/O. Measured on PPSSPP: snapshot 2–5 ms, compress+write 47–70 ms, apply 6–10 ms. For SUL's ring, compression and file I/O are off the hot path; only snapshot + apply are on it, and both are budgeted at < 200 µs p99.

Changed-blocks-only compression: the ring stores one full compressed slot plus a chain of deltas from the last restore point. The first snapshot is a full serialize + compress; subsequent snapshots are diffs against the previous, which compress 3× better (per the PPSSPP data: a full PSP save state is ~35–70 MB uncompressed, zstd compresses the changed blocks ~3×). This is the memory-amortization win for run_ahead = 2 where two snapshots are live.

Ring capacity ≥ 3 slots: run_ahead = 2 needs the current frame plus two historical frames, plus one slot for the run-ahead worker to write while the emu thread reads. Three is the minimum; four is the default.

Run-ahead orchestration: single-instance run-ahead (retro_run N+1 times per displayed frame, snapshot once, restore once) is what SUL implements. Two-instance run-ahead (secondary core for audio only) is A.92 research — the added complexity is not justified for the shipping release.

Integration: sul-gb implements SavestateSource natively. Its snapshot writes ~32 KB; its restore reads ~32 KB. Both complete in < 20 µs. sul-emu-libretro implements SavestateSource by calling retro_serialize into a Rust-owned buffer and retro_unserialize from the same buffer. The buffer is allocated once per core at retro_serialize_size(); it never resizes mid-session. The run-ahead subsystem (run_ahead.rs) is shared: for any SavestateSource, run-ahead snapshots once per displayed frame, runs the emulator N extra times, restores once, and returns the final frame. The cost is (N+1) × emu_frame_cost + 2 × snapshot_cost + 2 × restore_cost. A per-game run_ahead_frames config drives the run-ahead count; 0 disables it, 1 is the safe default, 2 is the aggressive setting that requires measurement per-emulator (RPCS3's baseline is already at ~25 ms input lag, so run-ahead 2 may not fit the budget).

Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_SAVESTATE_SIZE_MISMATCH	Size mismatch	Snapshot size differs from state_size()	Run-ahead disabled for the affected core (Mode C)
E_SAVESTATE_WORKER_STALLED	Worker stalled	Worker thread doesn't return within budget	Run-ahead disabled for the session (Mode C); persistent → Mode F
E_SAVESTATE_ROUND_TRIP_MISMATCH	Round-trip mismatch	Restore produces different state	Slot dropped without affecting emulator (Mode C)
Config:

toml
[emu.savestate]
ring_capacity = 4                          # slots; minimum 3 for run_ahead = 2, default 4
compression = "zstd"
compression_level = 1                      # 1 = fast, 3 = balanced, 6 = slow (not recommended for hot path)
worker_threads = 1
Validator rules:

ES-1: [emu.savestate] ring_capacity must be ≥ 3 when run_ahead_frames = 2 (E_CFG at load); the ring needs current + two historical frames + one write slot.

ES-2: [emu.savestate] compression_level must be 1 or 3 for the hot path; level 6+ is E_CFG (too slow for the < 200 µs p99 snapshot+restore gate).

ES-3: [emu.savestate] worker_threads must equal 1; any other value is E_CFG.

Dependencies: reuses zstd (already a workspace dependency). Owns its own buffers; wraps retro_serialize/retro_unserialize for libretro cores and calls SavestateSource::snapshot/restore for sul-gb. Single worker thread, pre-allocated ring slots. No new top-level deps.

Test requirements: Miri clean on all unsafe blocks (there are very few — the ring is safe Rust; only the libretro shim touches unsafe). Round-trip byte-identical after 100 iterations on every supported core. Snapshot / restore cost within budget for GB (~32 KB) and PS2 (~35 MB). Run-ahead at run_ahead = 2 snapshot+restore p99 < 200 µs. Zero allocations in the hot path (snapshot / restore / run-ahead orchestration). Worker thread does not block the emu thread on snapshot or restore — the only cross-thread call is worker.schedule(slot) which enqueues without blocking. Changed-blocks-only compression produces ≥ 3× compression on repeated snapshots (matches PPSSPP reference).

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=ss-1 (size mismatch).

Release: gated shipping component (A.91). R1 per releases.md.

2.7 sul-emu-libretro — libretro frontend
Purpose: Purpose-built libretro frontend. Direct symbol resolution, fixed-size vtable dispatch, persistent-mapped texture upload, fence-based sync. 1–2 frames of input-latency reduction and 15–25% CPU savings vs a generic frontend.

Performance contract:

Fixed-size vtable env dispatch ([Option<unsafe extern "C" fn(...)>; 64]), not match. ~30 ns → ~3 ns per call.

Persistent-mapped texture upload via glMapBufferRange with GL_MAP_PERSISTENT_BIT | GL_MAP_COHERENT_BIT. Zero-copy.

Fence-based frame-ready detection via glFenceSync + glClientWaitSync. ~2 ms/frame saved.

Cache env queries across frames. ~50 µs/frame saved.

Frame-skip in frontend, not core. ~3–5% CPU saved.

Frame pool allocator. Zero alloc per frame.

#![no_std] + alloc core, libloading for symbols.

run_ahead module exposes per-game run_ahead_frames config and save-state ring (§3.5.2).

Test requirements: Miri clean single/multi-thread; per-core env vtable coverage snapshot; fence-sync timeout recovery; frame pool correctness under resolution change; libretro_env_dispatch_ns < 10 (p99).

Explicit performance targets (measured on reference rig; each reproduces against a generic frontend on the same core):

Metric	Target	Test
Core function dispatch (cached)	~3 ns	libretro_env_dispatch_ns p99 < 10
Core function dispatch (first call)	~30 ns (dlsym miss, cached after)	measured
Frame-ready detection	~2 ms/frame saved vs glFinish	measured on RetroArch Gambatte
Texture upload	zero-copy via persistent-mapped buffer	measured — no CPU→GPU round trip per frame
Frame-skip cost	~3–5% CPU saved	measured on same core, frame-skip on vs off
Per-frame allocations	0	frame pool allocator + global allocator panic test
Input latency reduction vs generic frontend	1–2 frames	measured on same core
Total CPU reduction vs generic frontend	15–25%	measured on same core
SavestateSource integration: sul-emu-libretro implements the savestate::SavestateSource trait (§3.6) by wrapping retro_serialize/retro_unserialize in a Rust-owned Box<[u8]> sized at retro_serialize_size(). The buffer is allocated once per core load; it is never resized mid-session. Run-ahead (A.44) drives snapshots and restores through sul-savestate, so libretro cores and sul-gb share the same run-ahead subsystem with the same cost budget (snapshot+restore < 200 µs p99). This is the C-ABI-safe path: the libretro C-ABI still gets called, but the buffer it writes into is Rust-owned and does not alias any libretro-internal state.

Release: gated shipping component (A.2 category — no specific gate listed in the original spec; ships as part of the R1 emulation surface).

2.8 Game asset optimization (sul-optimize)
Purpose: Engine-aware archive repacking, BC7 texture encoding, KTX2 + Zstd container, streaming configurator. Elite Dangerous only. Disabled entirely when anti_cheat.kernel_level: true (structural).

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-optimize/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API
│   ├── archive_repacker.rs             # engine-aware archive detection + repacking
│   ├── bc7_encoder.rs                  # Tavrin/texture-compressor + hasenbanck/block_compression
│   ├── ktx2_container.rs               # Khronos KTX2 + Zstd container
│   ├── mip_chain.rs                    # mipmap_generator integration
│   ├── streaming_configurator.rs       # DirectStorage-adjacent streaming config
│   ├── emulation_downscale.rs          # P960/P1920 for emulators
│   ├── zstd_gpu/                       # DirectStorage 1.4 Zstd GPU decompression wrapper
│   │   └── direct_storage_shader.rs
│   └── anti_cheat_gate.rs              # structural refusal for kernel_AC titles
└── models/
    └── directstorage_zstd_1_4.spv      # Microsoft's open-source shader (vendored)
VRAM reduction attributed to downscale + mip optimization; BC7 contributes quality-per-byte and streaming-stutter reduction. mipmap_generator for mip chains. Disabled entirely when anti_cheat.kernel_level: true — structural, enforced by pack-type flag, not policy. zstd_gpu module wraps Microsoft's open-sourced DirectStorage 1.4 Zstd GPU decompression shader for 256 KB chunks. Archive container becomes DirectStorage-compatible Zstd, decompressed on GPU during streaming, not CPU. Gate A.43. Co-scheduling with frame generation is specified in §3.8.1 (optimize_only / fg_only / optimize + fg) and gated by A.76.

Config:

toml
[optimize]
enabled = false                            # gated shipping component
zstd_gpu = false                           # gated shipping component, A.43
Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_OPTIMIZE_AC_BLOCKED	Anti-cheat blocked	anti_cheat.kernel_level = true on target game	Pack type refused; sul-optimize not run for this title (Mode B)
Test requirements: BC7 encoding round-trip preserves PSNR > 40 dB on Elite Dangerous texture set. KTX2 + Zstd container validates against Khronos KTX validation tool. Streaming configurator produces DirectStorage-compatible archive container. Emulation downscale: P960 and P1920 profiles produce expected VRAM reduction. Anti-cheat gate: E_OPTIMIZE_AC_BLOCKED fires on kernel_level: true titles; the pack type is refused. zstd_gpu shader produces bit-identical decompression vs CPU Zstd on 10 GB test corpus. Gate A.43: GPU decompression reduces CPU overhead by ≥30% with no VRAM regression.

Release: gated shipping component (A.43). R2 per releases.md.

2.8.1 Optimize + FG co-scheduling (A.76)
The combined state where texture downscale and frame generation are simultaneously active, with the governor managing VRAM. Three modes:

optimize_only — texture downscale active, FG off.

fg_only — FG active, no downscale.

optimize + fg — both active, governor manages VRAM.

Ship if optimize + fg produces ≥1.2× effective framerate at ≤ same VRAM as native textures with FG off, with no frame corruption, on a 10-game test set (ED, 3 emulators, 6 native single-player titles). Gate A.76. Tier 1 event to enable (optimize:change_co_schedule).

2.9 Game build isolation (sul-sandbox)
Purpose: Windows Sandbox integration via launch_in_sandbox(path) — generates a .wsb config and launches WindowsSandbox.exe /file &lt;path&gt;. References: TarunKurella/sandboxrs-windows (AppContainer + Job Objects), Erio-Harrison/nanosandbox (Job Objects + Restricted Tokens), cpjet64/rappct (AppContainer toolkit), octocorvus/run_app_container, microsoft/mxc (sandboxed code execution), containers/libkrun (KVM/HVF/WHP). 4–8 h integration work.

Hardware passthrough and anti-cheat boundary: kernel-level anti-cheat multiplayer titles remain restricted to bare-metal host execution due to hypervisor detection barriers. This is not a policy choice — it is a technical constraint. nProtect GameGuard, Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, and Vanguard all detect hypervisor presence and refuse to launch (or ban on detection). SUL does not attempt to bypass this.

Deferred threat detonation: Automated threat detonation is out of scope. The A.51 entry tracks a future sandbox/malware-testing module — Windows Sandbox .wsb config generation + host read-only sharing + network disabled as default secure configuration. Not in the shipping release.

Config: [features] launcher.game_build_isolation = true (default on, R1).

Failure taxonomy: none at the sandbox level (the sandbox is Windows Sandbox, a Microsoft component). If WindowsSandbox.exe is unavailable (Windows edition without Sandbox feature), the feature is disabled with a warning.

Tier 1 events: none. sul-sandbox runs Windows Sandbox as-is; no security-sensitive toggles.

Release: shipping as part of R1 modding suite.

2.10 Mod building and staging suite (sul-mod)
Purpose: Mod manager with VFS integration. Reference: modde/modde (Rust mod manager with VFS — the primary reference for sul-vfs). Integration with ebkr/r2modmanPlus and ModOrganizer2/modorganizer patterns. Mod packages staged in isolated directories; activation via sul-vfs overlay (§3.12). Build/package integrity verified via Ed25519 signatures. Rollback via save-state ring (§3.6 / Ch. 12).

Config: [features] launcher.modding_suite = true (default on, R1).

Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_MOD_INSTALL_FAILED	Mod install failed	Staged package fails integrity or signature check	Package quarantined; install refused
E_SAVESTATE_*	(from §3.6)	Rollback failure	Per §3.6
Tier 1 events: none in releases.md's canonical list for sul-mod specifically; mod enable/disable is a per-session decision, not a Tier 1 config change.

Release: shipping as part of R1 modding suite.

2.11 Comprehensive modding and extraction (sul-unpack, sul-renpy, sul-arcade)
sul-unpack — zstd + rayon multi-threaded archiver. Handles generic archive extraction with parallel decompression. zstd crate (Rust binding) for compression; rayon for data parallelism.

Ren'Py Suite (sul-renpy) — AST decompilation of .rpyc compiled scripts, .rpa archive extraction, .rpy decompilation. Uses Tree-Sitter grammar for Ren'Py. Enables mod authoring on Ren'Py games.

sul-arcade — headless Ruffle Flash emulator (ruffle-rs/ruffle), 500 MB WebAssembly heap ceiling. Runs Flash content without a window. Miri-clean requirement (unsafe block audit) applies. sul-arcade integrates ruffle_core — the native Rust library — not the WASM/JS web client. The WASM build is what the Ruffle Chrome extension ships and carries a browser-sandbox and JS-bridge tax; the native ruffle_core runs at native speed with no WASM heap ceiling and no JS bridge. The 500 MB ceiling in this section is the AVM2 heap bound that sul-arcade enforces on the native build, not the browser's WASM memory limit. If the native build's action-script-heavy titles exceed 500 MB, the ceiling is a policy choice (the user is told the title exceeds the emulator's heap bound) rather than a hard browser constraint.

Helldivers 2 & Stardew: Boxofbiscuits97/HD2SDK-CommunityEdition (HD2 modding SDK), RaidingForPants/hd2-repatcher (HD2 patch alignment), RaidingForPants/hd2-audio-modder (HD2 audio modder), Floogen/Stardrop (Stardew SMAPI launcher). HD2 Modding Wiki as reference.

Config: [features] launcher.renpy_decompilation = true, [features] launcher.flash_content = true, [features] launcher.archive_extraction = true (all default on, R1).

Ruffle baseline:

toml
[emulation.ruffle]
heap_peak_mb = { median = 300, p99 = 500, higher_is_better = false, tolerance_pct = 20, status = "target", note = "ruffle_core native AVM2 heap; exceeds 500 MB → policy refusal, not browser WASM limit" }
Failure taxonomy: none at the crate level — extraction and decompilation failure is reported to the user, not a mode transition.

Tier 1 events: none.

Release: shipping as part of R1 modding suite. Note: sul-arcade requires Miri-clean unsafe block audit before shipping.

2.12 sul-vfs — WinFSP passthrough mode
Purpose: WinFSP integration with FSP_STATUS_PASSTHROUGH. Unmodified files return real NTFS handles. Zero user-mode overhead. References in R.12: billziss-gh/winfsp, winfsp/winfsp, SnowflakePowered/winfsp-rs (Rust WinFSP — ref for sul-vfs), dokan-dev/dokany, dokan-dev/dokan-rust. Only mod-modified files route through overlay. 5–10% of asset reads. Sector size 4096. Enables kernel-AC-safe modding. handle_cache module tightens test requirements — <2% frametime impact becomes <0.5% on open-heavy workloads; open latency within 1 ms of native.

Baselines:

toml
[vfs]
open_latency_ns = { median = 500, p99 = 1000, tolerance_pct = 20, status = "target" }
frametime_impact_pct = { median = 0.5, p99 = 0.5, higher_is_better = false, tolerance_pct = 10, status = "target" }
Test requirements: <0.5% frametime impact on open-heavy workloads; kernel-AC title runs unmodified; mod toggle <10 ms; concurrent access without torn reads; open latency within 1 ms of native.

Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_VFS_HANDLE_CACHE_STALE	Handle cache stale	Cached handle no longer valid	Fall back to non-cached passthrough
E_VFS_HANDLE_CACHE_STALE (VfsCacheMissReason telemetry)	ColdStart / HandleClosed / FileDeleted / VersionChanged	—	—
Config: [features] launcher.vfs_passthrough = true (default on, R1).

AST guards: sul-vfs not mounted on kernel-AC titles (structural refusal).

Tier 1 events: none.

Release: gated shipping component (A.2 category — no specific gate listed in the original spec; ships as part of R1).

2.13 Mod package scanning security
All mod packages scanned for malicious patterns before staging. Ed25519 Minisign signature verification against maintainer keys (Ch. 11 §11.15 / §11.18). Hive pack signing extends the same trust model — a malicious mod cannot execute without maintainer signature. Malware patterns scanned via community rules; any detection logged to sul-hive-mind threat log (Ch. 14 §14.13). Suspicious packages quarantined via sul-quarantine (copy → verify → record → verify → remove into encrypted quarantine).

Failure taxonomy: E_MOD_INSTALL_FAILED (from §3.10), E_QUARANTINE_RESTORE_FAILED (from Ch. 1 §3.4 base).

Tier 1 events: none at the config level (signature verification is always on; the user cannot disable it without a Tier 1 event that is not exposed in the shipping UI).

2.14 Steam IPC and Tauri bridge
Steam integration via Noxime/steamworks-rs (Rust Steamworks bindings). Steam Web API documentation in R.9. Game launch, achievement tracking, playtime. Tauri IPC bridge handles UI ↔ Steam shell communication via Tauri IPC custom protocol (declared network surface per Ch. 16 §16.15). Steam IPC exclusively reads — never writes to Steam's files. Session handoff via interprocess 2.2 cross-platform IPC.

Config: [features] launcher.steam_library_parsing = true, [features] launcher.steam_ipc = true (both default on, R0 — Steam library parsing is part of the R0 launcher substrate).

AST guards: sul-steam (or the Steam IPC path within sul-core) must not import HTTP client outside the declared Steam Web API surface.

Tier 1 events: none at the config level.

2.17 Emulation failure codes
Full emulation failure taxonomy (§11.11n's emulation subset):

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_GB_MAPPER_UNSUPPORTED	GB mapper unsupported	MBC5 rumble / HuC1 / MBC6	Refuse to load; Gambatte fallback (Mode B)
E_GB_ACCURACY_GATE_FAILED	Accuracy gate fail	A.90 gate fails on current hardware	Forced to libretro_gambatte (Mode B)
E_GB_ROM_CORRUPT	ROM corrupt	Header parse or ROM-size consistency mismatch	Quarantine lifecycle (Mode D)
E_SAVESTATE_SIZE_MISMATCH	Size mismatch	Snapshot size differs from state_size()	Run-ahead disabled for affected core (Mode C)
E_SAVESTATE_WORKER_STALLED	Worker stalled	Worker doesn't return within budget	Run-ahead disabled (Mode C); persistent → Mode F
E_SAVESTATE_ROUND_TRIP_MISMATCH	Round-trip mismatch	Restore produces different state	Slot dropped (Mode C)
E_EMU_CORE_LOAD_FAILED	Core load fail	libretro core .dll fails to load	Report to user; Gambatte fallback
E_OPTIMIZE_AC_BLOCKED	Anti-cheat blocked	kernel_level: true on target game	Pack type refused (Mode B)
E_VFS_HANDLE_CACHE_STALE	Handle cache stale	Cached handle no longer valid	Fall back to non-cached passthrough
Mode F classification:

E_GB_MAPPER_UNSUPPORTED — Mode B (Gambatte fallback).

E_GB_ACCURACY_GATE_FAILED — Mode B (Gambatte fallback).

E_GB_ROM_CORRUPT — Mode D (quarantine).

E_SAVESTATE_SIZE_MISMATCH, E_SAVESTATE_WORKER_STALLED, E_SAVESTATE_ROUND_TRIP_MISMATCH — Mode C (degraded — run-ahead disabled for affected core; emulation continues without run-ahead).

E_EMU_CORE_LOAD_FAILED — Mode D (quarantine if the core file is corrupt; otherwise user notification).

E_OPTIMIZE_AC_BLOCKED — Mode B (refuse).

E_VFS_HANDLE_CACHE_STALE — Mode C (fall back to non-cached).

AST guards:

sul-gb must not import wasapi.

sul-gb must not import ReadProcessMemory or any game memory access.

sul-savestate must not call retro_serialize outside its libretro shim (the shim is the only place the C-ABI is called, and it always writes into a Rust-owned buffer).

sul-savestate's libretro shim must allocate its buffer once at retro_serialize_size() and never resize mid-session.

[emu.savestate] worker_threads must be 1.

The original §13.6's emulation-relevant rows: none — the table's content was all AI, audio, vision, and sul-wire. The original §13.5's: none — all AI. The original §13.7's A.90 and A.91 are in §3.19 below; A.78 is in §3.19 below.

2.19 Gate entries (A.90 / A.91 / A.43 / A.44 / A.66 / A.78 / A.2)
Full text is in SUL-LEDGER/gates.md. Summary:

A.90 — sul-gb Game Boy / GBC core. R1. Nine sub-criteria (a)–(i) from §2.5.1. Failure blocks shipping; Gambatte remains the default.

A.91 — sul-savestate ring. R1. Six sub-criteria (a)–(f) from §2.6. Failure leaves run-ahead on the libretro-native save-state path.

A.43 — zstd_gpu decompression gate. R2. ≥30% CPU overhead reduction with no VRAM regression.

A.44 — Run-Ahead gate. R1. ≥16 ms latency reduction with no visible artifacting. Fallback run_ahead_frames = 0.

A.66 — Cross-Platform Screen Sharing, Share-Play & Remote Controller. R1. See §3.20.

A.78 — libretro Vulkan frontend for FG. R2. ≥95% of OpenGL frontend p99 frame time with zero visible artifacts.

A.2 category — sul-emu-libretro, sul-vfs. Both ship as gated shipping components without a specific A.x gate listed in the original spec. Part of R1's emulation surface.

2.20 Share-Play
Purpose: Share the SUL emulated game to a remote device (tablet, laptop) with low-latency video + input passthrough. Over WebRTC/QUIC or QUIC/WebTransport.

Emulation debut (R1, A.66): The emulation debut of Share-Play is a gated shipping component in the current release: A.66. It ships under the same gate as A.66: <50 ms end-to-end LAN latency, zero input corruption over 1000 sessions, ViGEm re-injection verified. Over QUIC/WebTransport (with ground-up QUIC/WebTransport as an explicit path). Open-source starting points in R.6: Kyber, punktfunk, LibreRemotePlay, stream-play-server.

Remote virtual gamepad: remote user's gamepad inputs re-injected into the host's sul-input via ViGEm (arounre/vigem-rust). Bandwidth-optimized (input is ~100 bytes/frame). Session authentication via Ed25519 challenge-response.

Reference implementations: tokio-rs/axum for signaling, tokio-rs/mio for I/O. Also from R.6: Kyber (QUIC/WebTransport kit), punktfunk (QUIC + ViGEm + SendInput), LibreRemotePlay (P2P), stream-play-server (WebRTC + ViGEm).

Config: [features] launcher.share_play = false (gated, default off; A.66).

Failure taxonomy: none at the crate level — a failed session terminates the remote viewer without affecting the host.

Tier 1 events: none in releases.md's canonical list for Share-Play specifically.

Non-emulation cross-OS share (deferred): the non-emulation cross-OS share (streaming the full desktop overlay) remains reference intent only, in Ch. 1 §1.18 / Brief §5.1. In the release ladder, Share-Play is R1 (its gate is A.66).

Dedicated Showcase Hub: first-party SUL games featured in a curated section of the library. Modding-friendly by design.

Seamless Game Library Ingestion for first-party titles: direct metadata import (title, cover art, description) without Steam or GOG. Signed manifest from maintainer.

Status: PARKED at A.67. Conditional on a first-party game existing, which it does not. Re-open automatically if a first-party SUL game is ever produced. The technical description above is preserved for the case where it re-opens.

Config: none (parked).

Failure taxonomy: none.

Tier 1 events: none.

2.22 Sandboxing hardware passthrough
This subsection is a reference note to §3.9 (sul-sandbox). The unique content from §13.4 not already in §3.9:

Hardware Passthrough & Anti-Cheat Boundary: Isolated VMs provide security for testing/tools, but kernel-level anti-cheat multiplayer titles remain restricted to bare-metal host execution due to hypervisor detection barriers. This is not a policy choice — it is a technical constraint. nProtect GameGuard, Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, and Vanguard all detect hypervisor presence and refuse to launch (or ban on detection). SUL does not attempt to bypass this.

Reference note: launch_in_sandbox is shipping as part of §3.9 (sul-sandbox). The automated threat detonation direction (and its re-purposing in A.51 as a future sandbox/malware-testing module) remains research. In the release ladder, sul-sandbox is R1 (it ships with the modding suite).

2.23 Emulation AST guards and cross-cutting concerns
The emulation module's AST guards (from Ch. 16 §16.15 / Ch. 1 §9):

sul-gb must not import wasapi.

sul-savestate's libretro shim must allocate its buffer once at retro_serialize_size() and never resize mid-session.
