History file (music_history.json in the diagnostics bundle, Ch. 1 §3.6): per-session music player state. Records MusicTelemetryMsg events (track-changed, position, playback-state, buffer-underrun, device-changed). Contains no audio data — only playback state and device events.

Failure-injection tests:

bash
cargo test -p sul-music --features=failure-injection -- --force-failure=mu-1
cargo test -p sul-music --features=failure-injection -- --force-failure=mu-2
mu-1 — music exclusive mode refused by device coordination; asserts fallback to shared mode with warning.

3.8 Gate entries (A.119 / A.120 / A.121 / A.122 / A.123 / A.124 / A.125)
Full text in SUL-LEDGER/gates.md. Summary:

A.119 — Music player bit-perfect path. R1. Verified with a loopback capture.

A.120 — Music player gapless. R1. FLAC, MP3 (LAME tag), OGG, WAV.

A.121 — Music player CPU overhead. R1. <1% playing, <3% with EQ, <5% with EQ + ReplayGain + resampling.

A.122 — Music player latency. R1. Exclusive mode buffer ≤256 samples, seek <50 ms, track-start <100 ms.

A.123 — Musicolet feature parity. R1. Every feature in §2.1 present and working.

A.124 — Music player device coordination. R1. Exclusive mode correctly refused when it would conflict.

A.125 — Native DSD over DoP. R4 (research).

The original §13.6's music rows (verbatim):

Feature	Status	Gate
Music player CPU overhead	Shipping gate	A.121
Music player latency	Shipping gate	A.122
Musicolet feature parity	Shipping gate	A.123
Music player device coordination	Shipping gate	A.124

3.9 AST guards and failure codes
AST guards (from Ch. 16 §16.15 base check list):

sul-music-engine must not import HTTP client.

sul-music must not import ReadProcessMemory.

sul-music-engine WASAPI exclusive path must not bypass the device-coordination check.

[music.playback] exclusive_mode = true must not be set without the device-coordination check having run.

Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_MUSIC_DEVICE_CONFLICT	Device conflict	Exclusive mode refused (device coordination)	Fall back to shared mode with warning (Mode B); UI shows reason
E_MUSIC_BIT_PERFECT_UNAVAILABLE	Bit-perfect unavailable	Exclusive mode unavailable or DSP active	Badge hidden; shared mode used (informational)
E_MUSIC_TAG_BACKUP_FAILED	Tag backup failed	Backup copy fails before tag write	Refuse tag write; user must resolve backup failure (Mode B)
MU-1	Exclusive mode refused	sul-audio loopback or voice loop active on same device	Music player falls back to shared mode, warning (Mode B)
MU-2	Bit-perfect path unavailable	Exclusive mode unavailable or DSP active	Bit-perfect badge hidden, UI shows reason (informational)
Mode F classification:

E_MUSIC_DEVICE_CONFLICT — Mode B (fall back to shared mode).

E_MUSIC_BIT_PERFECT_UNAVAILABLE — informational (bit-perfect badge hidden; no mode transition).

E_MUSIC_TAG_BACKUP_FAILED — Mode B (refuse tag write).

MU-1 — Mode B (same as E_MUSIC_DEVICE_CONFLICT).

MU-2 — informational (same as E_MUSIC_BIT_PERFECT_UNAVAILABLE).

3.10 Crate contracts
sul-music (top-level player):

Purpose: Queue manager, library index, scanner, playback state, sleep timers, A-B repeat, playback speed, audio cutter, IPC bridge.

Dependencies: symphonia, wasapi-rs, cpal, rodio, lofty, ebur128, oximedia-normalize, math_audio_iir_fir, biquad-rust, oxiaudio-dsp, rubato, soxr (feature), ardftsrc (feature), souvlaki, hound, flacenc, mp3lame-encoder, windows, serde, rusqlite (library index), notify (library watcher).

Compatibility: Separate process; communicates with sul.exe via sul-ipc ring buffer (MusicControlMsg / MusicTelemetryMsg).

Failure taxonomy: E_MUSIC_DEVICE_CONFLICT, E_MUSIC_BIT_PERFECT_UNAVAILABLE, E_MUSIC_TAG_BACKUP_FAILED.

Fallback chain: Exclusive mode → shared mode → refuse playback (device unavailable). Bit-perfect → shared with badge hidden. Tag write → refuse if backup fails.

Performance contract: CPU <1% playing (no DSP), <3% with EQ, <5% with EQ + ReplayGain + resampling. Audio callback allocation-free. Zero buffer underruns across 100 scripted sessions.

Test requirements: See §3.11 verification checklist.

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=mu-1, mu-2.

Release: R1 (ships as part of A.119–A.124).

sul-music-engine (bit-perfect playback engine):

Purpose: Symphonia decoder (integer samples where possible), WASAPI exclusive via wasapi-rs, WASAPI shared via cpal/rodio, device enumeration, format negotiation, rate switching, allocation-free callback, gapless preload, DSP chain (ReplayGain, EQ, resampler), time-stretch (WSOLA / phase vocoder).

Dependencies: symphonia, wasapi-rs, cpal, rodio, lofty, ebur128, oximedia-normalize, math_audio_iir_fir, biquad-rust, oxiaudio-dsp, rubato, soxr (feature), ardftsrc (feature).

Compatibility: Runs in sul-music.exe (separate process). WASAPI exclusive mode is gated by device coordination (Ch. 4 §4.3).

Failure taxonomy: E_MUSIC_DEVICE_CONFLICT, E_MUSIC_BIT_PERFECT_UNAVAILABLE.

Fallback chain: Exclusive mode → shared mode. Bit-perfect → shared with badge hidden.

Performance contract: Bit-perfect path verified by loopback capture (A.119). Gapless sample-accurate across FLAC/MP3(LAME)/OGG/WAV (A.120). CPU <1% playing (A.121). Exclusive buffer ≤256 samples (A.122).

Test requirements: Bit-perfect loopback verification (input bytes → output bytes match, no DSP active). Exclusive mode bypasses Windows mixer. Device rate-switching works for 44.1/48/96 kHz. Shared mode fallback works when exclusive unavailable. Gapless across FLAC/MP3 (LAME)/OGG/WAV is sample-accurate. ReplayGain track/album modes produce expected gain. EQ graphic and parametric work. Per-device profiles persist. Bypass-when-flat gives zero CPU cost. Resampler selection works for rubato_sinc/soxr/ardftsrc. Playback speed 0.25×–4.0× preserves pitch (spectral analysis). Audio callback is allocation-free (custom global allocator panic test). No buffer underruns across 100 scripted sessions. Exclusive mode buffer ≤256 samples, seek <50 ms, track-start <100 ms.

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=mu-1, mu-2.

Release: R1.

sul-music-tags (tag read/write wrapper over lofty):

Purpose: Batch tag read/write, album art extract/replace, backup before write.

Dependencies: lofty.

Compatibility: Runs in sul-music.exe.

Failure taxonomy: E_MUSIC_TAG_BACKUP_FAILED.

Fallback chain: Refuse tag write if backup fails.

Performance contract: N/A.

Test requirements: Batch tag read/write with backup. Album art extract/replace. Re-read after write to verify.

Failure-injection support: None specific.

Release: R1.

sul-music-lyrics (LRC parser + synchronized lyrics):

Purpose: Embedded lyrics (ID3 USLT, FLAC LYRICS, MP4 ©lyr), LRC sidecar, timeline sync, overlay ticker, full-screen view.

Dependencies: None beyond the workspace.

Compatibility: Runs in sul-music.exe.

Failure taxonomy: None.

Fallback chain: Embedded → LRC sidecar → off.

Performance contract: N/A.

Test requirements: LRC parser handles [mm:ss.xx], multiple timestamps per line, metadata tags ([ti:], [ar:], [al:], [by:], [offset:]). Embedded lyrics extraction from ID3 USLT / FLAC LYRICS / MP4 ©lyr. Timeline sync, offset, scroll.

Failure-injection support: None specific.

Release: R1.

3.11 Verification checklist
From the original §2.8, preserved verbatim:

Bit-perfect path verified (loopback capture, input bytes → output bytes match, no DSP active); exclusive mode bypasses Windows mixer; device rate-switching works for 44.1/48/96 kHz; shared mode fallback works when exclusive unavailable; gapless across FLAC/MP3 (LAME)/OGG/WAV is sample-accurate; ReplayGain track/album modes produce expected gain; EQ graphic and parametric work; per-device profiles persist; bypass-when-flat gives zero CPU cost; resampler selection works for rubato_sinc/soxr/ardftsrc; playback speed 0.25×–4.0× preserves pitch (spectral analysis); multiple queues (up to 20) persist; folder browsing linear and hierarchical; tag editor batch read/write with backup; lyrics embedded and LRC parse and sync; bookmarks and notes persist; playlists support multi-membership; sleep timer time-based and song-count-based; A-B repeat loops correctly; audio cutter exports FLAC/WAV/MP3 with metadata copied and ReplayGain recomputed; SMTC shows correct metadata and handles play/pause/next/prev/seek; overlay mini-player shows during gameplay and expands to lyrics; taskbar thumbnail toolbar works.

Performance: CPU <1% playing (no DSP), <3% with EQ, <5% with EQ + ReplayGain + resampling; audio callback is allocation-free (custom global allocator panic test); no buffer underruns across 100 scripted sessions; exclusive mode buffer ≤256 samples, seek <50 ms, track-start <100 ms.

Process coordination: Exclusive on same device as sul-audio refused; exclusive on different device allowed; voice loop active + game running + exclusive requested refused; player process spawns on demand, terminates when idle, restarts after crash with last state.

3.12 Ground-up builds
From the original §2.8, preserved verbatim:

sul-music process scaffold (~800 lines); sul-music-engine bit-perfect path (~2500 lines); sul-music-engine DSP chain (~1500 lines); pitch-preserving time-stretch (WSOLA / phase vocoder, ~500–1000 lines); sul-music-tags (lofty wrapper, ~600 lines); sul-music-lyrics (LRC parser + sync, ~600 lines); audio cutter (decode → trim → encode, ~700 lines); taskbar thumbnail toolbar (~200 lines).

3.13 Explicit rejections
From the original §2.8, preserved verbatim:

DSD native passthrough as a shipping feature (research only, A.125); streaming service integration (local-first launcher); online lyrics fetching (embedded or LRC sidecar, no network fetch); cloud library sync; Android Auto / Android widgets (replaced by SMTC + taskbar thumbnail toolbar + overlay mini-player); ad-supported or freemium.

3.14 UI components and libs
Music components:

MusicStatusIndicator — shows active track, playback state, bit-perfect status, exclusive mode status, device coordination state. Subscribes to MusicTelemetryMsg. Always visible in Settings → Music and in the overlay mini-player when [features.music.overlay_mini_player] is on.

MusicLibraryView — folder browsing (linear / hierarchical), multiple queues, playlists, tag editor, lyrics view, bookmarks, sleep timers, A-B repeat, playback speed, audio cutter. Reads local SQLite library; MusicControlMsg writes. Always visible in Settings → Music.

Music libs:

useMusicStatus.ts — subscribes to MusicTelemetryMsg. Returns active track, playback state, device state, bit-perfect status.

3.15 Tier 1 events
From releases.md:

music:enable_exclusive_mode — R1. Enabling [music.playback] exclusive_mode = true — it blocks other apps from using the device.

music:change_output_device — R1. Changing [music.playback] output_device from "auto" to a fixed device ID or vice versa.

music:enable_crossfade — R1. Enabling [music.playback] crossfade_ms > 0 — it disables gapless.

music:cutter_default_mp3 — R1. Enabling the audio cutter export to a lossy format ([music.cutter] default_format = "mp3") — lossy re-encode.

Rationale (from releases.md): music-player changes affect device availability (exclusive blocks sul-audio), playback quality (crossfade vs. gapless), and file fidelity (lossy export). None can be safely auto-applied by Tier 0.

3.16 Audio device coordination cross-reference
The music player participates in the Ch. 4 §4.3 device-coordination rules. The music player's failure modes (E_MUSIC_DEVICE_CONFLICT, MU-1) are the music side of that coordination; the sul-audio and sul-broadcast-audio sides are in Ch. 4 and Ch. 6 respectively.

3.17 Deferred: A.125 DSD over DoP
A.125 is the gate for native DSD over DoP (research only). Full text: "Bit-perfect DSD passthrough to a DoP-capable DAC. Research only; not a shipping gate."

SUL-ARCHITECTURE/Ch. 06 — Broadcast Engine.md
1. Purpose
A streaming and audio-mixing engine that replaces OBS and Voicemeeter and Voicemod with one integrated subsystem, and that uses SUL's own internals rather than treating the game as an opaque window. The core architectural bet is that OBS's audio model is the wrong shape for what the user is asking for, and that SUL can do better by building the mixer inside the broadcast engine instead of routing audio through a virtual device into OBS and then hoping OBS's six-track model can express the routing.

That bet is supported by the measured limitation: OBS can record up to six tracks, but only Track 1 is streamed, and only Twitch has a VOD track — YouTube, Kick, and every other RTMP target receive a single blended stream. Media players do not mix tracks, so a multi-track recording is not a multi-mix recording; it is one mix plus alternative audio that the consumer must choose between. Twitch's VOD track is a track OBS selects, not a mix it builds.

The user's requirement — "a dedicated channel toggle for it to play in OBS and VODs separately" — cannot be expressed cleanly in OBS's model. It can be expressed cleanly in a mixer that owns both the sources and the destinations, which is what this module is.

2. Architecture
2.1 Process model
sul-broadcast.exe — a separate process, spawned by sul.exe when broadcast is enabled or when the broadcast UI is opened, kept alive while streaming/recording, terminated when idle for 10 minutes. Separate process for four reasons:

Encoder isolation. NVENC/AMF/QSV driver faults take down the encoding process, not the launcher. The game keeps running, the user sees a "Broadcast engine crashed — restart?" toast, and the stream reconnects.

Real-time priority. The compositor thread and the audio callback run at THREAD_PRIORITY_TIME_CRITICAL; the inference threads run at BELOW_NORMAL. Putting the compositor in sul.exe would let a slow pack load or a WebView GC pause stall the stream.

VRAM accounting. The compositor's texture pool, the encoder's surface pool, and the ISO buffers all need to be budgeted against the 8 GB cap (Ch. 1 §5.3). Isolating them in their own process makes the budget line-item visible.

Licence separation. OBS is GPL-2.0+ and cannot be linked into SUL. Even if the user has OBS installed, SUL does not load obs.dll; the broadcast engine is clean-room (§6.2.1).

Communication with sul.exe is via sul-ipc ring buffers, same discipline as sul-music.exe:

BroadcastControlMsg — start/stop stream, start/stop recording, switch scene, set source transform, set channel gain/mute, set bus routing, request preview frame, set encoder preset.

BroadcastTelemetryMsg — stream state, dropped frames, encoder load, GPU utilization, audio underruns, per-bus levels, per-source frame timing, ISO file write status.

2.2 Crate layout
text
crates/sul-broadcast/              # top-level: scenes, sources, state, IPC bridge
  src/
    lib.rs
    scene.rs                       # declarative scene document (versioned)
    source.rs                      # source registry, transform, z-order
    state.rs                       # broadcast state machine (Idle / Preview / Live / Recording)
    ipc_bridge.rs
    iso.rs                         # ISO recording orchestration
    agent_api.rs                   # the method table (REST / WebSocket / CLI / MCP)
crates/sul-broadcast-video/        # capture → composite → encode → output
  src/
    capture/
      wgc.rs                       # Windows.Graphics.Capture (Win10 2004+)
      dxgi.rs                      # DXGI Desktop Duplication fallback
      game_hook.rs                 # optional game-capture hook (refused on kernel-AC)
      camera.rs                    # Media Foundation camera capture
      texture_bus.rs               # cross-process GPU texture sharing (D3D12 shared handles)
    composite/
      wgpu_renderer.rs             # wgpu scene graph renderer
      layout.rs                    # View / Rescaler / Crop / Color
      effects.rs                   # shader effects (chroma key, blur, LUT)
    encode/
      admission.rs                 # NVENC/AMF/QSV pixel-budget admission controller
      nvenc.rs                     # NVENC (H.264 / HEVC / AV1)

    output/

  src/

    vban.rs                        # VBAN network audio (in + out)
    recorder.rs                    # 8-channel recorder (MP3 / WAV / BWF / AIFF)
2.3 Clean-room constraint
The prior-art survey is unambiguous: every "OBS in Rust" that exists is a months-old alpha (Rivulet, GodwinMix, ROBS, rec-rs — all under 10 stars, most abandoned), and the two serious Rust projects adjacent to the goal are both unusable as dependencies. Smelter (Software Mansion) is a production-grade wgpu live compositor with the clearest agent-drivable API in existence, but its licence forbids bundling it into a distributed app without a deal starting at $1,000/month. libobs-rs wraps the real libobs but is GPL-3.0 and does not work on macOS. GPL is rejected on the same grounds as Ch. 16 §16.2 rejected the GPL lsfg-vk branch: SUL cannot ship GPL-linked code in a proprietary product.

The prior-art document's recommendation is therefore the one SUL follows: a clean-room, headless Rust core around a versioned, declarative scene document, built on permissively licensed per-OS capture crates and wgpu, with FFmpeg (LGPL build) or GStreamer as the encode/output back end only where a pure-Rust path does not exist. SUL differs from that recommendation in one place — it uses pure-Rust encoders and transports where they exist, and falls back to FFmpeg only for the codecs that do not.

2.4 Video pipeline
2.4.1 Capture
Three capture backends, in priority order:

Windows.Graphics.Capture (WGC) — the default. windows-capture wraps both WGC and DXGI Desktop Duplication in one crate; moq-video's capture module wraps WGC on Windows and delivers frames as wgpu textures with zero-copy imports on Metal and Vulkan, and on Windows uses Windows.Graphics.Capture without a Desktop Duplication or GDI fallback (it requires Win10 2004 / build 19041 or newer). WGC is the right default because it is external to the game process, it captures the composed window including any flip-model or external-DComp overlay that has been composited into it, and it does not trip anti-cheat injection detection.

DXGI Desktop Duplication — fallback for older Windows builds and for full-monitor capture where WGC's per-window API is a worse fit. win_desktop_duplication is explicitly designed for low-latency game streaming; dxgi-capture-rs and lx-capture are alternatives, with lx-capture using DXGI dirty and move metadata plus a 32×32 tile comparison to return only changed rectangles — a large win for desktop scenes where most of the frame is static.

Game-capture hook — opt-in only, refused on kernel_level: true titles. Same structural-refusal discipline as the overlay (Ch. 7 §7.1). The hook is for the small set of games that render fullscreen-exclusive and cannot be captured by WGC; it is never the default.

A fourth capture backend, cross-process GPU texture sharing, is what makes SUL's own overlay and vision pipeline first-class sources. sul-overlay already renders to a D3D12 texture; texture_bus.rs shares that texture with sul-broadcast.exe via a D3D12 shared handle, so the overlay is composited as a texture with zero CPU readback. This is the integration win that OBS cannot offer: OBS would need a virtual camera or a window capture to see SUL's overlay; SUL's broadcast engine gets the texture directly.

2.4.2 Compositor
The compositor is wgpu with a declarative scene graph. The scene graph is a versioned document (JSON, schema-versioned, Ed25519-signed when shared) with a tree of View / Rescaler / Crop / Color / Effect nodes — the same shape Smelter uses, which the prior-art document identifies as "the clearest existing model for an agent-drivable compositor." SUL's implementation is clean-room but borrows the shape of the API, which is not copyrightable. wgpu is already a workspace dependency (the overlay uses egui + eframe, which sits on wgpu; sul-vlm uses candle which can target wgpu). The compositor reuses the same wgpu device as the overlay where possible, so the shared-texture path is a wgpu::Texture import rather than a copy.

Animation, templates, and offline rendering (gated opt-in):
- **Theatre.js** (`[broadcast.scene.animation = "theatre"]`, optional): runs strictly in the React UI frontend to drive lower-thirds, transitions, and data-driven badges (MIT/ISC; `theatre` Cargo feature is optional, never `default`).
- **Friction templates** (`template_format = "friction" | "theatre" | "native"`): Friction SVG+keyframe exports are pre-rendered offline into frame sequences/clips so no Qt/OpenGL runtime is needed.
- **HyperFrames offline render** (`render_mode = "offline"`, R2, gated A.180): invokes HyperFrames inside an isolated container (no bundled Node.js in `sul.exe`) for deterministic HTML→MP4 tutorials/highlights, muxed by the existing ISO muxer with <2 GB peak RAM.
- **XSheet timeline** (`[broadcast.timeline]`, experimental, R4): OpenToonz-inspired frame-cell exposure sheet data model for stop-motion/frame-by-frame capture (pure data model, no C++ dependency).

Scene graph operations: add_source(id, capture_backend, transform), remove_source(id), set_transform(id, x, y, scale, rotation, crop), set_z(id, z), set_effect(id, effect_chain), set_visibility(id, bool), set_layout(id, layout) for multi-source layouts (PiP, side-by-side, grid), snapshot() returning the current scene as a versioned document (for rollback and for the agent).

2.4.3 Preview → Program safety
Every mutation happens on the preview scene. The program scene is what is on air. take() swaps preview to program (like a vision mixer's cut), and transition(kind, duration) does a crossfade / wipe / slide. This is the same Preview→Program model Isocast's prior-art document recommends, and it is the model that makes the agent safe: the agent mutates preview, shows the user a preview frame, and only commits on take(). preview_frame() returns a downscaled RGBA8 frame of the current preview scene as a PNG or a JPEG. This is the mechanism by which the agent "sees" what it is about to put on air — the prior-art document identifies the absence of this as the core weakness of every existing "AI controls OBS" wrapper.

2.4.4 Encoder admission control (the single largest optimization)
This is the most important architectural decision in the module, and it comes directly from Isocast's measured analysis of why OBS drops frames on fast GPUs. OBS defaults to NVENC preset P5, tune hq, multipass qres (two-pass), look-ahead enabled, 2 B-frames, and adaptive quantization — and it has no admission control. It just reports "encoding overloaded." On a single-NVENC card (RTX 5070, GB205, one 9th-gen NVENC), split-frame encoding cannot apply — SFE needs two or more NVENCs. One engine encodes roughly 521 fps of 1080p with HEVC P5/HQ, 947 fps with P3/HQ, 181 fps with P7/HQ, and 317 fps with H.264 P5/HQ. A 4K60 program plus a 4K60 screen ISO plus a 1080p60 camera ISO is 240 + 240 + 60 = 540 fps-equivalents, which exceeds P5 HEVC (~104%) and is impossible at H.264 P5 (~170%).

admission.rs computes the pixel budget before starting, and it is the first thing the engine does when the user clicks "Go Live."

Encoder capacity table:

Encoder	Preset	1080p fps capacity	4K60-equivalent capacity
NVENC HEVC	P7/HQ	181	~45 fps
NVENC HEVC	P5/HQ	521	~130 fps
NVENC HEVC	P3/HQ	947	~237 fps
NVENC H.264	P5/HQ	317	~79 fps
(Capacity is measured in 1080p60-equivalents at the reference card; 4K60 = 4 × 1080p60. The engine computes the budget from the actual card's reported throughput, not from these constants — the constants are the fallback when the driver query fails.)

The admission controller:

Queries the encoder's actual throughput at the configured preset (a 2-second probe at engine start, cached per driver version).

Sums the pixel budget of every enabled output (program at its resolution and preset, each ISO at its resolution and preset, each restream destination at its resolution and preset).

If the total exceeds 90% of capacity, downgrades in a fixed order (ISO presets first to P1–P3, no two-pass, no look-ahead, no B-frames; then restream presets; then program preset; then program resolution).

If the total still exceeds 100%, refuses to start with a specific message: "4K60 program + 4K60 screen ISO + 1080p60 camera ISO needs 540 fps-equivalent; this card's NVENC HEVC P5 does ~521. Reduce the screen ISO to 1080p60, or drop the program to 1440p60, or use P3."

ISOs default to P1–P3 with no two-pass, no look-ahead, and no B-frames. The program gets the higher preset only if the budget allows. This is the opposite of OBS's defaults, and it is the reason Isocast beats OBS on the same hardware.

2.4.5 Encoder fallback chain
ff-encode tries NVENC → QSV → AMF → VideoToolbox in order; ironav-hwaccel models CUDA/NVENC, VA-API, QuickSync, VideoToolbox, D3D11VA, AMF, Vulkan Video, and MediaCodec, and loads NVENC from the driver at runtime so the same binary runs on machines without NVIDIA hardware. SUL's chain is NVENC → AMF → QSV → Media Foundation hardware → openh264 software. The chain is probed once at startup and cached.

2.4.6 GPU frame handoff
The compositor renders to a wgpu texture. On NVIDIA, that texture is exported as a Vulkan external memory handle and imported into CUDA with timeline-semaphore ordering — the same zero-copy path ultra-streamer-rs uses (Vulkan external memory → CUDA, NVENC HEVC/AV1, sub-30 ms LAN latency) and moq-video uses (dedicated Vulkan RGBA8 slots imported into CUDA with timeline-semaphore ordering and completion-driven slot return, deliberately with no CPU pixel fallback). On AMD and Intel the equivalent is a D3D12 shared handle into AMF/QSV. The encode path never touches system RAM — this is the difference between "about half of OBS's CPU" and "OBS's CPU."

2.4.7 Output transports
arcly-stream ships RTMP, RTSP, SRT, and WHIP/WHEP ingestion, a lock-free zero-copy frame fan-out, an instant-start GOP cache, and a feature-gated pure-Rust media plane (MPEG-TS / HLS / fMP4). That is the transport layer. It is permissive-licensed and pure Rust, so it satisfies the clean-room constraint.

Transport	Use case	Crate
RTMP / RTMPS	Twitch, YouTube, Kick, X, TikTok	arcly-stream (feature rtmp)
SRT	Low-latency contribution, lossy networks	arcly-stream (feature srt)
WHIP	Sub-second latency to a WebRTC endpoint	arcly-stream (feature webrtc)
HLS	LAN preview, restreaming, OBS-as-consumer	arcly-stream (feature hls)
NDI	LAN production workflows, vMix/OBS as consumer	oximedia-ndi (clean-room, no official SDK) or grafton-ndi (NDI 6 SDK bindings, zero-copy)
Virtual camera	Zoom/Teams/Discord consumption	Windows virtual camera device (same USB/IP mechanism as the virtual audio devices, §2.8)
2.4.8 Multi-destination with per-destination mixes
This is the feature the user asked for and OBS cannot do. polyemesis is the reference model: "one ingest, many platforms, a different audio mix for each." SUL's broadcast engine does this natively — each RTMP/SRT/WHIP output subscribes to a named bus (§2.5), so the Twitch output can be on the Stream bus while the YouTube output is on Stream + Music and the local recording is on Record (which includes music for archival but the VOD bus does not).

2.4.9 ISO recording
Isocast records every source to its own file at native resolution alongside the program, all on one clock, and the resulting session file lines them up for the editor. SUL does the same, with one addition: audio ISOs are per-bus stems, not just per-source.

ISO type	Content	Format
Video program	The composited output	MKV (H.264/HEVC/AV1)
Video source ISO	Each captured source at native resolution	MKV, one per source
Audio program stem	The Stream bus mix	FLAC or WAV
Audio bus stems	One per bus (Stream, VOD, Record, Local, each B bus)	FLAC or WAV, sample-aligned
Audio channel stems	One per channel (game, mic, music, chat)	FLAC or WAV, sample-aligned
The multi-track recorder pattern from stems is the reference: it records every source feeding the sink into sample-aligned float WAV stems plus the sink mix. SUL's recorder does the same for every bus and every channel, so the user can remix the stream after the fact. One clock: all ISOs share the engine clock. Video timestamps come from the capture backend (WGC's SystemRelativeTime, DXGI's LastPresentTime), audio timestamps come from the WASAPI engine clock, and the ISO muxer aligns them to a single timebase at session start. This is the mechanism that lets the editor open the folder and have every file lined up.

2.5 Audio mixing engine
2.5.1 Topology
Voicemeeter Potato exposes 8 inputs (5 physical + 3 virtual VAIO) crossed to 8 buses (5 hardware A1–A5 + 3 virtual B1–B3), with A1 setting the master sample rate for the whole engine. SUL adopts that topology and extends it with four internal broadcast buses:

Bus	Type	Consumed by	Voicemeeter equivalent
A1	Hardware	Speakers (also sets engine sample rate)	A1
A2	Hardware	Headphones	A2
A3	Hardware	USB DAC / second output	A3
A4	Hardware	HDMI / capture card	A4 (Potato)
A5	Hardware	Spare	A5 (Potato)
B1	Virtual device	Discord, Zoom, DAW	B1
B2	Virtual device	OBS-as-external, vMix	B2
B3	Virtual device	Spare	B3
Stream	Internal	SUL's own RTMP/SRT/WHIP outputs	none
VOD	Internal	SUL's own VOD track (Twitch)	none
Record	Internal	SUL's own ISO recording	none
Local	Internal	Streamer's own monitor ("hear what the audience hears")	none
The four internal buses are the architectural difference from Voicemeeter. Voicemeeter's B buses are virtual devices that another application (OBS) picks up as a recording device — which means the mix is computed in Voicemeeter, shipped through a virtual cable, and re-mixed in OBS's six-track model. SUL's broadcast engine is the consumer, so it reads the buses directly, with no virtual cable in the path and no six-track ceiling.

The B buses still exist because other applications (Discord, Zoom, a DAW) need a virtual device. They use the same mechanism as Voicemeeter's virtual devices (§2.8), so the user can route B1 to Discord while SUL's own stream goes out the Stream bus with a different mix.

2.5.2 Per-channel strip
Each channel (a captured application, the microphone, the music player, a hardware line input, a virtual input) has a strip with the following processing, in this order:

Gain (−60 to +12 dB).

Mute / Solo (solo is monitor-only; it does not affect Stream/VOD/Record unless the user explicitly enables "solo follows stream").

Intellipan (2D pan + 3D binaural mode, matching Voicemeeter's Intellipan).

Color Panel EQ (a 10-band graphic EQ with draggable bands, matching Voicemeeter's Color Panel EQ; same DSP as the music player's graphic EQ, reusing math_audio_iir_fir).

Audibility (voice-oriented dynamics and filtering that keeps quiet speech intelligible on stream; implemented as a multiband compressor with a presence-band boost and a de-esser).

Noise Gate (threshold, ratio, attack, release, hold).

Compressor (soft-knee peak compressor with attack/release follower and make-up gain, matching oxideav_audio_filter's compressor).

Parametric EQ (up to 10 bands, peaking / shelf / LP / HP / notch, matching Voicemeeter Potato's parametric EQ).

Denoiser (spectral-subtraction / RNNoise-style denoiser, matching Voicemeeter Potato's denoiser; reuses sul-voice's cIRM model when [audio.voice] is enabled, falls back to a classical spectral denoiser when it is not).

Voice FX chain (see §2.5.3, only on channels flagged as voice).

Strip Limiter (brickwall limiter with optional look-ahead, matching Voicemeeter's per-strip limiter).

The DSP crates are already available: oximedia-effects provides noise gate, compressor, limiter, expander, de-esser, ducking, biquad IIR, filter bank, and parametric EQ, with no allocations in the process loops — the same allocation-free discipline as sul-dsp. dhvani provides biquad EQ, compressor, limiter, reverb, delay, de-esser, panner, noise gate, and normalize in a single crate. tunes::synthesis::effects provides Delay, Compressor, Gate, Limiter, and EQ chainable through an EffectChain. infinitedsp-core provides compressor, limiter, distortion, stereo panner, stereo widener, and timed gate. manguebyte-dsp provides state-variable filter, compressor, chorus, flanger, delay, reverb, limiter, and bitcrusher. The strip uses oxiaudio-dsp and oximedia-effects as the primary implementation, because they are the only ones explicitly documented as allocation-free in the process loop. sul-dsp's frozen-artifact pattern is used for the combined strip when the user saves a custom chain — the chain is frozen, stability-checked, and loaded as an artifact, same as the existing audio governor's DSP.

2.5.3 Voice FX chain (Voicemod parity)
Voicemod's feature set is documented: 200+ voice effects including reverb, echo, distortion, pitch, robot, radio; Auto-Voicetune with pitch-lock and full autotune; soundboard; built-in noise suppression and voice enhancement; AI voices trained with professional voice actors; and VoiceLab, a two-layer system combining characters, devices, surroundings, and pitch. SUL's chain, in signal order:

Stage	Effect	Implementation
1	Noise suppression	sul-voice cIRM when enabled; spectral subtraction otherwise
2	Pitch shift	Phase vocoder / PSOLA (the existing sul-voice-fx implementation)
3	Formant shift	Spectral envelope manipulation (existing sul-voice-fx)
4	Auto-Voicetune	Pitch detection (rustfft + YIN/MPM) → target pitch quantise → PSOLA re-pitch
5	Ring mod / bitcrush	Existing sul-voice-fx
6	EQ (low / mid / high)	Existing sul-voice-fx
7	Character preset	Composite of stages 2–6 with preset parameters
8	Surroundings (reverb)	Convolution reverb with impulse responses (church, room, stadium, cave)
9	Device emulation	Band-limit + saturation + noise floor (telephone, radio, walkie-talkie, megaphone)
10	AI voice	Gated — see below
The first nine stages reuse sul-voice-fx entirely. sul-voice-fx already has pitch shift, formant shift, character presets, ring mod, bitcrush, and EQ, with a sul-dsp graph and a ≤8 ms p99 budget at 512-sample / 48 kHz on AVX2 (A.88). The broadcast module adds the reverb, device emulation, and Auto-Voicetune stages on top. Auto-Voicetune is the only genuinely new DSP: a pitch detector (YIN or McLeod Pitch Method on rustfft), a target-pitch quantiser (chromatic scale, or a user-selected key/scale), and a PSOLA re-pitch stage with a glide time. Latency budget: ≤5 ms at 256-sample buffers. It is a ground-up build (~600 lines), not a wrapper.

AI voices (from A.131): research-gated. The user's non-negotiable — "voice cloning of a specific real person is refused" — applies unchanged. AI voices here are character voices (trained on licensed voice-actor data), not cloning. The gate requires: (a) the voice model is trained on data with explicit commercial-use rights; (b) the model has no zero-shot cloning capability — it can only produce the pre-trained character voices; (c) the API surface has no "upload a sample" path; (d) the refusal is structural, same as Ch. 16 §16.5.

Soundboard is a bank of short audio clips (user-supplied or from a licensed pack) that mix into the voice channel on demand. Clips are pre-loaded into RAM, played on a dedicated soundboard thread, and mixed with the live voice before the strip. Latency ≤10 ms from trigger to output.

Presets: 200+ presets, matching Voicemod's count. Each preset is a JSON document (versioned, signable, shareable) describing the parameter values for stages 2–9. Presets are signed by the maintainer when distributed through the hive; user-created presets are local and unsigned. A preset is not executable code — it is a parameter set, same discipline as the persona pack.

2.6 The routing matrix (the core feature)
This is the user's explicit requirement: "like how theres outputs for each channel on voicemeeter, there would be a dedicated channel toggle for it to play in obs and vods seperatly." The matrix is channels × buses. Each cell is a toggle plus a gain (default 0 dB when on, −∞ when off). The matrix is the single source of truth for routing; there is no hidden routing anywhere else.

Channel	A1	A2	A3	A4	A5	B1	B2	B3	Stream	VOD	Record	Local
Game	●	●							●	●	●	●
Microphone	●	●				●			●	●	●	●
Music player	●	●				●			●	○	●	●
Discord / chat	●	●				●			●	●	●	●
Browser	●	●							●	●	●	●
Soundboard	●	●							●	●	●	●
SUL agent (TTS)	●	●							●	●	●	●
Hardware line in		●							○	○	○	●
● = on by default, ○ = off by default, blank = not routed.

The Music player row is the answer to the user's question. The default is on for Stream, off for VOD, on for Record, on for Local — which means music plays on the live stream but is excluded from the Twitch VOD (avoiding the DMCA problem), and is present in the local recording for the editor. The user can flip the VOD cell on if they have rights to the music, or flip the Stream cell off if they want music to be local-only. This is exactly the behaviour that OBS cannot express without the Twitch VOD track workaround, and OBS's workaround only works on Twitch.

Per-destination mixes are computed by summing the rows that are enabled for that column, at the gains specified in the cells. The Stream bus is the sum of every row with Stream = ●. The VOD bus is the sum of every row with VOD = ●. There is no "master mix minus" trick — each destination is its own sum, computed from the same source buffers. This is more CPU than a single mix with mutes, but it is the only way to get genuinely independent mixes, and the CPU cost is trivial (a few hundred multiply-adds per sample across a dozen buses).

Personal vs stream mix toggles: the matrix is the advanced view. The simple view exposes two toggles per channel — "I hear it" (A1/A2) and "Stream hears it" (Stream) — matching SteelSeries Sonar's personal/stream mix model. The simple view writes into the same matrix; there is one routing state, two views of it.

Monitoring: Local is the "hear what the audience hears" bus — it mirrors the Stream mix (or the VOD mix, or the Record mix, user-selectable) so the streamer can verify the output. This is the Sonar "stream monitoring" feature, and it is what makes per-destination mixing usable without a second person watching the stream.

2.7 Config (consolidated)
This section merges the [broadcast.*] config block, the [features.broadcast.*] toggles, and the [performance.broadcast] block. Authority rule: [features.broadcast.*] is the release-gate view; [performance.broadcast] is the tuning view; [broadcast.*] is the runtime config. Per-game override wins over all three if a per-game broadcast block exists (currently none — the broadcast engine is global, not per-game, per Ch. 1 §2.8).

toml
[broadcast]
enabled = false
engine_sample_rate = 48000                    # follows A1 device; 44100 | 48000 | 96000

[broadcast.video]
capture_backend = "wgc"                       # "wgc" | "dxgi" | "game_hook"
compositor = "wgpu"
canvas_resolution = "1920x1080"               # program canvas
fps = 60
preview_resolution = "640x360"                # for preview_frame()

[broadcast.encoder]
backend = "auto"                              # "auto" | "nvenc" | "amf" | "qsv" | "mf" | "openh264"
codec = "h264"                                # "h264" | "hevc" | "av1"
preset = "p5"                                 # backend-specific
admission_control = true                      # the #1 optimization; never disable in production
probe_duration_ms = 2000                      # throughput probe at engine start

[broadcast.iso]
enabled = false
video_program = true
video_sources = true
audio_program = true
audio_buses = true
audio_channels = true
format_video = "mkv"

[broadcast.output]

[[broadcast.output.destinations]]
name = "twitch"

[broadcast.audio]
exclusive_monitoring = false                  # shared mode for monitoring; exclusive reserved for music

[broadcast.audio.virtual_device]

[broadcast.audio.vban]

[features]

broadcast.compositor = true
broadcast.encoder.admission_control = true

broadcast.output.rtmp = true
broadcast.output.srt = false
broadcast.output.whip = false
broadcast.output.hls = false
broadcast.output.ndi = false
broadcast.audio.mixer = true
broadcast.audio.voice_fx = true
broadcast.audio.autotune = false
broadcast.audio.soundboard = true
broadcast.audio.ai_voices = false             # gated A.131
broadcast.audio.virtual_device = true
broadcast.audio.vban = false

[performance.broadcast]
# Broadcast optimization — tuning view.
encoder_admission_control = true
zero_cpu_readback_encode = true
pre_allocated_command_buffers = true
fence_based_sync = true
spirv_compiled_at_build = true
iso_preset_p1_p3 = true
gpu_time_budget_multiplier = true
Validator rules (broadcast-specific; rules #61–#66):

B-61: [broadcast] enabled = true requires [broadcast.encoder] admission_control = true (E_CFG otherwise — disabling admission control is a Tier 1 event).

B-62: [broadcast.video] capture_backend = "game_hook" requires anti_cheat.kernel_level = false for all games (E_CFG otherwise — structural refusal).

B-63: [broadcast.audio] exclusive_monitoring = false (shared mode for monitoring; exclusive reserved for music) — E_CFG if true and music player is active.

B-64: [broadcast.output.destinations] each destination must have a unique name and a valid bus ("stream", "vod", "record", "local") (E_CFG otherwise).

B-65: [broadcast.audio.virtual_device] backend = "usbip" requires the USB/IP server to enumerate at startup; if enumeration fails, BR-2 fires and the backend falls back to "vban_bridge".

B-66: [broadcast.audio.vban] streams_in/streams_out must reference valid ports (E_CFG otherwise).

2.8 Per-application capture
WASAPI process loopback is a first-class Win32 API: ActivateAudioInterfaceAsync with AUDIOCLIENT_ACTIVATION_TYPE_PROCESS_LOOPBACK captures audio from a specific process, and the system-wide loopback uses AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_LOOPBACK on the default render endpoint. The sokuji-audio-host.exe reference implementation lists running processes as JSON and streams 24 kHz mono s16 PCM from a selected process, with a measured-continuous capture loop and pause/resume behaviour. SUL's process_loopback.rs does the same, with three additions:

Auto-routing — when a new process starts producing audio, the engine offers to create a channel for it, the SteelSeries Sonar "App Routing" drag-and-drop model, automated.

Per-channel EQ/FX — each process channel gets the full strip, so the user can EQ the game separately from the mic.

Fallback — when process loopback is unavailable (older Windows, protected process), the engine falls back to a virtual cable (B1/B2) that the user routes the app into, same as Voicemeeter.

2.9 Virtual devices without a custom driver
The Ch. 16 §16.5 non-negotiable is explicit: SUL does not build a virtual audio driver. The tarekwasfy01/Virtual-Cables project solves this without violating the constraint: instead of a custom kernel driver, it creates up to 32 virtual USB audio devices through USB/IP, and Windows connects them using its built-in USB audio class driver (via vadimgrn/usbip-win2). The device is a standard USB audio device from Windows' perspective; no driver signing, no WHQL, no kernel code. virtual_device.rs implements a userspace USB/IP server that presents N virtual audio devices (one per B bus and one for the virtual camera). Each device is a standard USB Audio Class device — Windows enumerates it, the user sees "SUL Virtual Audio B1" in the device list, and other applications can select it exactly as they would select Voicemeeter's virtual inputs. The audio data path is: SUL's bus → USB/IP server → Windows USB audio class driver → application's recording endpoint. This is materially better than Voicemeeter's approach for SUL's purposes:

No driver to sign or maintain (Windows updates do not break it).

No kernel attack surface (the USB/IP server runs in userspace).

No WHQL overhead.

Up to 32 devices, which is more than Voicemeeter Potato's 3 B buses.

SynchronousAudioRouter is the alternative if the USB/IP path proves unstable — it is a Windows audio driver that synchronises all virtual streams to the physical interface clock, reducing drift and buffer underruns. It is a kernel driver, so it violates Ch. 16 §16.5 and is therefore not the shipping path; it is listed only as a fallback in case USB/IP has a problem Microsoft will not fix.

2.10 VBAN
VBAN is Voicemeeter's network audio protocol: native 16/24-bit PCM, 1–8 channels, 11025 Hz–96 kHz, packet header with a 16-character stream name and a frame counter. sul-broadcast-audio implements VBAN send and receive, so SUL can:

Send a bus to another SUL instance on the LAN (multi-PC streaming setup).

Receive a VBAN stream as a channel (a second PC's game audio).

Bridge to a Voicemeeter instance (for users migrating from Voicemeeter, the B buses can be VBAN streams instead of USB/IP devices).

The VBAN implementation is ~800 lines (packet struct, sequence handling, jitter buffer, resampler at the boundary). It is a ground-up build because the existing Rust crates are thin and unmaintained.

2.11 Startup: broadcast binary check (Step 4.17)
If [broadcast] enabled = true, verify:

sul-broadcast.exe present.

Encoder admission controller probe succeeds.

WGC capture available.

USB/IP virtual audio device server enumerates devices without a SUL driver.

Per-destination bus routing valid.

Audio matrix has no sample-level drift over 1 hour.

ISO recording paths writable.

Agent API reachable.

Failure modes:

Condition	Error	Behavior
sul-broadcast.exe missing	E_CFG	Broadcast disabled; sul.exe continues.
Encoder probe fails	E_BROADCAST_ENCODER_OVERLOAD	Admission controller falls back to openh264; user notified.
WGC unavailable	E_BROADCAST_ADMISSION_REFUSED	Engine refuses to start.
USB/IP enumeration fails	BR-2	Fall back to VBAN bridge.
Bus drift exceeded	E_BROADCAST_BUS_DRIFT_EXCEEDED	Routing matrix disabled for session; base DSP pipeline continues.
ISO paths not writable	(warning)	ISO recording disabled; program output continues.
Agent API unreachable	(warning)	Agent method table disabled; manual control continues.
UI: BroadcastStatusIndicator shows stream state (Idle / Preview / Live / Recording), encoder load, dropped frames, GPU utilization, audio underruns, per-bus levels, ISO file write status. Subscribes to BroadcastTelemetryMsg. Always visible in Settings → Broadcast and in the overlay when [broadcast] show_broadcast_debug = true.

The VRAM figures matter for the Ch. 1 §5.3 budget: broadcast at 4K60 with three ISOs adds ~900 MiB, which on the reference 8 GB card means Combat Full and Deep cannot both be fully GPU-resident while streaming 4K. The compatibility validator surfaces this: enabling broadcast at 4K60 while Combat Full and Deep are both full-GPU triggers the over-budget warning, with the suggestion to drop broadcast to 1440p60 or offload 2–4 layers of Deep.

Failure-injection tests:

bash
cargo test -p sul-broadcast --features=failure-injection -- --force-failure=br-1
cargo test -p sul-broadcast --features=failure-injection -- --force-failure=br-2

2.13 Gate entries (A.126 / A.127 / A.128 / A.129 / A.130 / A.131 / A.132 / A.133 / A.134 / A.135)
Full text in SUL-LEDGER/gates.md. Summary:

A.126 — Encoder admission controller. R1. Verified on single-NVENC, dual-NVENC, AMF, and QSV cards.

A.127 — Zero-CPU-readback encode path. R1. No copy_to_host in encode path.

A.128 — Per-destination audio mixes. R1. Music on Stream and Record, off VOD; null-test verifying the two mixes differ by exactly the music content.

A.129 — USB/IP virtual audio device. R2. Windows enumerates SUL Virtual Audio B1/B2/B3 as standard USB audio devices, no kernel driver.

A.130 — Per-application capture. R1. WASAPI process loopback creates a channel per process, pause/resume works, fallback to virtual cable works.

A.131 — AI voices. R3 (research). Character voices trained on commercially licensed voice-actor data, no zero-shot cloning capability, no "upload a sample" API path, structural refusal of voice cloning.

A.132 — Preview→Program safety. R2. Agent cannot mutate program scene directly.

A.133 — ISO recording. R1. Every video source and every audio bus/channel written to its own file, sample-aligned on one clock.

A.134 — Audio performance. R1. 12 channels × 12 buses with all strip FX on <6% of one core, zero underruns over 60 minutes.

A.135 — VBAN send/receive. R3 (research). Interop with Voicemeeter's VBAN implementation on the LAN.

2.14 AST guards and failure codes
AST guards (from Ch. 16 §16.15 base check list):

sul-broadcast-video must not import ReadProcessMemory.

sul-broadcast-video must not hook IDXGISwapChain::Present.

sul-broadcast must not bypass the encoder admission controller.

[broadcast.encoder] admission_control must be true in shipped config.

sul-broadcast-audio must not import HTTP client.

sul-broadcast-audio virtual device server must not require a kernel driver.

[broadcast.video] capture_backend = "game_hook" must be refused on kernel-AC titles (AST check against game_registry.json).

Failure taxonomy (full):

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_BROADCAST_ADMISSION_REFUSED	Admission refused	Over-budget configuration	Refuse to start stream with specific message (Mode B)
E_BROADCAST_USBIP_ENUM_FAILED	USB/IP enumeration failed	Virtual audio device server fails to enumerate	Fall back to VBAN bridge (Mode C)
E_BROADCAST_BUS_DRIFT_EXCEEDED	Bus drift exceeded	Sample-level drift across buses over 1 hour	Disable routing matrix for session; base DSP pipeline continues (Mode E)
E_BROADCAST_ENCODER_OVERLOAD	Encoder overload	Admission controller downgrade exhausted, still over budget	Refuse stream start (Mode C)
E_BROADCAST_AUDIO_UNDERRUN	Audio underrun	Audio callback missed deadline	Governor adjusts buffer size / drops FX (Mode C)
Mode F classification:

E_BROADCAST_ADMISSION_REFUSED — Mode B (refuse stream start; game continues).

E_BROADCAST_USBIP_ENUM_FAILED — Mode C (fall back to VBAN bridge).

E_BROADCAST_BUS_DRIFT_EXCEEDED — Mode E (disable routing matrix for session; base DSP pipeline continues).

E_BROADCAST_ENCODER_OVERLOAD — Mode C (admission controller downgrade order; if still over, refuse).

E_BROADCAST_AUDIO_UNDERRUN — Mode C (governor adjusts buffer size / drops FX).

2.15 Crate contracts
sul-broadcast (top-level):

Purpose: Scenes, sources, state machine, IPC bridge, ISO recording orchestration, agent API.

Dependencies: windows-capture, wgpu, arcly-stream, oximedia-ndi, ff-encode, ironav-hwaccel, oxiaudio-dsp, oximedia-effects, dhvani, tunes, infinitedsp-core, manguebyte-dsp, rustfft, usbip-win2, serde, serde_json, tokio, axum, rkyv, sha2, ed25519-dalek.

Compatibility: Separate process (sul-broadcast.exe). Communicates with sul.exe via sul-ipc ring buffer (BroadcastControlMsg / BroadcastTelemetryMsg).

Failure taxonomy: E_BROADCAST_ADMISSION_REFUSED, E_BROADCAST_USBIP_ENUM_FAILED, E_BROADCAST_BUS_DRIFT_EXCEEDED, E_BROADCAST_ENCODER_OVERLOAD, E_BROADCAST_AUDIO_UNDERRUN.

Fallback chain: Admission controller downgrade order (ISOs first, then restream, then program preset, then program resolution) → refuse. USB/IP → VBAN bridge → shared-mode loopback. Bus drift → routing matrix disabled for session, base DSP continues.

Performance contract: See §2.12 baselines.

Test requirements: See §2.16 verification checklist.

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=br-1, br-2, br-3.

Release: R1 (core), R2 (full mixer + ISO + USB/IP + agent API).

sul-broadcast-video (capture → composite → encode → output):

Purpose: WGC/DXGI capture, wgpu compositor with declarative scene graph, encoder admission controller, NVENC/AMF/QSV/MF/openh264 chain, RTMP/SRT/WHIP/HLS output, ISO muxer with one-clock alignment, cross-process GPU texture bus.

Dependencies: windows-capture, wgpu, arcly-stream, ff-encode, ironav-hwaccel.

Compatibility: Runs in sul-broadcast.exe. VK_INSTANCE_LAYERS not set for this process (no FG in the broadcast engine — FG runs in the game's process).

Failure taxonomy: E_BROADCAST_ADMISSION_REFUSED, E_BROADCAST_ENCODER_OVERLOAD, E_BROADCAST_AUDIO_UNDERRUN.

Fallback chain: See §2.15 (top-level).

Performance contract: See §2.12.

Test requirements: See §2.16.

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=br-1.

Release: R1 (core), R2 (full).

sul-broadcast-audio (Voicemeeter replacement):

Purpose: Engine clock, bus summing, N×M routing matrix, channel strip DSP, voice FX chain (Voicemod parity), Auto-Voicetune, soundboard, USB/IP virtual audio devices, WASAPI process loopback, VBAN, 8-channel recorder.

Dependencies: oxiaudio-dsp, oximedia-effects, dhvani, tunes, infinitedsp-core, manguebyte-dsp, rustfft, usbip-win2.

Compatibility: Runs in sul-broadcast.exe. Virtual audio devices via USB/IP (userspace; no kernel driver).

Failure taxonomy: E_BROADCAST_USBIP_ENUM_FAILED, E_BROADCAST_BUS_DRIFT_EXCEEDED, E_BROADCAST_AUDIO_UNDERRUN.

Fallback chain: USB/IP → VBAN bridge → shared-mode loopback. Bus drift → routing matrix disabled for session.

Performance contract: See §2.12.

Test requirements: See §2.16.

Failure-injection support: --force-failure=br-2, br-3.

Release: R1 (core), R2 (full mixer + ISO + USB/IP + VBAN).

2.16 Verification checklist
From the original §2.9, preserved verbatim:

Video: admission controller refuses an over-budget 4K60+4K60+1080p60 configuration at H.264 P5 and downgrades correctly at HEVC P5; zero-CPU-readback path verified (GPU trace, no copy_to_host); WGC capture at 1080p60 has <80 ms p99 end-to-end latency to RTMP; DXGI fallback works on Windows 10 1909; game hook refused on HD2 with E_REFUSAL_POLICY; scene take() <16 ms p99; ISO recording produces one file per source plus program, all sample-aligned.

Audio: routing matrix: Music on Stream, off VOD, on Record, on Local; flipping the VOD cell makes music audible in the VOD; 12 channels × 12 buses with all strip FX on <6% CPU, zero underruns over 60 minutes; voice FX chain works with <10 ms p99 latency; Auto-Voicetune locks within 20 ms and releases cleanly; soundboard triggers within 10 ms; USB/IP virtual devices enumerate without a SUL driver; per-application capture works for a browser, a game, and Discord; VBAN interop with Voicemeeter (A.135).

Integration: overlay appears as a scene source with zero CPU readback; vision panel renders OCR'd game state; agent can switch scenes, mute channels, and start a stream; preview_frame() shows the pending change; take() commits; game launch auto-selects the scene; game exit auto-unmutes desktop; music player feeds the Music channel; now-playing metadata appears on stream.

Performance: 1080p60, 3 sources: <4% CPU, <250 MiB RSS, <350 MiB VRAM; 4K60, 6 sources, full effects: <15% CPU, <900 MiB VRAM; 60-minute soak: zero dropped frames, zero audio underruns.

Gates A.126–A.134 pass before release. A.131 and A.135 are research.

2.17 Ground-up builds
From the original §2.9, preserved verbatim:

Encoder admission controller (~800 lines); wgpu scene graph + compositor (~2500 lines); cross-process GPU texture bus (~600 lines); RTMP/SRT/WHIP output adapters over arcly-stream (~1200 lines); ISO muxer + one-clock alignment (~1000 lines); audio engine (clock, buses, summing) (~1500 lines); channel strip DSP (reuses oxiaudio-dsp / oximedia-effects) (~1200 lines); routing matrix (~500 lines); voice FX chain (reuses sul-voice-fx, adds reverb / device emulation) (~900 lines); Auto-Voicetune (pitch detect + quantise + PSOLA) (~600 lines); soundboard (~400 lines); USB/IP virtual audio device server (~1500 lines); WASAPI process loopback (~800 lines); VBAN send/receive (~800 lines); 8-channel recorder (~700 lines); agent method table (REST / WebSocket / CLI / MCP) (~1200 lines); scene document schema + versioning + signing (~600 lines); game-state scene automation (~400 lines).

2.18 Explicit rejections
From the original §2.9, preserved verbatim:

OBS as a library (libobs-rs) — GPL-3.0, incompatible with SUL's shipping licence, and does not work on macOS (same rejection as Ch. 16 §16.2's GPL lsfg-vk branch). Smelter as a bundled dependency — proprietary licence with a $1,000/month floor for distribution; reference for the scene-graph API shape only, implementation clean-room. Isocast as a dependency — MIT/Apache, but macOS/Linux only and no Windows lane yet; reference for the performance analysis and the ISO-on-one-clock model, implementation clean-room. A custom kernel-mode virtual audio driver — violates Ch. 16 §16.5; the USB/IP userspace approach is the shipping path. SynchronousAudioRouter as the shipping virtual device — kernel driver, violates Ch. 16 §16.5; fallback only. Streaming from OBS's multi-track model — OBS streams one track, only Twitch supports a VOD track, media players do not mix tracks; per-destination mixes must be computed in SUL's engine. Game-hook capture as the default — WGC is the default because it is external to the game process and does not trip anti-cheat; the hook is opt-in and refused on kernel-AC titles. AI voice cloning of a specific real person — refused, same as Ch. 16 §16.5; AI voices are character voices trained on licensed data with no zero-shot cloning path. Encoder presets without admission control — the admission controller is not optional; disabling it is a Tier 1 event with a warning. A virtual camera driver — the virtual camera uses the same USB/IP mechanism as the virtual audio devices; no kernel driver.

2.19 Integration with SUL
From the original §2.9, preserved verbatim:

Overlay as a source: sul-overlay renders to a D3D12 texture. texture_bus.rs shares that texture with sul-broadcast.exe via a D3D12 shared handle. The overlay becomes a scene source with a transform and z-order, composited with zero CPU readback. The user can place the overlay on stream (so viewers see the Combat Full status, the FPS counter, the music ticker) or hide it (so viewers see the clean game). This is something OBS cannot do without a window capture of the overlay window, which is fragile (the overlay is click-through and may be occluded) and which costs a full-frame copy.

Vision pipeline as a source or filter: sul-ocr and sul-vlm already produce structured output from the game screen. The broadcast engine can consume that: As a source — a "vision overlay" that renders the OCR'd text (mission objectives, shield %, ammo) as a composited panel. The data comes from the existing GameStateUpdated telemetry, not from a re-OCR. As a filter — an automatic scene switcher. "When the game state says combat, switch to the combat scene." This uses sul-governor's existing state machine, which already classifies ED and HD2 states. OBS cannot do this natively; it would need a custom Lua or Python script reading a file. SUL gets it from its own telemetry.

Agent control: The broadcast engine exposes a single method table over REST, WebSocket, CLI, and MCP — the Isocast prior-art pattern, which the document identifies as the right architecture for an agent-native compositor. Every operation is a method with typed arguments and typed errors:

text
scene.list() -> [SceneId]
scene.get(id) -> SceneDocument
scene.create(document) -> SceneId
scene.update(id, patch) -> SceneDocument
scene.delete(id)
scene.apply(id) -> PreviewState        # mutate preview, not program
scene.preview_frame() -> ImageHandle   # what the agent sees before committing
program.take() -> ProgramState         # commit preview to program
program.transition(kind, duration_ms)
source.list() -> [SourceInfo]
source.add(capture_spec) -> SourceId
source.remove(id)
source.set_transform(id, transform)
source.set_visibility(id, bool)
audio.channel.list() -> [ChannelInfo]
audio.channel.set_gain(id, db)
audio.channel.set_mute(id, bool)
audio.matrix.get() -> Matrix
audio.matrix.set(channel_id, bus_id, enabled, gain_db)
audio.matrix.bulk_set(cells)
stream.start(destinations) -> StreamState
stream.stop()
record.start(paths) -> RecordState
record.stop()
The agent mutates preview, calls preview_frame(), shows the user the frame, and only take()s on approval. The plan/apply and Preview→Program safety model is what makes this safe — the agent cannot accidentally put something on air.

Game state and library integration: sul-core knows which game is running (the library + the game_registry.json launch profile). The broadcast engine reads that and: Auto-selects the scene on game launch (ED → the ED layout; HD2 → the HD2 layout; no game → the desktop layout); Auto-mutes the game channel on game exit and unmutes the desktop channel; Applies per-game encoder settings (HD2 with its kernel-AC refusal for game-hook capture → WGC only; ED with DXVK → WGC); Applies per-game audio profiles (the ED audio strip has a different EQ than the HD2 strip, because the game's own mix is different). The agent can also query "what is the current game?" and "what scene should be live?" through the method table, so the user can say "go live with the combat scene" and the agent resolves it.

Music player integration: sul-music.exe (Ch. 5) feeds a Music channel in the broadcast mixer. The Music row in the routing matrix controls whether music reaches Stream, VOD, Record, and Local. The default is Stream on, VOD off — the user's explicit requirement. The music player also exposes its now-playing metadata as a scene source (a "now playing" panel) via BroadcastTelemetryMsg. The agent can use it for stream titles, and the overlay can render it as a ticker.

Combat Full and Deep integration: Combat Full's status (Instruct / Thinking / Conversation / Coding, router source, ReTrace state) is published on telemetry. The broadcast engine can render it as a small "AI status" panel on stream — useful for a tech demo, off by default. Deep's activity (which language profile is loaded, whether a task is in progress) is similarly available. The agent itself can be a scene source: sul-agent's TTS output (when the voice loop is enabled) routes to a TTS channel, which is on Stream and Local but off VOD by default (some users don't want their AI assistant in the VOD).

Frame generation interaction: Frame generation (sul-fg) runs as a Vulkan implicit layer inside the game. WGC captures the presented frames, which are post-FG — so the stream sees the generated frames. This is the user's choice: streaming the FG output doubles the apparent framerate to viewers, at the cost of the FG layer's VRAM (~300 MB at 1080p 2×). The broadcast engine accounts for FG's VRAM in the budget (§2.12) and warns if enabling both at 4K exceeds the cap. Frame generation is structurally refused on kernel-AC titles, so on HD2 the stream is the native framerate. The compatibility validator surfaces this at stream start: "HD2 has kernel-level anti-cheat; frame generation is disabled for this game, so the stream will be at native framerate."

2.20 Tier 1 events
From releases.md:

broadcast:enable — R1. Enabling or disabling broadcast ([broadcast] enabled).

broadcast:change_capture_backend — R1. Changing the capture backend between "wgc", "dxgi", "game_hook".

broadcast:disable_admission_control — R1. Disabling the encoder admission controller ([broadcast.encoder] admission_control = false).

broadcast:change_virtual_device_backend — R1. Changing the virtual audio device backend between "usbip" and "vban_bridge".

broadcast:enable_ai_voices — R1. Enabling AI voices ([broadcast.audio] ai_voices_enabled = true) — research-gated A.131.

broadcast:change_routing_defaults — R1. Changing the routing matrix defaults (the Music row's Stream/VOD/Record/Local cells).

Rationale (from releases.md): broadcast changes affect anti-cheat posture (game hook), stream stability (admission control), audio routing (device backends), and legal risk (VOD music routing). All are Tier 1.

2.21 Threat model
Threat: attacker enables the game-capture hook on a kernel-AC title (structural refusal), or enables broadcast exclusive monitoring on the same device as the music player (device conflict).

Defense: broadcast.capture.game_hook is refused on anti_cheat.kernel_level: true titles — the layer is not loaded, the env var is not set, and any attempt to force-enable is refused with E_REFUSAL_POLICY. Broadcast monitoring uses shared mode; exclusive mode is reserved for the music player. The compatibility validator (Ch. 1 §5) rejects broadcast.audio.exclusive_monitoring = true when the music player is active. USB/IP virtual audio devices run in userspace — no kernel driver, no anti-cheat attack surface. The audio matrix's per-destination mixes are computed from the same source buffers; no virtual cable in the path means no loopback capture conflict with sul-audio.

Threat: attacker uses the agent API to put content on air without the user's approval.

Defense: The Preview→Program model (§2.4.3) — the agent mutates preview, shows preview_frame(), and only take()s on approval. [broadcast.agent] require_approval_for_take = true enforces this. A scripted agent that attempts to bypass preview is caught by A.132's test.

Threat: attacker injects prompt injection into a scene source (a captured window, a vision panel) to cause the agent to switch scenes or mute channels.

Defense: Tool outputs from the broadcast engine flow through the same verification pipeline as every other tool output (Ch. 11 §11.6 OODA-Tool, Ch. 10 §10.9 destructive-action detection). The agent sees the output as data, not as instructions, and the Verifier checks any resulting tool call against the schema. The Preview→Program model means a malicious tool call can only change preview, not program. The user must approve before take().

2.22 UI components and libs
Broadcast components:

BroadcastStatusIndicator — shows stream state (Idle / Preview / Live / Recording), encoder load, dropped frames, GPU utilization, audio underruns, per-bus levels, ISO file write status. Subscribes to BroadcastTelemetryMsg. Always visible in Settings → Broadcast and in the overlay when [broadcast] show_broadcast_debug = true.

BroadcastSceneView — scene graph editor, source list, Preview→Program workflow, agent method table status. Always visible in Settings → Broadcast.

BroadcastAudioMixerView — routing matrix (channels × buses), per-channel strip controls, per-bus meters, virtual device status. Always visible in Settings → Broadcast → Audio.

Broadcast libs:

useBroadcastStatus.ts — subscribes to BroadcastTelemetryMsg. Returns stream state, encoder metrics, bus levels, ISO status.
