2. Architecture
2.1 sul-csi — WiFi CSI sensing and vital signs (A.136)
Purpose: WiFi CSI (Channel State Information) sensing for presence detection, pose estimation, breathing rate (6–30 BPM), and heart rate (40–120 BPM) through walls. Integrates ruvnet/ruview (WiFi DensePose) and anishshriram/esp32-csi-sensor.

Process: sul-csi.exe — a separate process, spawned by sul.exe when [features] vision.csi_sensing = true. Receives raw CSI data from ESP32 nodes via USB serial or network. Runs FFT-based vital sign extraction in Rust. Publishes CsiVitalsUpdated telemetry via sul-ipc.

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-csi/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API
│   ├── node_manager.rs                 # ESP32 node discovery + connection
│   ├── csi_stream.rs                   # CSI packet ingestion (USB serial + network)
│   ├── fft_processing.rs               # rustfft-based vital sign extraction
│   ├── presence.rs                     # Edge-compatible presence detection
│   ├── pose.rs                         # WiFi DensePose pose estimation
│   └── ring_integration.rs             # CsiVitalsUpdated telemetry
├── models/
│   ├── ruview_presence_int8.bin        # 4KB quantized INT8 for ESP32 edge inference
│   └── ruview_pose_q4.bin              # Host-side pose model
└── firmware/
    └── esp32/                          # ESP32 node firmware (CSI capture + edge presence)
Performance optimizations:

Edge inference: Run ultra-compact 4KB quantized models (INT8) directly on ESP32 nodes for presence detection, reducing wireless traffic.

Rust-native signal processing: Implement FFT-based vital sign extraction in Rust using rustfft for low-latency, host-side processing of raw CSI data.

Zero-copy data flow: Route all CSI data from the sensor service to the UI via sul-ring to avoid serialization overhead.

Integration: Toggle [features] vision.csi_sensing = false. Output feeds into sul-governor for God's Eye View fusion (§15.11). The CSI data is entirely local — USB serial or LAN to ESP32 nodes only, never over the internet.

Multi-camera vision pose fallback (`[sensing.vision_pose]`, R3, gated A.194): when ESP32/OpenBCI hardware is absent, 2–3 USB cameras can run `skellytracker` + `RTMPose` ONNX (Freemocap pattern, without full Python pipeline) as a BCI fallback (`E_POSE_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE` → Mode C).

Config:

toml
[csi]
enabled = false                        # gated A.136
edge_inference = true
pose_estimation = true

[features]
vision.csi_sensing = false             # gated A.136

[performance.csi]
edge_inference = true
fft_host_processing = true
zero_copy_data_flow = true
Validator rules (CSI-specific; rules #67–#68):

A-67: [csi] enabled = true requires at least one ESP32 node reachable at startup (E_CFG if none).

A-68: [csi] edge_inference = true requires ESP32 firmware with INT8 model support.

Baselines:

[csi] packet_to_ui_latency_ms = { median = 50, p99 = 100, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated", note = "A.136" }

[csi] heart_rate_accuracy_bpm = { median = 3, p99 = 5, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated" }

[csi] breathing_rate_accuracy_bpm = { median = 1, p99 = 2, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated" }

[csi] presence_detection_accuracy_pct = { median = 95, p99 = 98, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated" }

[csi] edge_inference_cpu_pct = { median = 1, p99 = 2, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated" }

Benchmarks (xtask csi-bench):

csi_bench.py::packet_to_ui — CSI packet-to-UI latency. Produces [csi] packet_to_ui_latency_ms.

csi_bench.py::vitals_accuracy — Heart rate and breathing rate accuracy vs reference. Produces [csi] heart_rate_accuracy_bpm, breathing_rate_accuracy_bpm.

csi_bench.py::presence_accuracy — Through-wall presence detection accuracy. Produces [csi] presence_detection_accuracy_pct.

Telemetry:

rust
pub enum TelemetryMsg {
    // ... base variants ...
    CsiVitalsUpdated { heart_rate_bpm: f32, breathing_rate_bpm: f32, presence_detected: bool, at: u64 },
}
Control messages:

rust
pub enum ControlMsg {
    // ... base variants ...
    SetCsiEnabled { enabled: bool },
    RequestCsiStatus,
}
Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_CSI_NODE_DISCONNECTED	CSI node disconnected	ESP32 node unreachable	Presence detection disabled; retain last known vitals with timestamp (Mode C)
E_CSI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED	CSI model load fail	Edge inference model corrupt	Fall back to host-side processing (Mode C); Mode D quarantine on the model file
CSI-1	CSI node disconnected	(same as E_CSI_NODE_DISCONNECTED)	Mode C
CSI-2	CSI edge model load fail	(same as E_CSI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED)	Mode C
Tier 1 events: csi:enable, csi:change_edge_inference, csi:enable_global_sensor_fusion. All R3.

UI components: HealthDashboard (Ch. 7 §2.6) — subscribes to CsiVitalsUpdated.

Diagnostics check: CSI check verifies sul-csi.exe present, ESP32 nodes reachable, FFT processing running. Reports heart rate and breathing rate accuracy against a reference (Ch. 12 §2.4).

History file: csi_history.json in the diagnostics bundle (Ch. 12 §2.9) — records CsiVitalsUpdated events. Contains no raw CSI data.

AST guards:

sul-csi must not import ReadProcessMemory or any game memory access.

sul-csi's edge firmware must not accept unsigned models (ESP32 secure boot enforced).

sul-csi must not import HTTP client (local USB/LAN only).

Gate: A.136 — <50ms latency from CSI packet to UI update; through-wall detection accuracy verified against a reference camera.

Threat model (from Ch. 16 §16.16): Attacker injects fake CSI data to spoof presence or vitals. Defense: CSI data comes only from paired ESP32 nodes over USB serial or local LAN; the ESP32 firmware is signed and verified via secure boot; a node whose firmware fails verification is refused. Faked presence/vitals cannot escalate to any destructive action — CSI data feeds the world model but the safety invariant is orthogonal. Users are shown a warning when CSI data is being fused with other sensors ([features] vision.global_sensor_fusion = true), and the modal lists exactly which sensors are being fused.

Release: R3 (gated A.136, prerequisite A.152).

2.2 sul-bci — brain-computer interface (A.139)
Purpose: MEG/EEG neural decoding to text using eugenehp/brain2qwerty-rs (Rust inference with numeric parity to Python — Pearson r ≥ 0.999999). Supports OpenBCI hardware for data ingestion.

Process: sul-bci.exe — a separate process, spawned by sul.exe when [features] bci.brain2qwerty = true. Ingests OpenBCI or MEG/EEG data, runs brain2qwerty-rs inference on a dedicated real-time thread. Publishes BciDecodedText telemetry via sul-ipc.

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-bci/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API
│   ├── ingestion.rs                    # OpenBCI serial data ingestion
│   ├── preprocessing.rs                # rustfft filtering + artifact removal
│   ├── decoder.rs                      # brain2qwerty-rs inference
│   ├── realtime_thread.rs              # dedicated real-time inference thread
│   └── ring_integration.rs             # BciDecodedText telemetry
└── models/
    └── brain2qwerty_q4.bin             # Quantized decoding model
Performance optimizations:

Real-Time Rust Inference: Use the Rust brain2qwerty-rs crate for inference on a dedicated real-time thread. Leverage RLX-accelerated Conformer for V2 pipelines.

Signal Preprocessing: Perform filtering and artifact removal in Rust using rustfft to minimize latency before the model.

Model Quantization: Quantize the neural decoding model (e.g., INT8) to reduce latency and memory.

Integration: Toggle [features] bci.brain2qwerty = false. Decoded text can control UI, send agent commands, or type into any application. The decoded text is flagged data_untrusted in the session packet (§15.17).

Config:

toml
[bci]
enabled = false                        # gated A.139
brain2qwerty = false                   # gated A.139
realtime_thread = true

[features]
bci.enabled = false                    # gated A.139
bci.brain2qwerty = false               # gated A.139

[performance.bci]
realtime_inference = true
rust_signal_preprocessing = true
int8_quantized_model = true
Validator rules (BCI-specific; rules #69–#70):

A-69: [bci] enabled = true requires OpenBCI hardware connected or brain2qwerty-rs model file present (E_CFG otherwise).

A-70: [bci] brain2qwerty = true requires [features] bci.enabled = true (E_CFG otherwise).

Baselines:

[bci] decoding_accuracy_pct = { median = 90, p99 = 95, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated", note = "A.139" }

[bci] end_to_end_latency_ms = { median = 200, p99 = 300, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated", note = "neural signal to text" }

[bci] inference_time_ms = { median = 50, p99 = 100, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated", note = "INT8 model" }

Benchmarks (xtask bci-bench):

bci_bench.py::decoding_accuracy — BCI decoding accuracy on eval set. Produces [bci] decoding_accuracy_pct.

bci_bench.py::end_to_end_latency — Neural signal to text latency. Produces [bci] end_to_end_latency_ms.

Telemetry:

rust
pub enum TelemetryMsg {
    // ... base variants ...
    BciDecodedText { text: FixedBytes<512>, confidence: f32, at: u64 },
}
Control messages:

rust
pub enum ControlMsg {
    // ... base variants ...
    SetBciEnabled { enabled: bool },
    RequestBciStatus,
}
Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_BCI_CALIBRATION_FAILED	BCI calibration failure	Signal quality too poor	Prompt for recalibration; disable BCI for session (informational)
E_BCI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED	BCI model load fail	brain2qwerty model corrupt	Fall back to no-BCI operation (Mode D quarantine on model file)
BCI-1	BCI calibration failure	(same as E_BCI_CALIBRATION_FAILED)	Informational
BCI-2	BCI model load fail	(same as E_BCI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED)	Mode D
Tier 1 events: bci:enable, bci:change_decoding_model. Both R3.

UI components: BCIControlPanel (Ch. 7 §2.6) — subscribes to BciDecodedText. Shows decoding accuracy, real-time decoded text, calibration status.

Diagnostics check: BCI check verifies sul-bci.exe present, brain2qwerty-rs model loaded, OpenBCI hardware connected. Reports decoding accuracy and latency (Ch. 12 §2.4).

History file: bci_history.json in the diagnostics bundle (Ch. 12 §2.9) — records BciDecodedText events. Contains no raw neural data.

AST guards:

sul-bci must not import ReadProcessMemory.

sul-bci's real-time thread must be pinned and must not block on allocations (custom global allocator panic test).

sul-bci must not import HTTP client (USB only).

sul-bci's decoded text must be flagged data_untrusted in the session packet (AST check on the packet-injection path).

Gate: A.139 — Decode a full sentence with >90% accuracy. End-to-end latency (neural signal to text) <200ms.

Threat model (from Ch. 16 §16.16): Attacker intercepts or spoofs neural signal. Defense: BCI uses a physical USB connection to OpenBCI hardware; there is no network surface. The decoding model is SHA-256 verified. A malicious signal source that is not the connected OpenBCI hardware is not readable by sul-bci.exe. The decoded text is treated as untrusted input — the same Verifier that checks tool calls checks any action the decoded text might trigger.

Release: R3 (gated A.139, prerequisite A.152).

2.3 sul-gev — God's Eye View and geolocation (A.137)
Purpose: Geospatial intelligence module for the "God's Eye View" surveillance visualization. Ingests public feeds (ADS-B, AIS, satellites) similar to bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view. Integrates Oldcircle/geo-sleuth as an agent skill for image geolocation.

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-gev/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs                          # public API
│   ├── feeds/
│   │   ├── adsb.rs                     # ADS-B aircraft tracking feed
│   │   ├── ais.rs                      # AIS maritime tracking feed
│   │   └── satellites.rs               # Orbital satellite feeds
│   ├── globe/
│   │   ├── renderer.rs                 # wgpu compute + graphics pipelines
│   │   ├── tile_cache.rs               # Local tile cache with prefetching
│   │   └── entities.rs                 # Dynamic entity (aircraft, ship) rendering
│   ├── geolocation.rs                  # geo-sleuth integration
│   └── ring_integration.rs             # GodsEyeViewRendered telemetry
└── assets/
    └── tiles/                          # Base globe tiles (vendored)
Performance optimizations:

WebGPU dynamic streaming: Render the 3D globe using wgpu compute and graphics pipelines to stream terabytes of terrain and orbital data at 60 FPS.

Tile-based caching: Cache geospatial tiles locally and fetch only for the visible viewport. Use predictive prefetching.

Zero-copy GPU buffers: Use wgpu buffer mapping to avoid CPU-GPU copies when updating dynamic entity positions.

Integration: UI component GodsEyeView (React/TS + wgpu). Toggle [features] geopolitics.gods_eye_view = false. Feeds are read-only — SUL never writes to any feed. Geolocation runs entirely locally (geo-sleuth model); no image is transmitted.

Config:

toml
[geopolitics]
gods_eye_view = false                  # gated A.137
geolocation = false                    # gated A.137
adsb_feed = true
ais_feed = true
satellite_feed = true

[features]
geopolitics.gods_eye_view = false      # gated A.137
geopolitics.geolocation = false        # gated A.137

[performance.gev]
webgpu_dynamic_streaming = true
tile_based_caching = true
zero_copy_gpu_buffers = true
predictive_prefetching = true
#### GEV layer taxonomy (reference: OSIRIS AI)

The GEV renderer adopts OSIRIS AI's layer taxonomy as a reference for the layer set, the renderer's visual target, and the per-layer toggle structure. OSIRIS AI (https://osirisai.live/) is a live geospatial-intelligence platform whose layer list is almost exactly what A.137 describes.

Layer set (each independently toggleable via `[gev.layers]`):

| Layer | Data source | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `maritime` | AIS (public feeds) | on |
| `satellites` | Orbital TLEs, public satellite feeds | on |
| `cctv_previews` | Publicly-available CCTV streams (read-only) | off |
| `live_news` | Public news feeds | off |
| `earthquakes` | Public USGS feed | on |
| `global_incidents` | Public incident feeds | off |
| `day_night` | Computed solar terminator (suncalc.org reference) | on |
| `cables` | Public submarine cable map data (submarinecablemap.com reference) | off |
| `adsb` | ADS-B aircraft tracking | on |
| `ais` | AIS vessel tracking | on |

Config:

```toml
[gev]
enabled = false
geolocation = false

[gev.layers]
maritime = true
satellites = true
cctv_previews = false
live_news = false
earthquakes = true
global_incidents = false
day_night = true
cables = false
adsb = true
ais = true
Renderer target: 10,000+ dynamic objects at 60 fps across ≥8 of the layer classes. wgpu compute + graphics pipelines. Zero-copy GPU buffers. Tile cache with predictive prefetching.

Geolocation reference: Picarta.ai (https://picarta.ai/) is a second geolocation model to compare against Oldcircle/geo-sleuth. If Picarta's model is usable (open weights or self-hostable) and beats geo-sleuth on the A.137 eval set by ≥5 percentage points, it replaces geo-sleuth as the default.

Gate A.137 criterion is extended: "render 10,000+ geospatial objects at 60 fps across at least 8 of the OSIRIS layer classes."

References: OSIRIS AI (https://osirisai.live/) — layer taxonomy and renderer target; Picarta (https://picarta.ai/) — geolocation comparison; suncalc.org — day/night computation reference; submarinecablemap.com — cable layer reference; earth.nullschool.net — weather layer reference (potential future layer).

Validator rules (GEV-specific; rules #71–#72):

A-71: [geopolitics] gods_eye_view = true requires wgpu-compatible GPU (E_CFG otherwise).

A-72: [geopolitics] geolocation = true requires geo-sleuth model file present (E_CFG otherwise).

Baselines:

[gev] object_count = { median = 10000, p99 = 50000, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated", note = "A.137" }

[gev] fps = { median = 60, p99 = 60, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated" }

[gev] geolocation_accuracy_pct = { median = 85, p99 = 95, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated" }

[gev] tile_cache_hit_rate_pct = { median = 80, p99 = 90, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated" }

Benchmarks (xtask gev-bench):

gev_bench.py::render_fps — Object rendering FPS with 10k+ objects. Produces [gev] fps.

gev_bench.py::geolocation_accuracy — Image geolocation accuracy. Produces [gev] geolocation_accuracy_pct.

Telemetry:

rust
pub enum TelemetryMsg {
// ... base variants ...
GodsEyeViewRendered { object_count: u32, fps: f32, at: u64 },
}
Control messages:

rust
pub enum ControlMsg {
// ... base variants ...
SetGevEnabled { enabled: bool },
RequestGevStatus,
}
Failure taxonomy:

Code Category Trigger Recovery
E_GEV_FEED_UNAVAILABLE Geospatial feed unavailable ADS-B/AIS/satellite feed timeout Fall back to cached tiles; retry with backoff (Mode C)
E_GEV_GEOLOCATION_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE Geolocation model unavailable geo-sleuth model file missing Disable geolocation; retain GEV visualization (Mode D quarantine on model file)
GEV-1 Geospatial feed unavailable (same as E_GEV_FEED_UNAVAILABLE) Mode C
GEV-2 Geolocation model unavailable (same as E_GEV_GEOLOCATION_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE) Mode D
Tier 1 events: gev:enable, gev:enable_image_geolocation. Both R3.

UI components: GodsEyeView (Ch. 7 §2.6) — 3D globe with public feeds (ADS-B, AIS, satellites). wgpu-based rendering at 60 FPS. Subscribes to GodsEyeViewRendered.

Diagnostics check: GEV check verifies GodsEyeView renders 10,000+ objects at 60fps, geolocation from image works (Ch. 12 §2.4).

History file: No dedicated history file. GEV events flow through the general telemetry ring.

AST guards:

sul-gev must not import ReadProcessMemory.

sul-gev's ADS-B/AIS/satellite feed parsing must use only declared network surfaces (the public feed URLs; listed in [gev] feed_urls in config.toml, user-verifiable).

sul-gev must not write to any feed.

sul-gev must not import any game-relevant memory access.

sul-gev's geolocation runs entirely locally — no image is uploaded.

Gate: A.137 — Render 10,000+ geospatial objects at 60fps. Geolocation from a single image <2s using local models.

Threat model (from Ch. 16 §16.16): Attacker poisons a public feed (ADS-B, AIS, satellite) to inject false geospatial data. Defense: feeds are read-only; SUL never writes to them. Feed data is displayed but does not trigger any automatic action — the user must explicitly act on what GEV shows. Geolocation from image runs entirely locally (geo-sleuth model); no image is transmitted. The GEV UI clearly labels each data source so the user can reason about feed reliability.

Release: R3 (gated A.137, prerequisite A.152).

2.4 rPPG vitals (A.138)
Purpose: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) — extract heart rate and respiratory rate from facial video via sul-vision. GPU-accelerated signal processing (bandpass filtering and ICA in wgpu compute shaders). ROI-specific processing using a lightweight face detector. Adaptive sampling based on subject motion. Output displayed in HealthDashboard and stored encrypted in the vault.

rPPG is not a separate process — it runs as part of sul-vision.exe (the OCR/VLM sidecar; Ch. 1 §2.6). It uses the same WGC capture path as the vision pipeline (Ch. 8 §8.2), processes only the user's own camera feed, and never processes remote video.

Config:

toml
[features]
vision.rppg_vitals = false # gated A.138

[performance.vision]

rPPG runs inside sul-vision; no separate performance block.
Baselines:

[rppg] heart_rate_accuracy_bpm = { median = 3, p99 = 5, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated", note = "A.138; within ±3 bpm vs. contact sensor" }

[rppg] cpu_overhead_pct = { median = 5, p99 = 5, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated", note = "for 720p 30fps stream" }

Benchmarks: rPPG measurement via xtask vision-bench (uses the rPPG-Toolbox reference impl). Produces [rppg] heart_rate_accuracy_bpm, cpu_overhead_pct.

Telemetry: rPPG data feeds HealthDashboard via the same CsiVitalsUpdated telemetry event (combined vitals stream) or a dedicated event if the implementation produces one. The spec's original §11.17 does not define an RppgVitalsUpdated variant; rPPG data flows through HealthDashboard's consumer without a distinct variant.

Failure taxonomy:

Code Category Trigger Recovery
E_RPPG_NO_FACE No face detected Face detector fails Skip frame, retry (Mode C)
E_RPPG_COMPUTE_FAILED Compute failed GPU compute shader fails Fall back to CPU path (Mode C)
Tier 1 events: rppg:enable. R3.

UI components: HealthDashboard (Ch. 7 §2.6) — shows heart rate, breathing rate, stress levels, activity trends over time. Data encrypted in the vault.

Diagnostics check: rPPG check verifies GPU compute shaders for bandpass filtering and ICA loaded. Reports HR accuracy and CPU overhead (Ch. 12 §2.4).

Gate: A.138 — Heart rate accuracy within ±3 bpm vs. contact sensor. CPU overhead <5% for 720p 30fps stream.

Threat model: rPPG runs only on the user's own camera feed — no remote video is processed. The GPU compute path is sul-vision's existing pipeline; no new attack surface.

Release: R3 (gated A.138, prerequisite A.152).

2.5 Browser automation (A.140)
Purpose: Integrate browser-use as an agent skill for headless browser control (direct CDP connection for ~50ms command latency). Use Crawl4AI for structured data extraction into LLM-ready Markdown (AsyncWebCrawler with CacheMode for optimized concurrency and caching). Persistent browser daemon between commands to eliminate startup cost.

Integration: The browser automation runs as an agent tool (browse_web(url, instructions); Ch. 11 §2.19). The browser runs in a sandboxed profile with no access to the user's cookies, saved passwords, or browser extensions.

Config:

toml
[features]
agent.web_browsing = false # gated A.140
Baselines: None specific (A.140's gate is the success-rate measurement; see below).

Benchmarks: A.140's gate is measured via a scripted 10-step task. Not a baselines entry — it is the gate itself.

Telemetry: Uses the general telemetry ring (no dedicated BrowserAutomationEvent variant in the spec). Per-step latency is logged to search_pipeline.log as a sub-stage of the search pipeline.

Failure taxonomy:

Code Category Trigger Recovery
E_BROWSER_NAV_FAILED Navigation failed Page load timeout Retry once, then report failure
E_BROWSER_CDP_DISCONNECTED CDP disconnected Browser daemon crash Restart browser daemon; user notified
E_BROWSER_SANDBOX_ESCAPED Sandbox escaped Sandbox violation detected Kill browser; quarantine profile; user notified
Tier 1 events: agent:enable_web_browsing. R3.

UI components: None specific (the browser runs headless; user-facing state is surfaced through the agent's messages).

Diagnostics check: Browser automation check verifies the persistent browser daemon is running; not a user-facing check.

AST guards:

browser.use and crawl4ai must not import any SUL-internal crate (they run as external processes in a sandboxed profile).

The browser profile is separate from the user's default browser profile (AST check on profile path).

Gate: A.140 — Agent completes a 10-step task (e.g., "find price of X on Y site and add to spreadsheet") with >95% success rate.

Threat model (from Ch. 16 §16.16): The browser automation runs in a sandboxed profile with no access to the user's cookies, saved passwords, or browser extensions. The browser process is isolated from sul.exe. A compromised browser cannot reach the vault, the WebView, or any SUL process. The user must authorize each browsing session (Tier 1 event).

Release: R3 (gated A.140, prerequisite A.152).

2.6 sul-security-toolkit — security tools (A.141, A.142)
Purpose: Wraps and manages security tools for authorized pentesting, password auditing, and network analysis.

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-security-toolkit/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│ ├── lib.rs # public API
│ ├── hashcat.rs # GPU password recovery wrapper
│ ├── nuclei.rs # Vulnerability scanner wrapper
│ ├── mitmproxy.rs # mitmproxy_rs traffic interception
│ ├── shannon.rs # Shannon autonomous pentester wrapper
│ ├── container.rs # Docker container lifecycle (isolated execution)
│ └── ring_integration.rs # SecurityToolkitEvent telemetry
├── containers/
│ ├── shannon/ # Shannon Lite container image
│ └── security-toolkit/ # Unified security tools container
└── wordlists/
└── common/ # Curated wordlists (for authorized cracking)
Performance optimizations:

Isolated execution: Run Shannon in a container with enforced CPU/memory limits to contain exploits and prevent resource starvation of SUL processes.

Parallel scanning: Orchestrate multiple Shannon instances in parallel for different targets or modules.

GPU saturation: Ensure hashcat uses optimal kernels (-O) and workload profiles (-w 3/-w 4).

Concurrent execution: Use tokio for async process management of Nuclei scans.

Zero-copy interception: Use mitmproxy_rs's Rust API to intercept and analyze traffic without copying data between processes.

Tools wrapped:

Tool Purpose Container Gate
Shannon Autonomous pentester (white-box, exploit-driven; 96.15% XBOW) Yes A.141
hashcat GPU password recovery Yes A.142
nuclei Vulnerability scanner Yes A.142
mitmproxy_rs Traffic interception Yes A.142
Ghidra MCP Binary audit (193+ tools) Yes A.150 (§15.14)

Additional tools
Tool	Purpose	Container	Gate
Zero-Breach IOC	Offline spyware IOC scan (`[security_toolkit.spyware_scan]`)	Local	A.193
aircrack-ng (`wifi_audit`)	WiFi security audit (`[security_toolkit.network]`, external process)	External	A.184
GIMP (docker-gimp)	Image editing	Yes	A.170
ArchiveBox	Web page archiving	Yes	A.167
Changedetection.io	Web page change detection	Yes	A.168
Stirling PDF	PDF manipulation (merge/split/edit)	Yes	A.170
LibreTranslate	Local translation	Optional container or library	A.166
Each runs in a container with the same isolation as hashcat/nuclei/mitmproxy_rs: no network by default, read-only filesystem except for the specific input, resource limits enforced. The image digests are pinned in crates/sul-security-toolkit/containers/VERSIONS.toml.

WASM isolation (A.163)
The security toolkit's tool isolation has two implementations: Docker (default) and WASM (via Wasmtime or WASM Micro Runtime, gated by A.163). WASM has lower overhead and no daemon, but some tools (hashcat, nuclei) require native code and cannot run in WASM. The WASM path is an additional isolation layer for tools that can run in it, not a replacement for Docker.

A.163 criterion: WASM isolation ships as an additional option if (a) at least 50% of the security toolkit's tools can run in WASM, (b) the WASM sandbox has ≤50 ms overhead per tool invocation, (c) the AST guard verifies that WASM-executing tools cannot reach the host filesystem or network beyond their declared surface.

Reference: wasm-micro-runtime (https://github.com/wasm-micro-runtime/wasm-micro-runtime).

Config:

toml
[security]
toolkit = false # gated A.142
shannon = false # gated A.141
hashcat = false
nuclei = false
mitmproxy = false
ghidra_mcp = false

[security_toolkit.container]
backend = "docker" # "docker" | "wasm"

[features]
security.toolkit = false # gated A.142
security.shannon = false # gated A.141

[performance.security]
hashcat_gpu_optimization = true
nuclei_concurrent_execution = true
mitmproxy_rs_interception = true
shannon_isolated_execution = true
Validator rules (security-toolkit-specific; rules #73–#75):

A-73: [security] toolkit = true requires Docker available for container-based tools (E_CFG otherwise).

A-74: [security] shannon = true requires [security] toolkit = true (E_CFG otherwise).

A-75: [security] hashcat = true requires CUDA or OpenCL GPU available (E_CFG otherwise — CPU cracking is too slow).

Baselines:

[security_toolkit] hashcat_speed_hashes_per_sec = { median = 1000000, p99 = 5000000, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated", note = "A.141, A.142" }

[security_toolkit] nuclei_scan_throughput_hosts_per_min = { median = 50, p99 = 100, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated" }

[security_toolkit] mitmproxy_interception_latency_ms = { median = 5, p99 = 10, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated" }

[security_toolkit] shannon_container_startup_ms = { median = 2000, p99 = 5000, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated" }

Benchmarks (xtask security-bench):

security_bench.py::hashcat_speed — Hashcat hashes/sec. Produces [security_toolkit] hashcat_speed_hashes_per_sec.

security_bench.py::nuclei_throughput — Nuclei scan throughput. Produces [security_toolkit] nuclei_scan_throughput_hosts_per_min.

security_bench.py::mitmproxy_latency — Mitmproxy interception latency. Produces [security_toolkit] mitmproxy_interception_latency_ms.

Telemetry:

rust
pub enum TelemetryMsg {
// ... base variants ...
SecurityToolkitEvent { tool: SecurityTool, action: SecurityAction, result: SecurityResult, at: u64 },
}

pub enum SecurityTool { Shannon, Hashcat, Nuclei, Mitmproxy, GhidraMcp }
pub enum SecurityAction { StartScan, CompleteScan, CrackHash, InterceptTraffic, BinaryAudit, Report }
pub enum SecurityResult { Success, Failed, Refused, Pending }
Control messages:

rust
pub enum ControlMsg {
// ... base variants ...
SetSecurityToolkitEnabled { enabled: bool },
RequestSecurityToolkitStatus,
}
Failure taxonomy:

Code Category Trigger Recovery
E_SECURITY_TOOL_CONTAINER_FAILED Security tool container failure Docker container fails to start Report error; do not execute scan (Mode B)
E_SECURITY_TOOL_GPU_UNAVAILABLE Security tool GPU unavailable Hashcat requires GPU, none available Refuse cracking; suggest CPU-based alternative (Mode B)
SEC-1 Security tool container failure (same as E_SECURITY_TOOL_CONTAINER_FAILED) Mode B
SEC-2 Security tool GPU unavailable (same as E_SECURITY_TOOL_GPU_UNAVAILABLE) Mode B
Tier 1 events: security:enable_toolkit, security:enable_shannon, security:enable_hashcat, security:enable_nuclei, security:enable_mitmproxy, security:enable_ghidra_mcp. All R3. These enable active offensive security capabilities on the user's machine.

UI components: SecurityToolkitPanel (Ch. 7 §2.6) — displays tool status, running scans, cracking progress, intercepted traffic. Subscribes to SecurityToolkitEvent.

Diagnostics check: Security toolkit check verifies hashcat, nuclei, mitmproxy_rs, Shannon Lite available and functional. Reports GPU utilization during cracking and scan throughput (Ch. 12 §2.4).

History file: security_toolkit_history.json in the diagnostics bundle (Ch. 12 §2.9) — records SecurityToolkitEvent events. Contains no sensitive target data.

AST guards:

The container must be enforced (AST check that no tool runs outside the container).

sul-security-toolkit's hashcat/nuclei/mitmproxy wrappers must not import wasapi or ReadProcessMemory.

sul-security-toolkit must refuse to run any tool against a target the user has not explicitly authorized (a signed consent file must exist).

sul-security-toolkit's scan output must be flagged data_untrusted in the session packet (AST check on the packet-injection path).

Gates:

A.141 (Shannon): Successfully run a pentest against OWASP Juice Shop and produce a report with valid findings.

A.142 (toolkit): Each tool passes a functional test (crack known hash, find known vuln, intercept and log HTTP traffic).

Threat model (from Ch. 16 §16.16): Attacker uses the toolkit against a target the user did not authorize. Defense: every tool call requires a signed consent file (§15.19 AST guard) that the user created in the security toolkit UI before running the tool. The container isolation means a compromised scan cannot escalate to the host. The tools run in a Docker container with enforced CPU/memory limits; the container has no access to the vault, the WebView, or any SUL process. The security toolkit is opt-in per session; it is off by default and requires a Tier 1 event to enable.

Release: R3 (gated A.141/A.142, prerequisite A.152).

2.7 sul-voicestudio — voice synthesis and dubbing (A.143)
Purpose: Integrate debpalash/VoiceStudio as a separate process (like sul-music.exe) running a local voice cloning, TTS, and dubbing engine (646 languages).

Process: sul-voicestudio.exe — a separate process, spawned by sul.exe when [features] voice.voicestudio = true. Runs VoiceStudio TTS and voice cloning engine (excluding voice cloning of specific real persons, which is structurally refused). Communicates via sul-ipc ring buffer.

Architecture:

text
crates/sul-voicestudio/
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│ ├── lib.rs # public API
│ ├── tts.rs # TTS engine wrapper
│ ├── dubbing.rs # Video dubbing pipeline
│ ├── voice_cache.rs # VoiceClonePrompt LRU cache
│ ├── ipc_bridge.rs # sul-ipc communication
│ └── ring_integration.rs # VoiceStudioEvent telemetry
└── models/
└── voicestudio/ # TTS and character voice models
Performance optimizations:

Process isolation: Run VoiceStudio in its own process to isolate GPU/memory usage from sul.exe.

Low-latency streaming: Use MeanVC2 streaming for 110ms end-to-end first-packet latency.

VoiceClonePrompt caching: Cache voice-clone prompt embeddings (LRU keyed by ref_path + mtime + ref_text) to eliminate per-request re-encoding latency.

Integration: Toggle [features] voice.voicestudio = false. Agent tools: speak(text, voice), clone_voice(audio_sample) (Tier 1 event, structural refusal per Ch. 16 §16.5).

The voice-cloning refusal (structural, non-negotiable):

The clone_voice(audio_sample) tool accepts only character voice preset IDs from the vendored catalog (trained on licensed voice-actor data with explicit commercial-use rights). Any attempt to pass a raw audio sample of a specific real person is refused with E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED. The API surface has no parameter that could accept a target person. This is enforced by the AST guard (Ch. 16 §16.15) — any PR that introduces a "target person" parameter is rejected regardless of its other merits.

The refusal is not a config toggle. The [voice] voicestudio = true toggle enables the tool, but the tool itself has no cloning-a-real-person code path. This is the same structural refusal as Ch. 16 §16.5.

Config:

toml
[voice]
voicestudio = false # gated A.143

[features]
voice.voicestudio = false # gated A.143

[performance.voicestudio]
process_isolation = true
low_latency_streaming = true
voice_clone_prompt_caching = true
Validator rules (VoiceStudio-specific; rules #76–#77):

A-76: [voice] voicestudio = true requires VoiceStudio model files present (E_CFG otherwise).

A-77: [voice] voicestudio = true with voice cloning enabled requires the character voice models to be loaded from licensed data only — the config does not have a "clone specific person" toggle because the API surface structurally refuses it.

VoxCPM engine (A.143 comparison)
VoxCPM (https://voxcpm.net/) is a second character-voice engine option alongside debpalash/VoiceStudio (default). The A.143 comparison evaluates both on:

Character-voice-similarity gate (>90% similarity for the vendored character voice catalog).

TTS latency gate (<100 ms first sentence).

The better engine is the default. Structural refusal applies unchanged. VoxCPM's "voice cloning" must be restricted to the character voice catalog; no specific real person. This is the same AST guard that already exists (sul-voicestudio must not expose a "clone specific person" code path). VoxCPM is a voice engine, not a bypass.

Reference: voxcpm.net.

Baselines:

[voicestudio] tts_first_packet_latency_ms = { median = 110, p99 = 200, higher_is_better = false, status = "gated", note = "A.143" }

[voicestudio] dubbing_throughput_seconds_per_minute = { median = 10, p99 = 15, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated" }

[voicestudio] voice_clone_similarity_pct = { median = 90, p99 = 95, higher_is_better = true, status = "gated", note = "character voices only; cloning of specific real persons is structurally refused" }

Benchmarks (xtask voicestudio-bench):

voicestudio_bench.py::tts_latency — TTS first-packet latency. Produces [voicestudio] tts_first_packet_latency_ms.

voicestudio_bench.py::clone_similarity — Character voice clone similarity (NOT specific person). Produces [voicestudio] voice_clone_similarity_pct.

Telemetry:

rust
pub enum TelemetryMsg {
// ... base variants ...
VoiceStudioEvent { action: VoiceStudioAction, latency_ms: u32, at: u64 },
}

pub enum VoiceStudioAction { Speak, CloneCharacterVoice, DubVideo, CachePrompt }
Control messages:

rust
pub enum ControlMsg {
// ... base variants ...
SetVoiceStudioEnabled { enabled: bool },
RequestVoiceStudioStatus,
}
Failure taxonomy:

Code Category Trigger Recovery
E_VOICESTUDIO_MODEL_MISSING VoiceStudio model unavailable TTS or character voice model missing Fall back to Piper TTS; log (Mode C)
E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED Voice clone refused Attempt to clone specific real person Refused; the refusal is the intended behavior (informational)
VS-1 VoiceStudio model unavailable (same as E_VOICESTUDIO_MODEL_MISSING) Mode C
VS-2 Voice clone attempt detected (same as E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED) Informational
Tier 1 events: voicestudio:enable, voicestudio:enable_character_voice_cloning, voicestudio:attempt_clone_specific_person. All R3. The clone-specific-person attempt is Tier 1-core (structural refusal attempt) and lives in R0's refusal:voice_clone_attempt.

UI components: VoiceStudioPanel (Ch. 7 §2.6) — UI for TTS and voice cloning (character voices only). Subscribes to VoiceStudioEvent.

Diagnostics check: VoiceStudio check verifies sul-voicestudio.exe present, TTS engine loaded, voice cloning structural refusal in place. Reports TTS latency and clone similarity (Ch. 12 §2.4).

History file: voicestudio_history.json in the diagnostics bundle (Ch. 12 §2.9) — records VoiceStudioEvent events. Contains no voice samples.

AST guards:

sul-voicestudio must not expose a "clone specific person" code path (AST check on the API surface — hard invariant).

sul-voicestudio must not import HTTP client.

sul-voicestudio's character voice models must be loaded from signed manifests with per-model license identifiers.

Gate: A.143 — Zero-shot voice cloning (character voices only) with >90% similarity. TTS latency <100ms for first sentence.

Threat model (from Ch. 16 §16.16): Attacker attempts to use the voice cloning capability to clone a specific real person. Defense: the API surface has no code path that accepts a "target specific person" parameter — the AST guard rejects any PR that introduces one. The clone_voice tool only accepts character voice preset IDs from a vendored catalog of licensed voice-actor data. Any attempt to pass a raw audio sample of a specific person as a cloning target is refused with E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED. This is a structural refusal (Ch. 16 §16.5), not a config toggle — the code path does not exist.

Release: R3 (gated A.143, prerequisite A.152).

2.8 Uncensored models (A.144, A.145)
§15.9.1 sul-heretic — build-time abliteration (A.144):

Purpose: Pre-apply abliteration to GGUF models (Combat Full, Deep) at build time. This is a build-time tool, not a runtime dependency.

Architecture: Build-time integration. The p-e-w/heretic CLI runs on base GGUF models during the release build pipeline. Pre-computed abliterated models are shipped alongside the base GGUFs; the [features] ai.uncensored toggle selects which file to load. No runtime abliteration.

Quality gate: Run comprehensive eval (A.63-like) to ensure abliterated models retain >98% of original benchmark performance (BFCL, HumanEval). Benchmark data for similar models (e.g., Gemma-4-E2B-Heretic) shows competitive MMLU scores.

Integration: [features] ai.uncensored = false (default). Tier 1 event to enable. Abliterated models ship alongside the base GGUFs; the toggle just selects which file to load.

Config:

toml
[features]
ai.uncensored = false                  # gated A.144; Tier 1 to enable
Baselines: A.144's gate is the quality retention measurement (>98% of original benchmark performance). Not a baselines entry — it is the gate.

Telemetry: No dedicated telemetry variant. Uses the general telemetry ring; the loaded model is reported through the standard QuantMethodActive event (Ch. 10 §10.22) with a note indicating abliterated variant.

Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_HERETIC_QUALITY_GATE_FAILED	Quality gate failed	Abliterated model regresses >2%	Do not ship the abliterated GGUF; toggle remains hidden
Tier 1 events: ai:enable_uncensored. R3. Tier 1-core-class in spirit (loads models whose safety behavior is modified), but assigned R3 because the safety layer is enforced below the model (see A.154).

Safety invariant (A.154, DECIDED): The safety invariant (destructive-action → Thinking), the Verifier's tool-call check, the structural refusals in Ch. 16 §16.5, and the persona constraints in the always-loaded context are enforced at the agent/router level, not at the model level. An abliterated model does not bypass any of them. This is a documentation clarification — the mechanism was already correct.

UI components: The model-loading indicator (standard QuantStatusIndicator in Ch. 10 §10.15) shows the abliterated variant when loaded.

Diagnostics check: None specific; the standard model-file check (Ch. 10 §10.24) covers the abliterated GGUF's SHA-256 and manifest.

AST guards:

sul-heretic runs at build time only, not at runtime — AST check that no runtime code path imports heretic.

The abliterated GGUFs follow the standard model-file signing chain.

Gate: A.144 — Abliterated models retain >98% of original benchmark performance.

Threat model: Attacker (or the user) enables abliterated models. Defense: Tier 1 event. The safety invariant, Verifier, and structural refusals are enforced at the agent/router level (A.154). The user is shown a warning in the overlay when uncensored models are loaded.

Release: R3 (gated A.144, prerequisite A.152).

§15.9.2 Local uncensored models (A.145):

Purpose: Support for locally-uncensored third-party models as an alternative to abliterated GGUFs.

Same quality gate as A.144 — the model must retain >98% of the base model class's benchmark performance, and the model must be from a source with a compatible license (verify per-model).

Config:

toml
[features]
ai.local_uncensored = false            # gated A.145; Tier 1 to enable
Failure taxonomy:

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_LOCAL_UNCENSORED_LICENSE_INVALID	License invalid	Model license incompatible	Refuse to load; toggle remains hidden
E_LOCAL_UNCENSORED_QUALITY_GATE_FAILED	Quality gate failed	Model regresses >2%	Refuse to load; toggle remains hidden
Tier 1 events: ai:enable_local_uncensored. R3.

Safety invariant: Same as A.144 (A.154 applies).

UI components: Same as A.144.

Diagnostics check: None specific; the standard model-file check (Ch. 10 §10.24) covers the model.

AST guards: Same as A.144.

Gate: A.145 — Same quality gate as A.144, plus license verification.

Threat model: Same as A.144.

Release: R3 (gated A.145, prerequisite A.152).

2.9 400B model distillation (A.146 — research)
Status: Research track, no shipping obligation, no date, no owner. Release class R4 per releases.md.

Purpose: Distill knowledge from a 400B model into SUL's 2B/7B models using a data-generation → distillation → evaluation pipeline.

Method: Use the 400B model to generate a 1M-example instruction-following dataset. Train SUL models via KL divergence and sequence-level KD. Evaluate against SUL benchmarks. If successful, distilled models integrate via the existing model update pipeline (Tier 1 event).

Research budget: ~$200–500 in rented compute per iteration (varies with the 400B model chosen and the number of iterations).

Gate: None (research; no gate). Graduates into a future R-release if the eval harness (A.8) confirms the distilled model improves over baseline.

Config: None (research; no runtime config).

Release: R4 (research).

2.10 Global sensor fusion (A.147)
Purpose: Fuse data from CSI (§15.2), rPPG (§15.4), BCI (§15.3), geolocation (§15.3), audio, and camera feeds into a single, coherent world model in sul-governor. This is the true "God's Eye View" for situational awareness.

Integration: fuse_sensor_data(sensors) tool (Ch. 11 §2.19). Gated by [features] vision.global_sensor_fusion = false.

Config:

toml
[features]
vision.global_sensor_fusion = false    # gated A.147
Baselines: A.147's gate is the world-model accuracy + overhead measurement (see gate). Not a baselines entry — it is the gate.

Benchmarks: A.147's gate measurement via a dedicated scripted eval (not a baselines entry).

Telemetry: Uses the general telemetry ring; the fusion result feeds the sul-governor world model. No dedicated telemetry variant in the spec.

Failure taxonomy: None specific; sensor-level failures are handled by their owning modules.

Tier 1 events: csi:enable_global_sensor_fusion. R3. This is the single most privacy-sensitive toggle in the spec — the modal must show the specific list of sensors being fused.

UI components: HealthDashboard (Ch. 7 §2.6) shows the fused world model's health-related outputs. The general agent UI shows the fused state.

Diagnostics check: None specific; the individual sensor checks (CSI, BCI, GEV, rPPG) cover the inputs.

AST guards:

The fusion path must enumerate its inputs explicitly (AST check on the fuse call).

The fusion path must show the sensor list to the user before the first session (Tier 1 modal requirement).

Gate: A.147 — The fused world model must outperform any individual sensor's state estimation by ≥15% on a benchmark eval set, with ≤2× the CPU overhead of the most expensive individual sensor.

Threat model: The fused world model combines data from multiple sensors, each of which has its own threat model (Ch. 16 §16.16). The fusion itself is a privacy amplifier — the user sees a Tier 1 modal listing every sensor being fused. Cross-cutting research (A.160) covers how the sensors interact; if any interaction is found that weakens the safety invariant, that interaction blocks the shipping release of the affected combination until it is resolved.

Release: R3 (gated A.147, prerequisite A.152).

2.11 Predictive analytics and simulation (A.148)
Purpose: Integrate a MiroFish-style multi-agent prediction engine to simulate outcomes of events ("what happens if we deploy this resource here?"). Used for strategic planning and risk assessment in strategy games and simulation contexts.

Config: None specific (runs as an agent tool).

Baselines: A.148's gate is the human-evaluator rating (see gate). Not a baselines entry.

Telemetry: Uses the general telemetry ring.

Failure taxonomy: None specific.

Tier 1 events: None specific in releases.md's canonical list (the prediction engine runs as an agent tool, gated by the general agent enable).

UI components: None specific (the prediction outputs are surfaced through the agent's messages).

Diagnostics check: None specific.

AST guards: The prediction engine runs in the agent's process; it must not import ReadProcessMemory or any game memory access.

Gate: A.148 — The prediction engine must produce action recommendations that a human evaluator rates as "useful" on ≥70% of test scenarios.

Threat model: The prediction engine reasons over the world model; it does not act on it. Its recommendations are subject to the same Verifier and safety invariant as any other agent output.

Release: R3 (gated A.148, prerequisite A.152).

2.12 Personal health dashboard (A.149)
Purpose: Expand rPPG/CSI vitals into a comprehensive dashboard tracking stress, sleep (via CSI), and activity over time. All data stored encrypted in the vault.

Config: None specific; the dashboard is a UI feature of the existing sensor modules.

Baselines: A.149's gate is a UI completeness + data-encryption verification (see gate). Not a baselines entry.

Telemetry: Consumes CsiVitalsUpdated (and rPPG data if a dedicated event exists).

Failure taxonomy: None specific; sensor-level failures are handled by their owning modules.

Tier 1 events: ai:enable_health_dashboard. R3.

UI components: HealthDashboard (Ch. 7 §2.6) — the dashboard itself.

Diagnostics check: None specific; the sensor checks (CSI, rPPG) cover the inputs.

AST guards:

The health data must be encrypted in the vault (AST check on the dashboard's data path).

The dashboard must not store plaintext vitals outside the vault (AST check).

Gate: A.149 — HealthDashboard UI is complete, all vitals are accurate (per A.136, A.138), and all data is verified to be encrypted in the vault (no plaintext on disk, verified by the vault's own integrity tests).

Threat model: The health data is stored encrypted in the vault (Ch. 2 §2.10). The dashboard reads from the vault; a compromised dashboard cannot exfiltrate vitals without the vault being unlocked. The user must explicitly enable the dashboard (Tier 1 event).

Dependencies: A.136 (CSI), A.138 (rPPG), A.92 (vault).

Optional read-only companion export (`[companion]`, gated opt-in, D-135): exports `health_trends.sulpack` for offline mobile viewing (PocketPal-style GGUF summary) without turning SUL into a mobile companion product.

Release: R3 (gated A.149, prerequisite A.152).

2.13 Agentic code review and binary audit (A.150)
Purpose: Use Ghidra MCP (bethington/ghidra-mcp, 193+ tools, batch operations for 93% API call reduction) and reverse engineering capabilities to allow the agent to audit third-party binaries (mods, game files) for security issues. Integrates with sul-quarantine — any flagged binary is quarantined automatically.

Config: None specific; the binary-audit tool runs as part of the security toolkit (§15.6) and requires [security] ghidra_mcp = true.

Baselines: A.150's gate is the malicious-binary detection accuracy (see gate). Not a baselines entry.

Telemetry: Emits SecurityToolkitEvent with action: BinaryAudit (Ch. 15 §15.6's telemetry).

Failure taxonomy: Inherits from sul-security-toolkit (§15.6).

Tier 1 events: ai:enable_binary_audit. R3.

UI components: SecurityToolkitPanel (Ch. 7 §2.6) — displays binary audit results.

Diagnostics check: Security toolkit check (Ch. 12 §2.4) covers Ghidra MCP availability.

AST guards: Inherits from sul-security-toolkit.

Gate: A.150 — The agent successfully audits a scripted set of known-malicious binaries and identifies the malicious behavior on ≥90% of them, with zero false positives on the clean binary set.

Threat model: The agent audits binaries but does not execute them. Flagged binaries are quarantined automatically (Ch. 14 §14.13). The feature is opt-in per binary and requires a Tier 1 event to enable. The Ghidra MCP server runs in a container (same isolation as the other security tools).

Release: R3 (gated A.150, prerequisite A.152).

2.14 Automated vulnerability remediation (A.151)
Purpose: When Shannon or Nuclei finds a vulnerability in a user-built web app, the agent can automatically propose a patch using its coding capabilities (Deep or Combat Full Coding).

Config: None specific; runs as an agent tool.

Baselines: A.151's gate is the patch success rate (see gate). Not a baselines entry.

Telemetry: Emits SecurityToolkitEvent (for the scan that found the vuln) and the general agent telemetry (for the patch proposal).

Failure taxonomy: Inherits from sul-security-toolkit (§15.6) and sul-agent (Ch. 10 §10.13).

Tier 1 events: ai:enable_auto_remediation. R3.

UI components: The agent's message surface (patch proposals are shown as diffs the user reviews).

Diagnostics check: Inherits from sul-security-toolkit.

AST guards: The patch proposal path must go through the standard Verifier and Gate A/B protocol (Ch. 14 §14.3). No patch is applied without user acceptance.

Gate: A.151 — The agent produces a working patch on ≥70% of a scripted set of common vulnerability classes (SQLi, XSS, CSRF, path traversal, broken auth).

Threat model: The agent proposes patches but does not apply them. Each patch proposal requires explicit user acceptance before being applied. The Verifier and Gate A/B checks apply to every patch. The patch applies to the user's app, not to SUL itself.

Release: R3 (gated A.151, prerequisite A.152).

2.15 Legal and ethical framework (A.152)
Purpose: A dedicated section defining legal and ethical boundaries for GEV and surveillance features, including strict data retention, encryption, and user consent policies.

Structure: The section is drafted, reviewed internally, and added to the spec as a new top-level section (likely §20 in the final document, or as a subsection of Ch. 16 — the exact placement is determined when the framework is written). The framework defines:

Consent requirements: Every sensing feature requires explicit user consent via the Tier 1 modal. The modal lists every sensor being used, what data is collected, how long it is retained, and where it is stored.

Data retention policies: CSI vitals, rPPG vitals, BCI decoded text, GEV feed data, and security toolkit scan output each have a defined retention period. Default is session-only unless the user explicitly opts into persistent storage (which requires vault encryption).

Encryption requirements: All persistent health data is encrypted in the vault (Ch. 2 §2.10). All persistent security toolkit scan output is encrypted in the vault. All geolocation history is encrypted in the vault.

User control: The user can delete any stored data at any time. The user can export their data in a standard format. The user can revoke consent for any sensing feature at any time (which disables the feature and deletes its session data).

Legal boundaries: GEV ingests only public feeds. The security toolkit runs only against targets the user has explicitly authorized. No feature is used for unauthorized surveillance of third parties. The user is responsible for compliance with local laws governing the use of these tools.

Ethical boundaries: The sensing features are for the user's own situational awareness, not for surveilling others. The security toolkit is for the user's own security testing, not for attacking third parties. The voice synthesis is for character voices, not for impersonation of real persons (the structural refusal in Ch. 16 §16.5 enforces this).

Gate: A.152 — The section is complete, all features in §15.2–§15.15 are reviewed against it, and any features that do not comply are removed or gated further.

Failure: the handoff features do not ship. This is a prerequisite for A.137 (GEV), A.147 (global sensor fusion), A.150 (binary audit), A.151 (auto-remediation), and — by extension — every other R3 handoff feature, because the framework defines the consent and retention baseline those features must meet.

The framework is not a shipping gate for the existing SUL features (which are already compliant — they don't collect data on anyone but the user).

Release: R3 prerequisite (A.152 itself is not a feature; it is a condition for shipping the R3 features).

2.16 Handoff telemetry, control, and failure codes (consolidated)
§15.17.1 Telemetry:

rust

§15.17.3 Failure codes (consolidated):

Code	Category	Trigger	Recovery
E_CSI_NODE_DISCONNECTED	CSI node disconnected	ESP32 node unreachable	Presence detection disabled; retain last known vitals (Mode C)
E_CSI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED	CSI edge model load fail	Edge inference model corrupt	Fall back to host-side processing (Mode C); Mode D quarantine
E_BCI_CALIBRATION_FAILED	BCI calibration failure	Signal quality too poor	Prompt for recalibration (informational)
E_BCI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED	BCI model load fail	brain2qwerty model corrupt	Fall back to no-BCI (Mode D)
E_GEV_FEED_UNAVAILABLE	Geospatial feed unavailable	Feed timeout	Use cached tiles; retry with backoff (Mode C)
E_GEV_GEOLOCATION_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE	Geolocation model unavailable	geo-sleuth model missing	Disable geolocation; retain GEV visualization (Mode D)
E_SECURITY_TOOL_CONTAINER_FAILED	Security tool container failure	Docker container fails	Report error; do not execute scan (Mode B)
E_SECURITY_TOOL_GPU_UNAVAILABLE	Security tool GPU unavailable	GPU required, none available	Refuse cracking; suggest CPU alternative (Mode B)
E_VOICESTUDIO_MODEL_MISSING	VoiceStudio model unavailable	TTS/character voice model missing	Fall back to Piper TTS (Mode C)
E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED	Voice clone refused	Clone specific real person attempt	Refused; informational
E_HERETIC_QUALITY_GATE_FAILED	Heretic quality gate failed	Abliterated model regresses >2%	Do not ship; toggle hidden
E_LOCAL_UNCENSORED_LICENSE_INVALID	Local uncensored license invalid	Model license incompatible	Refuse to load
E_LOCAL_UNCENSORED_QUALITY_GATE_FAILED	Local uncensored quality gate failed	Model regresses >2%	Refuse to load
E_BROWSER_NAV_FAILED	Browser navigation failed	Page load timeout	Retry once, then report failure
E_BROWSER_CDP_DISCONNECTED	Browser CDP disconnected	Browser daemon crash	Restart browser daemon
E_BROWSER_SANDBOX_ESCAPED	Browser sandbox escaped	Sandbox violation detected	Kill browser; quarantine profile
E_RPPG_NO_FACE	No face detected	Face detector fails	Skip frame, retry (Mode C)
E_RPPG_COMPUTE_FAILED	rPPG compute failed	GPU compute shader fails	Fall back to CPU path (Mode C)
CSI-1	CSI node disconnected	(same as E_CSI_NODE_DISCONNECTED)	Mode C
CSI-2	CSI edge model load fail	(same as E_CSI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED)	Mode C
BCI-1	BCI calibration failure	(same as E_BCI_CALIBRATION_FAILED)	Informational
BCI-2	BCI model load fail	(same as E_BCI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED)	Mode D
GEV-1	Geospatial feed unavailable	(same as E_GEV_FEED_UNAVAILABLE)	Mode C
GEV-2	Geolocation model unavailable	(same as E_GEV_GEOLOCATION_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE)	Mode D
SEC-1	Security tool container failure	(same as E_SECURITY_TOOL_CONTAINER_FAILED)	Mode B
SEC-2	Security tool GPU unavailable	(same as E_SECURITY_TOOL_GPU_UNAVAILABLE)	Mode B
VS-1	VoiceStudio model unavailable	(same as E_VOICESTUDIO_MODEL_MISSING)	Mode C
VS-2	Voice clone attempt detected	(same as E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED)	Informational
Mode F classification (from Ch. 1 §3.4):

E_CSI_NODE_DISCONNECTED, E_CSI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED — Mode C (fall back to host-side processing) / Mode D (quarantine).

E_BCI_CALIBRATION_FAILED — informational (prompt recalibration; no mode transition).

E_BCI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED — Mode D (quarantine).

E_GEV_FEED_UNAVAILABLE — Mode C (use cached tiles).

E_GEV_GEOLOCATION_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE — Mode D (quarantine).

E_SECURITY_TOOL_CONTAINER_FAILED — Mode B (refuse scan; do not execute).

E_SECURITY_TOOL_GPU_UNAVAILABLE — Mode B (refuse cracking; suggest CPU alternative).

E_VOICESTUDIO_MODEL_MISSING — Mode C (fall back to Piper TTS).

E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED — informational (structural refusal — the refusal is the intended behavior).

E_HERETIC_QUALITY_GATE_FAILED, E_LOCAL_UNCENSORED_LICENSE_INVALID, E_LOCAL_UNCENSORED_QUALITY_GATE_FAILED — gate failures (no shipping release; toggle hidden).

E_BROWSER_* — Mode C (retry / restart).

E_RPPG_* — Mode C.

Mode F escalation (from Ch. 14 §14.12): persistent E_CSI_NODE_DISCONNECTED across sessions → Coder reviews the ESP32 node discovery protocol; persistent E_CSI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED → Coder reviews the edge inference model integrity path; persistent E_BCI_CALIBRATION_FAILED on a specific user → Coder reviews the calibration wizard flow; persistent E_BCI_MODEL_LOAD_FAILED → Coder reviews the model manifest; persistent E_GEV_FEED_UNAVAILABLE across multiple networks → Coder reviews the feed ingestion retry logic; persistent E_SECURITY_TOOL_CONTAINER_FAILED → Coder reviews the container lifecycle; persistent E_VOICESTUDIO_MODEL_MISSING → Coder reviews the model provisioning.

2.17 Handoff diagnostics, history, and benchmarks (consolidated)
§15.18.1 Diagnostics checks: From Ch. 12 §2.4 (the handoff-specific diagnostics):

CSI check: Verifies sul-csi.exe present, ESP32 nodes reachable, FFT processing running. Reports heart rate and breathing rate accuracy.

rPPG check: Verifies GPU compute shaders for bandpass filtering and ICA loaded. Reports HR accuracy and CPU overhead.

BCI check: Verifies sul-bci.exe present, brain2qwerty-rs model loaded, OpenBCI hardware connected. Reports decoding accuracy and latency.

Security toolkit check: Verifies hashcat, nuclei, mitmproxy_rs, Shannon Lite available and functional. Reports GPU utilization during cracking and scan throughput.

VoiceStudio check: Verifies sul-voicestudio.exe present, TTS engine loaded, voice cloning structural refusal in place. Reports TTS latency and clone similarity.

GEV check: Verifies GodsEyeView renders 10,000+ objects at 60fps, geolocation from image works.

§15.18.2 History files: From Ch. 12 §2.9 (the handoff-specific history files):

csi_history.json — Records CsiVitalsUpdated events. Contains heart rate, breathing rate, presence detection — no raw CSI data.

bci_history.json — Records BciDecodedText events. Contains decoded text and confidence — no raw neural data.

security_toolkit_history.json — Records SecurityToolkitEvent events. Contains tool name, action, result — no sensitive target data.

voicestudio_history.json — Records VoiceStudioEvent events. Contains action type and latency — no voice samples.

GEV and rPPG do not have dedicated history files; their events flow through the general telemetry ring and the standard diagnostics bundle.

§15.18.3 Benchmarks (consolidated): From Ch. 12 §2.10 and §15.2–§15.8:

xtask csi-bench — CSI packet-to-UI latency, vital sign accuracy, presence detection, edge inference CPU.

xtask bci-bench — Decoding accuracy, end-to-end latency, INT8 inference time.

xtask gev-bench — Object rendering FPS, geolocation accuracy, tile cache hit rate.

xtask security-bench — Hashcat speed, nuclei throughput, mitmproxy latency, Shannon startup time.

xtask voicestudio-bench — TTS first-packet latency, dubbing throughput, clone similarity.

xtask vision-bench (rPPG subtest) — HR accuracy, CPU overhead.

2.18 Handoff AST guards
From Ch. 16 §16.15 (the handoff-specific AST guards):

sul-csi must not import ReadProcessMemory or any game memory access.

sul-csi's edge firmware must not accept unsigned models (ESP32 secure boot enforced).

sul-csi must not import HTTP client (local USB/LAN only).

sul-csi's global sensor fusion path (when [features] vision.global_sensor_fusion = true) must emit a user-visible modal listing every sensor being fused before the first session.

sul-bci must not import ReadProcessMemory.

sul-bci's real-time thread must be pinned and must not block on allocations (custom global allocator panic test).

sul-bci must not import HTTP client (USB only).

sul-bci's decoded text must be flagged data_untrusted in the session packet.

sul-gev must not import ReadProcessMemory.

sul-gev's ADS-B/AIS/satellite feed parsing must use only declared network surfaces.

sul-gev must not write to any feed.

sul-gev must not import any game-relevant memory access.

sul-gev's geolocation runs entirely locally — no image is uploaded.

sul-security-toolkit's container must be enforced (AST check that no tool runs outside the container).

sul-security-toolkit's hashcat/nuclei/mitmproxy wrappers must not import wasapi or ReadProcessMemory.

sul-security-toolkit must refuse to run any tool against a target the user has not explicitly authorized (a signed consent file must exist).

sul-security-toolkit's scan output must be flagged data_untrusted in the session packet.

sul-voicestudio must not expose a "clone specific person" code path (AST check on the API surface — hard invariant).

sul-voicestudio must not import HTTP client.

sul-voicestudio's character voice models must be loaded from signed manifests with per-model license identifiers.

sul-heretic runs at build time only, not at runtime — AST check that no runtime code path imports heretic.

The abliterated GGUFs follow the standard model-file signing chain.

The browser automation (browser.use, crawl4ai) must run in a sandboxed profile separate from the user's default browser profile.

2.19 Handoff threat model (consolidated)
The full threat model is in Ch. 16 §16.16. This subsection is the summary:

CSI sensing (sul-csi): Attacker injects fake CSI data to spoof presence or vitals. Defense: CSI data comes only from paired ESP32 nodes over USB serial or local LAN; ESP32 firmware is signed and verified via secure boot; a node whose firmware fails verification is refused. Users are shown a warning when CSI data is being fused with other sensors, and the modal lists exactly which sensors are being fused.

BCI (sul-bci): Attacker intercepts or spoofs neural signal. Defense: BCI uses a physical USB connection to OpenBCI hardware; no network surface. The decoding model is SHA-256 verified. Decoded text is treated as untrusted input.

GEV (sul-gev): Attacker poisons a public feed to inject false geospatial data. Defense: feeds are read-only; SUL never writes to them. Feed data is displayed but does not trigger any automatic action. Geolocation runs entirely locally; no image is transmitted. The GEV UI labels each data source.

Security toolkit (sul-security-toolkit): Attacker uses the toolkit against a target the user did not authorize. Defense: every tool call requires a signed consent file. Container isolation. The security toolkit is opt-in per session and requires a Tier 1 event to enable.

VoiceStudio (sul-voicestudio): Attacker attempts to use the voice cloning capability to clone a specific real person. Defense: the API surface has no code path that accepts a "target specific person" parameter — the AST guard rejects any PR that introduces one. The clone_voice tool only accepts character voice preset IDs from a vendored catalog of licensed voice-actor data. Any attempt to pass a raw audio sample of a specific person is refused with E_VOICESTUDIO_CLONE_REFUSED.

Uncensored models (ai.uncensored / ai.local_uncensored): Attacker (or the user) enables abliterated or third-party uncensored models. Defense: Tier 1 events. The safety invariant, Verifier, and structural refusals are enforced at the agent/router level, not at the model level. The user sees a warning when uncensored models are loaded.

Global sensor fusion (vision.global_sensor_fusion): The single most privacy-sensitive toggle in the spec. Defense: Tier 1 event with a modal listing every sensor being fused. Cross-cutting research (A.160) covers how the sensors interact; any interaction that weakens the safety invariant blocks the shipping release of the affected combination.

Predictive analytics (A.148): The prediction engine reasons over the world model; its recommendations are subject to the same Verifier and safety invariant as any other agent output.

Personal health dashboard (A.149): All health data is encrypted in the vault. The user must explicitly enable the dashboard (Tier 1 event).

Binary audit (A.150): The agent audits binaries but does not execute them. Flagged binaries are quarantined automatically. The Ghidra MCP server runs in a container.

Auto-remediation (A.151): The agent proposes patches but does not apply them. Each patch proposal requires explicit user acceptance. The Verifier and Gate A/B checks apply to every patch.

Legal and ethical framework (A.152): The prerequisite for all R3 handoff features. Defines consent, data retention, encryption, and user control policies.

2.20 Handoff Tier 1 events (consolidated)
From releases.md's tier1_events_added for R3:

SUL-ARCHITECTURE/Ch. 16 — Threat Model, Licensing, Anti-Cheat.md
1. Purpose
Three cross-cutting concerns that span every module:

Threat model: what SUL defends against, and what it explicitly does not.

Third-party licensing: what ships, under what license, and why.

Anti-cheat compatibility policy: what SUL does and does not do inside an anti-cheat boundary.

Structural refusals: what SUL categorically refuses, as code, not policy.

AST guards, network tripwires, and CI gates: the enforcement layer that makes the above invariants real.

The threat model, licensing analysis, and anti-cheat policy are module-agnostic — they hold regardless of which module is active. The structural refusals are code-level invariants that the AST guards enforce at build time. The AST guards are the mechanism by which every other chapter's rules become enforceable.

2. Architecture
2.1 Third-party licensing
SUL's dependency tree is dominated by MIT, Apache-2.0, and BSD-licensed crates. A handful of dependencies have licenses that require analysis. This section is the authoritative license ledger; it is produced and signed by cargo xtask license-audit at release time.

§16.2.2 Frame generation licensing boundary:

lsfg_native requires the user-supplied Lossless.dll (from the paid Lossless Scaling application, not redistributed). lsfg_layer requires the upstream lsfg-vk layer (MIT through v1.0, GPL-3.0 after v2.0.0-dev — vendoring the GPL branch requires the vendored code to remain GPL, which is a license incompatibility with SUL's MIT/Apache license). win_fg is clean-room (no proprietary weights, fully redistributable).

The shipping release of sul-fg uses lsfg_native (user-supplied Lossless.dll) + win_fg (clean-room). lsfg_layer is gated shipping (A.72) — vendoring the MIT branch is legal, vendoring the GPL branch is not. If lsfg_layer ships, it ships against the MIT branch only.

See Ch. 9 §2.10 for the full text.

§16.2.3 Vault licensing:

sul-vault-core uses the ring crate (ISC + Apache 2.0 + MIT, permissive). chacha20poly1305 (Apache 2.0 / MIT). blake3 (CC0 / Apache 2.0 / MIT). windows-dpapi (MIT). hardwareseal (MIT). secrecy (Apache 2.0 / MIT). redoubt (Apache 2.0 / MIT). secmem-alloc (Apache 2.0 / MIT). cynapse (MIT). astraguard (MIT). anti-dbg (MIT). All permissive. No license incompatibility.

§16.2.4 KV compression licensing:

sul-kv-compress uses star-kv (Apache 2.0), gaac (Apache 2.0), palquant (MIT), puzzlekv (Apache 2.0), jolt (Apache 2.0), turboquant (Apache 2.0), tcq (MIT). All permissive. No license incompatibility.

§16.2.5 Training data licensing:

jarvis_combat_full_tools.lora training data: Salesforce/xlam-function-calling-60k is CC-BY-NC-4.0 (commercial use prohibited). This is resolved by A.63's two-path approach: (a) synthetic data generated from SUL's own tool schemas via APIGen (CC-BY-4.0 for the public release, verify against the tag before shipping) or ToolOrchestrationReward (verify license), or (b) licensed-subset path (xLAM splits must be verified individually; if none qualify, this path is closed). The synthetic path is the recommended path because it produces commercially-usable data and is also higher quality for SUL's specific tool set.

jarvis_deep_tools.lora training data: SUL's own agentic-coding traces (owned by SUL). No license issue.

jarvis_persona_7b_k2.lora and jarvis_structured_k2.lora training data: user-provided tuples (the user owns the data). No license issue.

The ToolPRM distillation training data (ToolPref-Pairwise-30K) must be verified before shipping. If its license is not compatible with commercial use, the synthetic path is the only remaining option.

§16.2.6 WebView licensing:

Tauri 2 is MIT. WebView2 is Microsoft-distributed and comes from Windows Update. The Tauri plugins (updater, single-instance, window-state, notification, log, shell, fs, sql, autostart, deep-link) are MIT. The React/TypeScript toolchain is MIT/ISC. No license incompatibility.

§16.2.7 Music player licensing:

sul-music uses Symphonia (MPL-2.0 — file-level copyleft, compatible with SUL's MIT/Apache as long as the MPL-licensed files remain MPL; no virality to SUL's code). wasapi-rs (MIT/Apache 2.0). cpal (Apache 2.0). rodio (MIT/Apache 2.0). lofty (MIT). ebur128 (MIT). oximedia-normalize (Apache 2.0). math_audio_iir_fir (MIT/Apache 2.0). biquad-rust (MIT). oxiaudio-dsp (Apache 2.0). rubato (MIT). soxr (LGPL-2.1 — dynamically linked, or feature-gated off by default; SUL ships rubato_sinc as default and soxr as opt-in, so the LGPL path is not in the default binary). ardftsrc (MIT/Apache 2.0). souvlaki (MIT). hound (Apache 2.0). flacenc (Apache 2.0 / MIT). mp3lame-encoder (LGPL — feature-gated, only enabled when the user selects MP3 export; the default FLAC/WAV path does not link it). All permissive or file-level copyleft with dynamic linking. No license incompatibility for the default binary.

§16.2.8 Broadcast engine licensing:

sul-broadcast uses windows-capture (MIT/Apache 2.0). wgpu (MIT/Apache 2.0). arcly-stream (MIT/Apache 2.0 — permissive, pure Rust). oximedia-ndi (clean-room, no official SDK — MIT/Apache 2.0) or grafton-ndi (NDI 6 SDK bindings — the NDI SDK has its own license; grafton-ndi is MIT but the NDI runtime is not redistributable without a NewTek license; SUL uses oximedia-ndi as the default and grafton-ndi only if the user has a valid NDI license). ff-encode (LGPL-2.1 — dynamically linked, or feature-gated; SUL prefers pure-Rust encoders and falls back to FFmpeg only for codecs that do not have a pure-Rust path, with the LGPL build dynamically linked). ironav-hwaccel (MIT/Apache 2.0). oxiaudio-dsp (Apache 2.0). oximedia-effects (Apache 2.0). dhvani (MIT/Apache 2.0). tunes (MIT). infinitedsp-core (MIT/Apache 2.0). manguebyte-dsp (MIT). usbip-win2 (BSD-3-Clause / MIT — the USB/IP virtual device server is userspace, no kernel driver). tarekwasfy01/Virtual-Cables (MIT — reference only; SUL implements its own USB/IP server). All permissive or dynamically-linked copyleft. No license incompatibility for the default binary.

§16.2.9 App auth licensing:

sul-auth-app reuses sul-vault-core's auth primitives (ring, DPAPI, TPM) and adds no new licensed dependencies beyond the workspace set. The Win32 modal uses the windows crate (MIT/Apache 2.0). No license incompatibility.

No new license incompatibilities. The three areas that need per-tag verification before shipping are: the specific character voice models in VoiceStudio (commercial-use rights on voice-actor data), the geo-sleuth geolocation model, and the ruview presence/pose models. All three are gated shipping components (A.137, A.143, A.136), so the shipping release is not blocked on them.

§16.2.11 Unified license ledger:

cargo xtask license-audit produces a full third-party license ledger at release time. The ledger covers every direct dependency, every transitive dependency, and every vendored submodule. The audit fails on:

Any GPL/AGPL-3.0 dependency in the shipping path (unless it is explicitly vendored as a separate process like shannon and nuclei).

Any dependency whose license changes between the pinned version and the current upstream (the pinned version's license is what ships).

Any model file whose manifest does not include a license identifier.

Any container image whose digest does not match the pinned version.

The ledger is signed by the release signing key and shipped alongside the release artifacts. Users can inspect it locally without connecting to any network.
